text:
David Robinson was the league’s MVP.

Against Hakeem Olajuwon in the 1995 Western Conference Finals, even that distinction offered no protection.

Robinson had the size, speed and defensive instincts to ruin an opponent’s night. That is what makes this series extraordinary. Hakeem was doing this to someone equipped to stop almost anybody.

Across six games, Olajuwon averaged 35.3 points, 12.5 rebounds, 5.0 assists and 4.2 blocks, shooting 56 percent from the field.

Houston won the series in six.

The numbers establish the dominance. The footwork explains the helplessness.

Hakeem could show a defender a shot worth contesting, then use that reaction to create a better one. His shoulders sold one direction. His feet preserved another. He could pivot away from pressure without surrendering his balance or the ability to finish.

A defender’s correct first reaction could become the opening for Hakeem’s next move.

That is the cruelty of a complete offensive repertoire. Stay down and he could shoot over you. Commit to the contest and he could step through. Lean toward the baseline and he could turn back into the middle.

The moves worked together because each threat was credible.

In Game 2, he scored 41 points. The reigning champion was making the newly crowned MVP solve problems that kept changing after the possession had begun.

None of this makes Robinson’s award undeserved. A regular season MVP recognizes a season, and Robinson had earned his standing.

It makes Hakeem’s performance more impressive.

Reducing Robinson to a punchline removes the very thing that gives this series its weight. An extraordinary defender met an extraordinary scorer operating at the height of his powers.

Robinson could take away an option.

Hakeem kept having another.

2026 APEC Leaders' Shenzhen Outlook
The 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting adopted 2026 APEC Leaders' Shenzhen Outlook on Thursday.

2026 APEC Leaders' Shenzhen Outlook
Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together

1. We, the Economic Leaders of APEC, gathered in Shenzhen, China, on November 18 to 19, 2026. Decades after APEC's establishment, our sustained efforts have helped make our region a key engine of global growth and a champion of regional economic cooperation. Under the theme "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together", we have built on our work throughout the year with China's APEC 2026 priorities "Openness, Innovation, Cooperation", and advanced our shared objectives toward realizing an open, dynamic, resilient, and peaceful Asia-Pacific community, guided by the Putrajaya Vision 2040.

2. The world today is changing rapidly, with new opportunities emerging alongside complex challenges. Technological breakthroughs are contributing to the economic growth, resilience, and dynamism of our region. We endeavor to work together to maintain macroeconomic stability, promote productivity and dynamism, and boost economic growth for the benefit of all our people.

3. APEC has long been at the forefront of regional economic cooperation, and its enduring role remains relevant in the current economic context. We reaffirm our commitment to APEC as the premier forum for regional economic cooperation, guided by its voluntary, non-binding and consensus-building principles, and to making APEC a more modern, efficient, and effective incubator of ideas.

Trade and Investment

4. We underscore that supporting efforts to improve the trade and investment environment is important to our region. We reaffirm our commitments to strengthening supply chain resilience and deepening regional economic cooperation to build robust and resilient economies, contributing to sustained economic growth and prosperity of our region.

5. We will continue advancing economic integration in the Asia-Pacific region in a manner that is market-driven, including through the work on the Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific (FTAAP) agenda. We recognize that the FTAAP agenda plays an important role in building economies' capacity to participate in high standard and comprehensive regional undertakings.

6. We recognize the important role of digitalization as a driver for innovation, productivity, and economic growth across the region, and its benefit to facilitating trade. In this context, we welcome the APEC Trade Digitalization Cooperation Framework (2027-2030) to guide our efforts to foster a supportive policy environment, strengthen policy exchange and promote use of digital technologies for trade digitalization. We will continue to facilitate trade, including through measures to advance paperless trade and cross-border e-commerce. We are also committed to harnessing the benefits of emerging technologies for trade.

7. Recognizing the contribution of the services sector to economic growth and job creation, and the expanding role of digitally-delivered services, we will continue to enhance the competitiveness of the APEC economies in the sector. We note the impacts of environmental and related challenges and encourage APEC economies to consider how capacity building and exchanges of experience can help meet their respective environmental and trade objectives. We also recognize APEC's past and ongoing work to foster cooperation in advancing resilient business models. We acknowledge the positive contribution of the cultural and creative industries (CCIs) to economic growth, and affirm the importance of robust intellectual property protections. We are committed to enhancing the protection and enforcement of intellectual property rights, as well as continued efforts to address challenges faced by innovators, creators, and other right holders.

Connectivity

8. We affirm that connectivity has served as a conduit for economic growth, facilitating the flow of goods, services, capital, and people, including as supported by safe and resilient transport links. We appreciate the efforts made by APEC to advance regional connectivity over the past decade. Building on this progress, we endorse the APEC Connectivity Blueprint, through which we encourage economies to continue efforts towards achieving a seamlessly and comprehensively connected and integrated Asia-Pacific, by further strengthening the three pillars: physical, institutional, and people-to-people. We will continue to advance connectivity to deliver tangible benefits for all. We will enhance cooperation on quality infrastructure development and investment. We also underscore the importance of investment, including through ex-ante investment in disaster risk reduction.

9. In the face of supply chain challenges impacting our region, we reaffirm our commitment to maintaining resilient supply chains, particularly for essential goods. We recognize that it is in our mutual interest that our region remains interconnected and trade corridors remain open to facilitate trade flows, including energy supplies and other essential goods. We affirm our resolve to work together and with other trade partners to ensure trade continues to flow and critical infrastructure continues to support the viability and integrity of supply chains globally. We support efforts to enhance supply chain resilience, address chokepoints, and leverage existing platforms in APEC to advance supply chain connectivity and trade facilitation. We welcome the final review of Phase Three of the Supply Chain Connectivity Framework Action Plan (SCFAP III) (2022-2026). We also recognize the importance of transparency of measures that may affect trade or disrupt supply chains.

10. We will continue cooperation to advance innovation and foster ICT resilience in the transport sector. We will continue to promote good regulatory practices, strengthen cooperation on standards and conformity assessment procedures, pursue structural reform to improve the business environment. We will also foster practical exchange of experience on trade digitalization, supply chains, trade facilitation, advance digitalization of customs and trade-related procedures. We encourage business mobility through the APEC Business Travel Card, and welcome economies' efforts to advance tourism facilitation, strengthen education, skills development and cultural exchanges.

Innovation

11. We recognize that technology and innovation are profoundly reshaping our economies and rapidly driving economic growth in the Asia-Pacific region. We will leverage technological advancement to pursue innovation-driven and productivity-led growth, improve quality of life, and promote prosperity and opportunity for all our peoples. To this end, we support science, technology, and innovation cooperation to foster a competitive, resilient and secure innovation ecosystem. We encourage the voluntary exchange of good practices to support the growth of local innovation ecosystems.

12. We reaffirm our commitment to growing the digital economy and sharing the benefits of digital transformation with all our peoples. We encourage economies to advance digital connectivity and bridge digital divides across all segments of society and across regions between urban and rural areas, strengthen accessible and resilient digital infrastructure, promote digital transformation for economic growth, enhance digital literacy and skills, and promote the development of digital platforms. We encourage economies to address potential risks such as data breaches, online scams and deliberate misuse of digital and emerging technologies for malicious purposes, to strengthen and enhance the digital environment. We recognize the importance of respecting intellectual property rights in the development of digital and emerging technologies. We recognize the vital role of data in powering digital transformation. We will continue our cooperation on facilitating the flow of data across borders, strengthening business and consumer trust in digital transactions, and ensuring data protection and privacy.

13. We underscore that digital and emerging technologies present transformative opportunities to boost productivity, efficiency, competitiveness, resilience, and economic growth across the Asia-Pacific. We commend APEC's efforts to advance discussions on digital and emerging technologies including the APEC AI Initiative (2026-2030), and endorse APEC Statement on Harnessing Digital and Emerging Technologies for Employment and Prosperity in the Asia-Pacific Region to continue this important work. We will support human-centric innovation, responsible approaches, and the adoption of digital and emerging technologies across all sectors of the economy for the benefit of all our peoples. We support driving digital and emerging technologies transformation across key sectors, harnessing digital and emerging technologies to improve public service delivery, including strengthening healthcare systems, fostering an enabling environment for businesses, promoting market-oriented and innovation-driven approaches, and empowering micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) with accessible digital tools. We will continue to invest in infrastructure related to digital and emerging technologies and advance data utilization to fuel innovation.

Economic Growth

14. We recognize that the economic empowerment of all is an important way to boost productivity and innovation and strengthen participation in the economy. We emphasize the importance of preparing our workforce for the future of work to capture the benefits of technological advancement and respond to demographic changes in line with the APEC Collaborative Framework for Demographic Changes. We reaffirm our commitment to modernizing human resources development through promoting high-quality, full, productive and decent employment, lifelong learning, vocational training, reskilling and upskilling, protecting the rights of workers and continuing efforts to promote international labour standards in the changing world of work, and optimizing social security systems as appropriate.

15. We emphasize the importance of credible and flexible fiscal, monetary and financial policy frameworks to manage shocks, maintain macroeconomic and financial stability. We note that global imbalances have persisted, creating risks to growth and stability. We recognize that global rebalancing is in our common interest and agree to strengthen communication and cooperation in this regard. We encourage fiscal policies to support households and promote financial access, opportunity and literacy for all, recognizing that financial literacy is important to financial health and well-being.

16. We seek to strengthen comprehensive security across all energy sectors and technologies and jointly address energy security challenges, ensuring uninterrupted, reliable, and affordable access to energy to enable economic prosperity. We encourage strengthened energy security through cooperation on supply chain resilience, secure cross-border infrastructure interconnection, and risk assessment. We recognize the benefits of timely restoration of critical energy infrastructure such as power plants, electric grids, submarine power cables and pipelines, and encourage sharing of economies' experiences on market mechanisms, emergency preparedness and response, and strategic reserve management. We recognize the importance of secure and uninterrupted energy flows and cooperation across the whole supply chain including between producers and consumers in a mutually beneficial manner as well as fostering energy cooperation in the region. We will promote universal access to high-quality energy that is secure, reliable, abundant, resilient, and affordable, including for remote and rural areas. We encourage deepening voluntary cooperation on mutual enhancement between digital and emerging technologies and energy by supporting reliable, resilient and affordable energy for digital and emerging technologies development while harnessing digital and emerging technologies to enhance energy systems that deliver benefits for all. We recognize that conventional and zero and low emission energy sources and technologies provide a foundation for energy security, and strong and sustainable economic growth, and that each economy will choose an energy system mix consistent with its domestic priorities.

17. We will work towards promoting open, fair, transparent, productive, resilient, and innovative agri-food systems that benefit all. We will strengthen policy partnership on food security, boost agricultural productivity and efficiency, enhance the resilience of regional food systems and supply chains, including through innovation and digitalization, promote the transformation of agri-food systems, advance food safety and nutrition for all, and prevent and reduce food loss and waste. We support science- and evidence-based, technology-enabled agriculture, including utilizing tools such as digital and emerging technologies and the advancement in agricultural biotechnology. We reaffirm our commitment to strengthening economic opportunities in rural areas.

18. We recognize the multiple values and contributions that forests provide for economic growth, biodiversity conservation, and the resilience and prosperity of communities across the Asia-Pacific region. We support cooperation on combating illegal logging and associated trade while promoting legally harvested forest products, sustainable forest management, and halting and reversing forest loss and degradation. We will also collaborate to improve the resilience of marine and coastal communities and promote the conservation and management of ocean resources, including by combating illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing and addressing the growing challenge of marine debris, while leveraging science- and technology-based approaches.

19. We are committed to fostering an enabling business environment that supports the growth of MSMEs and startups through opportunities to become more competitive and innovative. We will promote greater access for MSMEs to capital, assets, skills training and digital tools, support MSMEs' participation in value chains, and encourage economies to continue providing support for MSMEs capacity building. We encourage the development of accessible, easy-to-use and cost-effective products and solutions that help MSMEs boost productivity and efficiency, expand market participation, accelerate digital transformation and facilitate the transition of economic actors from the informal to the formal and global economies.

20. We recognize the detrimental impact of corruption as a threat to economic growth, eroding public trust, harming trade and fair competition, diverting resources away from vital areas, and facilitating crimes, including organized crime. We resolve to promote growth and prosperity through effective anti-corruption and integrity measures, and continue our joint efforts to fight against corruption, including cross-border corruption, deny safe haven to corruption offenders including people who benefit from corruption and illicit assets, and strengthen cooperation on asset recovery and return.

21. As part of our collective endeavors to deepen regional cooperation across all fronts, we note the convening of the 2026 sectoral ministerial meetings for Women and the Economy, Trade, Tourism, Digital and AI, Forestry, Food Security, Small and Medium Enterprises, Energy, Transportation, Human Resources Development, Finance, as well as other high-level events including during the Digital Weeks. We commend the outcomes of the 37th APEC Ministerial Meeting as an important basis for future cooperation, including the adoption of the five-year review of the Aotearoa Plan of Action.

22. Our business communities and other stakeholders bring creativity, dynamism, and energy to APEC and remain vital partners in our work. We look forward to further strengthening multi-stakeholder engagement, as appropriate, including with the APEC Business Advisory Council (ABAC) and Pacific Economic Cooperation Council (PECC).

23. We extend our sincere gratitude to the People's Republic of China and the people and city of Shenzhen, Guangdong Province for their warm hospitality and thorough arrangements. We look forward to the upcoming APEC host years of Viet Nam (2027), Mexico (2028), Singapore (2030), Japan (2031), Chile (2032), Papua New Guinea (2033), and Peru (2034). (via Xinhua News)

text:
SURAH AL-JINN
Number of verses: 28 | Period: Mecca (in all likelihood after the journey to Taif) | Pedagogical order: 88
Subject: The Limit of the Unseen — Human Responsibility
Reference Frame: Qur'an Tafsir Reference Protocol v27 | Foundational Axiom: an-Nisa 136 | Epistemic Limit: Allah knows best.
INTRODUCTION: CONTEXT, THE HISTORICAL READING OF THE “JINN”, AND THE EPISTEMOLOGICAL CRISIS
The surah was sent down in the heaviest years of siege of the Meccan period, in all likelihood after the journey to Taif. It was revealed in a time when the Prophet was confronted with pressures from without, with a sense of loneliness from within, and with the systematic campaign of discredit waged by the Meccan oligarchy. As required by article 0b of the Protocol, the historical context of the surah is the key of the interpretation: the Meccan elites, by labeling the Prophet as a “soothsayer” (a diviner, one who gives news of the future) or as “possessed by jinn” (majnun), were trying to tie the source of the message he brought to networks of the unseen, dark, and untrustworthy. Surah al-Jinn is a manifesto that answers this accusation directly, structurally collapses the epistemological crisis of the age, and assigns the source of truth to Allah alone.
The analysis must be begun in the light of an-Nisa 136, the unalterable foundational axiom of the Protocol: faith in Allah, in His Prophet, in the Book sent down upon him, and in the books sent down before. The structure of this verse shows that faith is a continually renewed orientation; to “those who have believed” the command “believe” is given anew. The scope carries the four pillars together: Allah, the Prophet, the Qur'an, and the previous original revelations. A critical distinction must be made here: the Torah and the Gospel to which the Qur'an refers are not the versions shaped by human hands and compiled from the memories of the apostles that are accepted today by church or synagogue authorities. The reference is to the pure, original, tawhid-centered revelations of the time they were first sent down. The Qur'an came down as the verifier, the protector, and the final criterion that separates truth from falsehood (the Furqan) of these original messages. The emphasis of tawhid in Surah al-Jinn directly supports the continuity of this chain of original revelation and the Qur'an's position of protector within this chain.
The concept of “jinn” is not supernatural beings; it is the foreign delegations who concealed their identity to escape the pressure and embargo of the Meccan oligarchy (the intelligence apparatus of the Quraysh), who remained in the darkness, who listened in secret; the leading men of far regions (Nasibin, Yemen) or the early secret sympathizers of Medina (the Ansar).
1. Historical and Siyer Verification: the Theory of “the Hidden Human Beings”
The great majority of the classical tafsirs convey this event as a supernatural miracle, reflecting the mythological perception among the common people (the jinn upon the mountain). But Abu Muslim al-Isfahani (the twelfth-century rationalist exegete) and contemporary academic researchers refuse this reading, drawing attention to the internal consistency of the verses and to the historical context (the Siyer).
The Siyer Context (Protocol 0b): the Prophet, gravely wounded from the journey to Taif, is returning to Mecca under a psychological and sociological blockade (boycott). The Meccan oligarchy (the Quraysh) had wholly cut his contact with the outer world, with the tribes and the leading men, and was applying an “intelligence embargo.” No one could speak with him openly; those who listened to him were being declared “mad” or “sorcerer” and cast out of society.
The group that listened in secret to the Prophet while he recited the Qur'an by night in this valley of “Nakhla” or “Qarnu'l-Manazil” is defined, in the academic literature and the rationalist reading, as “foreign delegations come from far regions who were obliged to conceal their identity, Jewish/Christian scholars (from Nasibin or the region of Yemen), or the elites in search of an early secret alliance (the forerunners of the Ansar of Medina) who feared the pressure of Mecca.”
Why were they called “Jinn” (the hidden)? The Arabic root J-N-N means “to cover, to hide, to remain in darkness, to conceal one's identity.” These delegations, to escape the spy networks of the Meccan oligarchy (of the Quraysh), to avoid a diplomatic crisis or a physical lynching, listened to the Prophet incognito — concealing their identities in the darkness of night, in the hollows of the valleys (the metaphor of “the stations of the heaven / the secret listening posts” in verses 8-9).
The Possibility of the Leading Men of Medina: the leading men of the tribes of Medina (Yathrib), the Aws and the Khazraj, were conducting their first contacts with the Prophet (before the pledges of Aqaba) in the utmost secrecy, because they feared the pressure of Mecca. These “secret listeners / elites in search of a secret alliance,” not wishing to live an open tension with the Meccan oligarchy, escaped the surveillance of the Quraysh and listened to the revelation in the darkness of night. The Qur'an reverses, in an ironic language, the smear propaganda of Mecca, “none but the jinn (madness / invisible powers) listen to him”: “those secret listeners whom you took for 'invisible beings / jinn' (the elites of the far regions, the hidden delegations) surrendered before the rational power of the revelation.”
2. Semantic and Logical Proofs (Protocols 0d and 17)
The internal structure of the verses cries out that these listeners are not ontological “aliens/ghosts” but a sociological group of human beings:
A. “When they returned to their people...” (al-Jinn 11-14): the jinn's returning to their people as warners (nadhirs) is biologically and ontologically impossible. But the secret delegates come from Nasibin, from Yemen, or from Medina's returning to their own people / leading men and saying “We heard a rational truth (a Furqan)” is a historical and sociological reality.
B. “The mosques belong to Allah alone...” (al-Jinn 18): this verse stresses that the public spaces, the diplomatic meeting points, and the houses of worship must be cleansed of the idols / intermediary authorities of the oligarchy. This is the theological approval of a proposal of “public space and alliance” that the secret delegations or the Medinan sympathizers offered to the Prophet.
C. Protocol 17d (Symbolic Language): just as with the Prophet Solomon's listening to the ants (the peasants at the very bottom of society, whose voice is not heard), so the Prophet Muhammad's listening to, and addressing, the persons of “invisible / jinn” status whom Mecca counted as non-existent, who remained in the darkness and were forced into hiding (the secret delegates, the foreign scholars) is the establishing of a revolutionary network of equality and communication.
3. The Axiom of Nisa 136 and Contact with the “Original Revelation”
When this historical reading is joined with the unalterable axiom of the Protocol, Nisa 136, it gains a magnificent epistemological depth.
If these “secret listeners” (the jinn) are Jewish/Christian scholars come from Nasibin or the region of Yemen, or the elites of far tribes possessing knowledge of the original Torah/Gospel, then the reaction they gave upon hearing the Qur'an (verse 2: “We heard a wondrous Qur'an that guides to rushd (to rational maturity / the right)”) is precisely the shock of encountering the original, uncorrupted, pure revelation that Nisa 136 affirms.
The churches and the chief rabbinate seats of the age had corrupted the Torah and the Gospel and produced a theology that ascribed to Allah a “son” or “partners” (the confession of al-Jinn 3-4: “one of us who was foolish would say outrageous things about Allah”). But when these “secret listeners / scholars of the far regions” heard the pure tawhid faith the Qur'an brought (that Allah is free of taking a consort or children — tanZih), they recognized at once that this was the lost or distorted original message.
Their confession, “We shall never again set up any partner to our Lord” (al-Jinn 2), is the breaking away from the human dogmas produced by the church councils or the rabbinical assemblies, and the proclamation of the return to the first and pure revelation of Moses and Jesus (Nisa 136). These scholars, who hid in the darkness to escape the pressure of the Meccan oligarchy, had found the light of the truth.
4. The Breaking of the Epistemological Blockade
The Collapse of the Secret Networks and the Oligarchic Embargo (Verses 1-5):
The Meccan oligarchy had isolated the Prophet and was waging a psychological war, claiming that his message addressed only “dark powers / the jinn” (that is, the marginals outside society, or madness). But the Qur'an structurally collapses this intelligence embargo. “Say: It has been revealed to me that a group of the jinn (delegates concealing their identity, remaining in the darkness, fearing the pressure of Mecca / secret Medinan sympathizers / scholars of far regions) listened to the Qur'an...”
This verse is a message of immense consolation and geopolitical victory given to the Prophet and the first believers. The message is this: “They think you alone and besieged. But your voice has passed beyond the intelligence networks of Mecca (the satans' listening to the heaven / Protocols 8-10) and reached the far regions, the hidden elites, and the heirs of the original revelation. They saw how the Furqan you brought (the criterion that separates truth from falsehood) collapsed the superstitions produced by the corrupted authorities of religion (the fools), and they surrendered to the pure tawhid (Nisa 136).”
The first verse of the surah opens with the expression, “Say: It has been revealed to me that a community of the jinn listened to the Qur'an and said: 'Surely we have heard a wondrous Qur'an.'” Article 0g of the Protocol is decisive in the reading of this verse. The root of “jinn” (J-N-N) carries the meaning “to cover, to hide, to remain in the dark.” In the cultural perception of the jahiliyya, the soothsayers claimed to receive knowledge of the unseen from “the jinn.” In the perception of the audience of the age this meant the secret networks of information, the intelligence sources, the invisible strata of society, and the manipulative webs of the soothsayers. The Protocol makes it binding that the concept of jinn be understood not as an ontologically independent species (an alien, ghost, or independent spiritual category of being) but as a near companionship and role that leads a person astray, that whispers, that produces secret knowledge, that manipulates. Just as in the story of the Prophet Solomon's speaking with the ants, where what is in question is not a literal dialogue with insects but the symbolic telling of the hearing, by a just ruler, of the rights of the peasants living in the Valley of the Ants, at the lowest stratum of the people, whose voice is not heard; so the “listening of the jinn” in Surah al-Jinn is not a literal supernatural event but the symbolic telling of the surrender, before the rational truth of the Qur'an, of the secret networks of the age, the manipulative webs, and the soothsayers' sources of information. The expression “wondrous Qur'an” (Qur'anan 'ajaban) proclaims that even these hidden networks felt astonishment and admiration before the logical consistency, the universal moral message, and the epistemological soundness of the Qur'an — that is, that the truth is not in the monopoly of the dark webs, but that, as an evident Furqan, it penetrates to everyone.
The second verse declares that this Qur'an “guides to the right” (yahdi ila'r-rushd), and that they have believed in it and will never again set up partners to their Lord. The word “rushd” carries the meaning of the maturing of the reason, the capacity to find the right path, the conscious orientation. This is directly connected with the concept of “lubb” (the enlightened intellect) in article 6d of the Protocol. The secret networks, the manipulative webs, and the sources of whispering, accepting the structure of the Qur'an that leads to rushd (to rational maturity), abandon the setting up of partners (the associating of partners with Allah). Shirk here is not only the worshipping of idols; as the Protocol defines it, it is the placing of the ego, the desires, worldly interests, hidden centers of power, or other authorities before the teaching of Allah. The soothsayers' claim to receive knowledge “from the jinn” was the raising of these secret networks to the position of partners in divine knowledge; the Qur'an structurally collapses this partnership.
The third and fourth verses establish the tanZih dimension of tawhid: “The majesty of our Lord is exalted; He has taken neither a consort nor a child.” This expression is the direct application of the binding principle of tanZih in article 20a of the Protocol: Allah is the one who creates and is perfect with absolute perfection; time, space, weakness, mortality, need, and dependence are the attributes of the created, not of the Creator. The expressions “taking a consort” and “taking a child” are a direct refusal of the deviations seen in the idolatrous Arab theology of the age (the claim that the angels were the daughters of Allah) and in the human interpretations later added to the previous traditions of revelation (the corrupting of the pure tawhid of the original Gospel and the producing of the myth of the divine son). While the Qur'an re-establishes the pure tawhid in the original revelations affirmed by Nisa 136, it sifts out the human layers added afterward. The word “sefih” (foolish, deficient of mind, destitute of thought) in the fourth verse defines the epistemological position of those who make outrageous claims about Allah: these are they who reduce the divine authority to human categories, who set idols, hidden powers, or ideological leaders in the place of Allah.
The fifth verse continues with the expression, “We thought indeed that men and jinn would never speak falsehood against Allah.” The soothsayers, the rabbis, and the councils of the church (their priests) were presenting, ascribing it to Allah, the knowledge they claimed to receive “from the jinn” (from the secret sources of information); and society believed that this knowledge came from Allah. But with the coming down of the Qur'an it came to light that these secret sources had spoken falsehood in the name of Allah, had produced fabricated knowledge, and had manipulated the people. The expression “men and jinn” covers both the open (human) and the hidden (jinn) manipulators; both categories possess the capacity of speaking falsehood against Allah, and the Qur'an lays this capacity bare.
THE HISTORICAL DECIPHERMENT OF VERSE 5 OF SURAH AL-JINN: THE MECHANISM OF “SPEAKING FALSEHOOD IN THE NAME OF ALLAH” AND THE ACTORS OF MANIPULATION
Reference Protocol: the Qur'an Tafsir Reference Protocol v27 (articles 0b, 0d, 0g, 17, 18, 26, and the Axiom of Nisa 136).
The Text of the Verse and Its Epistemological Frame
The fifth verse of Surah al-Jinn says: “Ve enna zannenna en len tekule'l-insu ve'l-cinnu alallahi keziba” — “We thought indeed that men and jinn would never speak falsehood against Allah.”
This sentence is a most shattering epistemological confession. The “secret listeners” of the age (the delegations in the role of jinn, the scholars of far regions, the secret sympathizers) confess that they had lived before with this assumption: “No one who speaks in the name of Allah speaks falsely.” If the soothsayer says “I received it from Allah,” if the rabbi says “the Torah says thus,” if the priest says “this is the decree of the Gospel,” the truth of these words could not be doubted, they supposed. But when they listened to the rational, shattering, and pure tawhid message of the Qur'an, they understood what a dangerous delusion this assumption had been.
The unalterable axiom of the Protocol, Nisa 136, sets here a key distinction: the Torah and the Gospel that the Qur'an affirms are not the versions shaped by human hands and dogmatized by the decisions of councils that are read today in synagogues or churches. The reference is to the first, pure, original tawhid message revealed to Moses and to Jesus. But this original message was systematically manipulated through history by certain actors. Verse 5 is precisely the decipherment of this manipulation: to speak falsehood in the name of Allah is to instrumentalize the divine authority for human interests.
The Category of “Men”: the Manipulation of the Open Authorities
The expression “men” (al-ins) in the verse covers the religious actors who stand in a position legitimate, visible, and authoritative in the eyes of society. These are not “hidden” (jinn) but “open” (human) manipulators; they speak from the pulpit, from the prayer niche, from the synagogue, or from the temple. The Qur'an documents the manipulation mechanisms of these actors concretely in more than one surah:
The Soothsayers (the Arab Tradition of the Jahiliyya): the soothsayers of the jahiliyya period were presenting, ascribing it to Allah, the knowledge they claimed to receive “from the jinn” (from secret sources of information, from intelligence networks). Society did not question the source of this knowledge; for the soothsayer was speaking “in the name of Allah.” This is the nakedest form of the deed of “speaking falsehood against Allah” in verse 5: the attributing of fabricated information to the divine authority. The Qur'an structurally collapses this practice with the metaphor of the “shihab” (blaze) in al-Mulk 3-5: the truth is closed to the manipulation of the soothsayers; the claim of “stealing news from heaven” is invalid.
The Rabbis and the Doctors of Religion (the Rabbinic Tradition): the Qur'an documents this manipulation openly in Al-e Imran 78: “There is a party among them who twist their tongues with the Book, that you may suppose it to be part of the Book, though it is not part of the Book; and they say, 'It is from Allah,' though it is not from Allah, and they speak falsehood against Allah while they know.” This verse gives the historical counterpart of the deed of “men's speaking falsehood against Allah” in verse 5. The rabbis, adding to the original text of the Torah their human interpretations, the Talmudic traditions, and their own fatwas, presented these as “the word of Allah.” In al-Baqara 79 this is expressed yet more sharply: “Woe to those who write the Book with their hands and then sell it for a small price! Woe to them for what their hands have written!” Here the “small price” is the converting of religious authority into economic and political rent. In at-Tawba 34, with the expression “the rabbis and the monks consume the goods of the people unjustly and turn them from the way of Allah,” the converting of religious authority into “a vehicle of transfer of wealth” (Protocol 31e: Legal Corruption and Bribery) is cursed.

Washington State 

THE INMATES ARE RUNNING THE ASYLUM 

As budget gap looms, Washington progressives say state isn’t spending enough

Nov. 19, 2026

TACOMA — As state lawmakers and agencies brace for budget cuts amid a projected $4 billion shortfall, some members of Washington’s progressive community think the state should actually be spending, and taxing, more.

Business groups and Democratic Gov. Bob Ferguson have indicated they don’t want to see new taxes on the table for next year. But progressives insist that this month’s decisive election win for the state’s new “millionaires tax” shows that voters are on board with increased spending and shifting the tax burden from the poor to the wealthy. 

“There is a mandate to continue to fix our upside-down tax code and have enough revenue to support the programs that people clearly want more investment in, like education (and) healthcare,” said Eli Taylor Goss, executive director of the left-leaning Washington State Budget and Policy Center, during the group’s annual policy summit at Tacoma’s Asia Pacific Cultural Center on Tuesday.

The half-day event, which attracts various advocacy groups, offered a glimpse of progressive policy objectives ahead of the state legislative session that will begin in January. 

At last year’s summit, state Sen. Noel Frame, D-Seattle, previewed a proposal for the new tax on high-earner income. This year’s lineup didn’t feature lawmakers or lay out specific legislation. And it’s far from clear what appetite state legislators may have for additional revenue.

State Senate Majority Leader Jamie Pedersen recently floated the idea of a state corporate income tax to replace Washington’s archaic business and occupation tax. However, the Seattle Democrat made clear he wants a “neutral” change that doesn’t raise additional tax revenue for the state. He also said a bill calling for the switch is not likely before 2028.

On Monday, Ferguson directed state agencies to propose cuts to deal with a $4 billion projected shortfall in the state’s next fiscal year, and his top budget official insisted that “we’re not considering new revenue as part of our solution for the budget problem.”

Another major uncertainty for progressives is whether a state income tax, which is central to many of their tax plans, will be upheld by the courts.

Those uncertainties didn’t dampen the mood at the summit or keep advocates from touting ideas for new revenue — including a corporate income tax and a wealth tax — along with new strategies to turn those concepts into viable legislation.

“Transforming our tax code requires us to transform how we win, who we work with, and how we work together in coalition,” said Taylor Goss. 

One big focus is winning over voters who might not have backed progressive causes in the past, advocates said Tuesday. 

That includes residents in Central and Eastern Washington, where there is often little trust in the Democratic Party and skepticism toward state government generally, said Elana Mainer, executive director of Rural People’s Voice, an advocacy organization based in north-central Washington.

Mainer said her group’s approach is to focus on shared goals around economic class — such as taxing billionaires, or protections for working-class families — rather than trying to get conservative voters to change parties or embrace government. 

“There’s no way I can win on that conversation,” Mainer said. When she knocks on doors, she added, “I am really clear that I’m not there to go to bat for the Democratic Party.”

Progressives also think they need to stop letting tax opponents control the narrative about the budget crisis.

Many business leaders and Republicans, for example, have argued that the state’s current budget shortfall results not from inadequate revenue, but from decades of overspending. 

That has also been the message of former Govs. Christine Gregoire and Gary Locke, both Democrats.

text:
I got a lot of overwhelming responses and DMs on the back of this post. Thank you brothers and sisters, who are all in various stages of your own journey. I’d like to clarify a few things at the outset to the many comments on the post .thought I’ll address it as one big write up. 

- i am very clear that my journey started when i was 22, back in 2011 . 
- I am not comparing this to someone who is the same age in 2026, 
- i am aware of the many difficulties your generation faces like the entry level job market , the US doors being shut due to Trump administration, agentic AI stealing jobs , cost of living.

Now to the specifics of my journey 

- at 22, I had a BTech in IT. I did not land a campus job, though many of my peers did. So I had to crack an off campus grid and I got a Tech Mahindra offer after 4 rounds in one day. 

- many of peers post training phase there went into development. Wanting to relocate to my hometown chennai I took up a support project opportunity , it was application support, which was looked down upon by many. It also was rotational shifts so wasn’t easy on the body either. 

- many nights I’ve been the only one in office doing maintenance, woken up weekend mornings and festival days doing oncall. Wasn’t easy but first 3.5 years learnt the ropes of corporate IT , customer client support, projects. Picked up SQL ,App support, Linux skills , soft skills that would aid me for rest of my life.

- whole of 2014 while working this job, I studied for MBA exams on the side and ran the gauntlet - CMAT, CAT, XAT, SNAP, IIFT. Got a few high 90s but due to caste wasn’t enough to land any college I actually wanted. No IIMs 

- in 2015 I switched to TCS after 3 years in TechM. Worked a year there with added responsibility but wasn’t considered for an onsite opportunity I had worked hard for, office politics .

- so decided to write GRE and target a masters degree in USA, which I did in 2015, got a score of 319. Had no arrears in BTech, applied to 5 colleges, got University of Florida., MS in CS.

- my dad had purchased lands with his savings, used this as collateral to get a student loan to go to USA. I acknowledge this is a privilege many don’t have. 

- August 2016 I went there , had a rough time in my masters, scraped thru with a GPA 3.4 , homesick, hated cooking all the time. But I made good friends for life too there. Graduated in December 2018 cause I had to do an extra sem caused I failed a subject and had to repeat it. But December 2018 I also landed a startup company in Atlanta as a Cloud operations engineer. 

- Jan 2019- July 2019 worked in the startup learnt the ropes of Cloud and distributed systems, Devops and SRE.

- August 2019 saw a Microsoft job posting for Azure cloud , applied, cracked it and worked there for roughly 4 years till June 2023. Experienced Layoff with Microsoft

- worked a interim job posting layoff in a consulting company in USA, till I applied to AWS in December 2023 and cracked it.

- worked with AWS till July 2026. 

- after about 10 years in USA, I took a personal call to return to India, now I know I’ll get a lot of opinions on this, I did so for my parents, both of who are hard of hearing and mute, they made an enormous sacrifice to get me so far, so I made this call that I’m tired of living away from them for long lengths of time and that’s why I am back in india now.

- I’ll share my LinkedIn definitely when I feel safe enough, but most of time here is a political handle opposing the DMK, so revealing my identity isn’t without significant risk . 

- that’s all I felt like sharing at this moment. Thank you all for your support. Stay blessed. Never give up, never quit, the night is always darkest before it’s dawn.

Leadership in Motion: A Week of Diplomacy, Innovation & National Pride 

This week, His Excellency President Dr. @edmnangagwa demonstrated decisive leadership across foreign policy, digital governance, innovation, and sports accelerating Zimbabwe’s march toward #Vision2030.
Here is a look at the key milestones from the week:
1. Results-Driven Global Diplomacy
On November 18, President Mnangagwa appointed nine new ambassadors to key global postings, including the USA, South Africa, the UAE, Cuba, Canada, and Ghana. Addressing the envoys in Harare, he issued a clear mandate: turn diplomatic missions into engines of economic growth by attracting FDI, expanding exports, boosting tourism, and protecting Zimbabweans in the diaspora.
2. Chairing Cabinet & Advancing AI Governance
Presiding over Cabinet, the President steered major approvals to modernize the economy. Cabinet adopted the Zimbabwe National Artificial Intelligence Charter to operationalize the National AI Strategy (2026–2030) across agriculture, mining, health, and education, alongside legislative principles to amend the National Arts Council Act in support of the digital and creative economy.
3. Celebrating Sporting & Youth Excellence
At a special State House reception on November 18, His Excellency honoured Zimbabwe’s sporting ambassadors celebrating the Warriors’ 3–0 triumph over Equatorial Guinea at the refurbished National Sports Stadium and congratulating 17-year-old sprinter Ropafadzo Liberty Mzondo on winning Zimbabwe’s historic first Youth Olympic gold medal in the men's 200m at Dakar 2026. The President also pledged accelerated upgrades to sports facilities nationwide to nurture grassroots talent.
4. Scaling Homegrown Innovation (Education 5.0)
Continuing his push for heritage-based Education 5.0, the President challenged universities, banks, and industry players to back student startups and commercialize local innovations that drive job creation and import substitution.
From global re-engagement and AI readiness to celebrating our youth on the world stage, His Excellency continues to lead from the front in building a modern, prosperous Zimbabwe.

My wife and I [MF] spent the weekend with another couple [MF] and had an accidental night time mix-up.

Last year, my wife, Lily, and I were invited by another couple to stay in their family cabin in rural Michigan. The couple, Alice and Robert, had their first child about 18 months prior and were taking their first vacation since. text:
$GAP Q3 2026 earnings: Gap Inc.'s profit rose, but it now plans flat sales

Gap Inc., the owner of Old Navy, Gap and Banana Republic, earned more while its sales hardly moved. Sales rose 2%, while profit per share excluding one-offs grew far faster, helped by lower overhead and buybacks. Chief executive Richard Dickson said a warm October then slowed demand. So the company now plans no sales growth for the year, with the holiday quarter flat or slightly down.

• Net sales: $𝟒.𝟎𝟏 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 (+1.8% from a year ago; comparable sales unchanged)
• Profit per share, excluding one-offs: $𝟎.𝟖𝟐 ($0.62 a year ago, +32%)
• Gap brand comparable sales: +𝟗% (+7% a year ago)
• Full-year sales outlook: 𝐂𝐮𝐭 𝐭𝐨 𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐠𝐡𝐥𝐲 𝐟𝐥𝐚𝐭 (previously up 1% to 1.5%)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🔴 Bearish

The story got worse, because Gap Inc. cut its yearly sales plan for a third time and lowered its profit forecast too. The good news: the Gap brand kept growing against a strong year-ago quarter, and lower overhead lifted the quarter's operating margin.

The question now is whether Old Navy, which brings in over half of sales, can grow again without cutting prices. Either lower prices win back shoppers who stay, or discounts only keep sales level while profit per item shrinks. Holiday-quarter results, due in early 2027, will tell.

[Model: Claude Opus 5.5. Full article with charts - link in bio]

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐆𝐚𝐩 𝐁𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐑𝐨𝐬𝐞 𝟏𝟏% 𝐀𝐠𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐬𝐭 𝐓𝐨𝐮𝐠𝐡 𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐢𝐬𝐨𝐧
Gap Inc. owns four clothing brands, and the one that shares its name now drives its growth. The worry was that the Gap brand would slow against its strong 2025 quarters. A year earlier, its comparable sales, which count only stores and websites open at least a year, had risen 7%.

The brand passed that test. Its comparable sales rose 9%, and net sales climbed 11%. It was the 12th straight quarter of gains, with "broad-based strength across Men's, Women's, and Kids and Baby", the company said.

• Share of Gap Inc. sales: 26%, from 24% a year ago
• Sales outside North America: up 18%
• Comparable sales over two years combined: 16 points, from 14 last quarter

This matters because Gap Inc. tied its higher merchandise margin, the profit on goods before store costs, to "another quarter of strength at the Gap brand". That gain covered lower prices and heavier discounts at Old Navy.

What to watch: the brand's holiday-quarter comparable sales, due in early 2027, against a 7% gain a year earlier. Another rise would show the growth rests on the brand itself, not on a few popular collections.

🟢 𝐋𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐎𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐡𝐞𝐚𝐝 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐋𝐢𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐥𝐲 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭
Gap Inc. spent less on operating expenses: store staff, advertising and head office. Those costs fell 2% while sales grew, so they took 1.3 percentage points less of sales than a year ago.

Chief executive Richard Dickson said the group "exceeded our profit expectations". Lower overhead explains that result, because gross margin excluding one-offs stayed level. Operating margin excluding one-offs reached 9.8%, against 8.5% a year earlier.

The holiday plan asks for more of the same, about 1 percentage point off the cost share. But the retailer does not say which costs fell, so readers cannot judge how much will last.

What to watch: the holiday quarter's operating costs as a share of sales, due in early 2027. Hitting the planned drop would show the savings are lasting.

🟢 𝐁𝐮𝐲𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐬 𝐋𝐢𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐒𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐅𝐚𝐫 𝐀𝐛𝐨𝐯𝐞 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬
Gap Inc. keeps buying back its own shares. Its diluted share count fell 5% from a year ago, so each share claims more of the profit. That is why profit per share excluding one-offs rose 32%, far ahead of sales.

The retailer returned $788 million to shareholders in nine months, $601 million of it through buybacks. About $399 million remains under its buyback approval.

One caution: by our math, tariff refunds and a legal settlement supplied nearly all of this year's free cash flow. Without them, about $16 million remains, before tax on those gains.

What to watch: full-year free cash flow, due in early 2027. A result well below the cash returned would mean the buybacks are drawing down savings.

🟢 𝐏𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐭𝐞𝐬𝐭
Gap Inc. has started several new lines meant to add sales beyond its core clothing. The release gave no figures for any of them, so this quarter neither helped nor hurt the case for them.

• Old Navy Sport: about 40 shop-in-shops due this autumn; a sales figure for the line would show whether it lifts Old Navy
• Beauty: the company describes a "continuing strategic expansion into the beauty category"; beauty sales would show its size
• Gap bags: due to launch with Fashion Week in September; accessories sales would show demand beyond clothing
• Fanatics sports collection: Old Navy's first exclusive range of licensed team clothing was due this quarter; any sales figure would test it

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐎𝐥𝐝 𝐍𝐚𝐯𝐲 𝐇𝐞𝐥𝐝 𝐈𝐭𝐬 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐛𝐲 𝐂𝐮𝐭𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐏𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐞𝐬
Old Navy is Gap Inc.'s budget clothing chain, and it brings in more than half of group sales. Chief executive Richard Dickson said: "Gap posted another outstanding quarter, and we delivered meaningful sequential improvement at Old Navy." The improvement is real, because Old Navy's comparable sales went from a 4% fall last quarter to no change.

But Old Navy got there by charging less. The company said the chain's average selling price dropped because of "planned pricing adjustments at Old Navy" and "higher promotional activity at Old Navy and Athleta". Net sales at the chain rose only 1%, a year after a 6% jump in comparable sales.

This matters because Old Navy now asks less for each item, so steady sales can still hide thinner profit. The group does not report profit by brand, so readers cannot check. Nor does the holiday plan show a rebound, because the retailer now expects total sales to slip.

What to watch: Old Navy's holiday-quarter comparable sales, due in early 2027, against a 3% gain a year earlier. A rise without deeper discounts would show that shoppers came back for the product, not the price.

🔴🔴 𝐆𝐚𝐩 𝐈𝐧𝐜. 𝐍𝐨𝐰 𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐬 𝐍𝐨 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡
Gap Inc. started the year planning sales growth of 2% to 3%. It lowered that plan in the spring and again in the summer. Now the retailer expects sales roughly level with last year's, and a holiday quarter flat or down 1%.

By our math, the summer plan needed holiday-quarter sales to rise 3% to 4%. The company blamed "a slower than expected start to the fourth quarter", and said trends improved as the weather returned to normal. It also lowered its plan for profit per share excluding one-offs by about 4% at the middle of the range.

This matters because, until now, higher profit plans had made up for lower sales plans. This time both moved down together. The plan puts operating margin excluding one-offs at about 7.2% for the year, below last year's 7.3%. So earnings growth now rests on buybacks and a lower tax rate.

What to watch: holiday-quarter sales, due in early 2027. A result inside the new range would show that the weak start cost only a few weeks of demand.

🔴 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧 𝐌𝐢𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐚𝐧𝐲'𝐬 𝐎𝐰𝐧 𝐏𝐥𝐚𝐧
Gross margin is the share of sales left after the cost of goods and stores. Gap Inc. had planned a rise of up to 0.75 percentage points, helped by lower tariffs. Excluding one-offs, it stayed at 42.4%, level with a year ago.

Tariff relief did arrive: the retailer collected its refunds, and its outlook now counts $46 million more relief. But lower Old Navy prices, heavier discounts and dearer fuel used it up. Rent, occupancy and depreciation also took 0.4 percentage points more of sales. So the yearly plan now has gross margin slipping slightly, after a small gain before.

What to watch: holiday-quarter gross margin, due in early 2027, against a 38.0% to 38.3% plan. A result below it would show price cuts still cost more than tariffs save.

🔴 𝐀𝐭𝐡𝐥𝐞𝐭𝐚 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐁𝐚𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐚 𝐑𝐞𝐩𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐜 𝐁𝐨𝐭𝐡 𝐋𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬
Athleta, the women's sportswear brand, has posted falling comparable sales for seven quarters. This quarter they dropped 15%, the steepest decline in that run. Gap Inc. cited "limited traction from efforts to modernize the assortment and marketing", and named Ashley Kechter as Athleta's next chief executive.

Banana Republic also lost ground after five quarters of gains. Its comparable sales fell 3%, which the company tied to its women's autumn range and "delayed demand for cold-weather categories".

This matters because both brands now work against the Gap brand's gains while leaders change. Old Navy also got a new chief executive on November 2.

What to watch: Athleta's comparable sales in the first seasons Kechter shapes. A smaller decline would show the reset has started to work.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐖𝐚𝐫𝐦 𝐖𝐞𝐚𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐒𝐥𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐲 𝐇𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐲 𝐃𝐞𝐦𝐚𝐧𝐝
Chief executive Richard Dickson said "demand softened in October and early November, amidst warmer weather". Trends improved "as temperatures have cooled", he added. Gap Inc. built that pattern into its holiday plan, which assumes a slow start and then a recovery. Weather shifts sales of coats and sweaters between months, so the full quarter matters more than any single week.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐄𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐢𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐲 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟐.𝟑𝟏 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Stock on hand fell 6% from a year ago, even as sales rose. Inventory growth ran near 7% at the start of the year, held around zero in spring and summer, and has now turned negative. Leaner shelves leave fewer goods to clear at a discount after the holidays.

𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐬𝐡𝐨𝐫𝐭-𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐦 𝐢𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟐.𝟗𝟕 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
The cash pile rose 18% from a year ago. By our math, tariff refunds and a legal settlement account for about $799 million of it. Without those, the balance would sit about 14% below last year, after a year of heavy buybacks.

𝐂𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 (𝐟𝐢𝐫𝐬𝐭 𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐦𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐡𝐬): $𝟒𝟖𝟑 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Spending on stores and systems jumped 48% from a year ago, to about 4% of sales. The yearly plan of about $650 million still holds. By our math, that leaves about $167 million for the holiday quarter. More spending lifts depreciation, part of the store costs that held gross margin back.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐧𝐞𝐭 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬: 𝐑𝐨𝐮𝐠𝐡𝐥𝐲 𝐟𝐥𝐚𝐭 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫-𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫-𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫 (𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟓: $𝟏𝟓.𝟒 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧)  ⇘ decelerating
🠇 cut from Up 1% to 1.5% year-over-year
Cut. The plan now has sales roughly level with last year's $15.4 billion. Third cut this year; the middle of the range moved -1.0, -0.25 and -1.25 points. By our math, sales so far leave about $4.21 billion for the holiday quarter, slightly below a year ago.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧, 𝐞𝐱𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐧𝐞-𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐬: 𝐃𝐨𝐰𝐧 𝐬𝐥𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭𝐥𝐲 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫-𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫-𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫 (𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟓: 𝟒𝟎.𝟖%)  ⇘ decelerating
🠇 cut from Up slightly year-over-year
Cut. The plan now has gross margin excluding one-offs slightly below last year's 40.8%, where it had been slightly above. Lower prices at Old Navy and rising store costs outweigh the extra tariff relief.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐞 𝐚𝐬 % 𝐨𝐟 𝐧𝐞𝐭 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬, 𝐞𝐱𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐧𝐞-𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐬: 𝐋𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐬𝐥𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭𝐥𝐲 (𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟓: 𝟑𝟑.𝟓%)  ⇒ stable
🠇 cut from About flat year-over-year
Lowered, which helps profit. The company now expects operating costs to take slightly less of sales than last year's 33.5%, rather than the same share. Third-quarter savings and a planned holiday-quarter drop drive the change.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧, 𝐞𝐱𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐧𝐞-𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐬: 𝐀𝐩𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐱𝐢𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐥𝐲 𝟕.𝟐% (𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟓: 𝟕.𝟑%)  ⇘ decelerating
🠇 cut from About 7.4% to 7.6%
Cut. The forecast now has operating margin excluding one-offs a little below last year's 7.3%. By our math, that leaves about 6.5% for the holiday quarter, against 5.4% a year earlier. It is the first cut after two earlier updates held or raised the figure.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭, 𝐧𝐞𝐭, 𝐞𝐱𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐧𝐞-𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐬: 𝐀𝐩𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐱𝐢𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐥𝐲 $𝟐𝟒 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐨𝐟 𝐧𝐞𝐭 𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞  ⇒ stable
🠅 raised from Approximately $20 million
Raised. Gap Inc. now expects about $4 million more interest income than three months ago. Larger cash balances, helped by the tariff refunds, earn the extra income.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐞𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐭𝐚𝐱 𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞, 𝐞𝐱𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐧𝐞-𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐬: 𝐀𝐩𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐱𝐢𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐥𝐲 𝟐𝟓%  ⇒ stable
🠇 cut from Approximately 25% to 26%
Lowered slightly. The plan now sits at the bottom of the earlier range, well under last year's 27.9%. The lighter tax bill adds to profit per share while operating profit stands still.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐝𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐰𝐞𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐚𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭: 𝐀𝐩𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐱𝐢𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐥𝐲 𝟑𝟔𝟔 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 (𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟓: 𝟑𝟖𝟒 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧)  ⇘ decelerating
🠇 cut from Approximately 367 million
Lowered by 1 million shares. The count would sit about 5% below last year's. Buybacks so far this year drive the drop, and fewer shares lift profit per share even when total profit does not grow.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐝𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐏𝐒, 𝐞𝐱𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐧𝐞-𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐬: $𝟐.𝟐𝟗 𝐭𝐨 $𝟐.𝟑𝟒 (𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟓: $𝟐.𝟏𝟑)  ⇘ decelerating
🠇 cut from $2.35 to $2.45
Cut. By our math, the middle of the range means about 9% growth on last year's $2.13. That leaves about $0.60 for the holiday quarter, against $0.45 a year ago, also by our math. Fourth change this year; the middle moved +$0.075, +$0.05, then -$0.085.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐫𝐞𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐝𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐏𝐒: $𝟑.𝟕𝟏 𝐭𝐨 $𝟑.𝟕𝟔  ⇘ decelerating
🠇 cut from $3.77 to $3.87
Cut. This figure includes the tariff refunds and the legal settlement. The company counts about $0.89 a share from net tariff refunds, and the cut mirrors the lower plan excluding one-offs.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐜𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞𝐬: 𝐀𝐩𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐱𝐢𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐥𝐲 $𝟔𝟓𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 (𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟓: $𝟒𝟕𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧)  ⇗ accelerating
🠆 unchanged from Approximately $650 million
Unchanged. The retailer still plans about $650 million, up from $470 million last year, with the extra money going to stores and technology.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐧𝐞𝐭 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐚𝐧𝐲-𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐜𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐮𝐫𝐞𝐬: 𝐀𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐟𝐥𝐚𝐭  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from About flat
Unchanged. Gap Inc. expects to open about as many company-run stores as it closes. So far this year it has added 8 stores, net.

𝐐𝟒 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐧𝐞𝐭 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬: 𝐅𝐥𝐚𝐭 𝐭𝐨 𝐝𝐨𝐰𝐧 𝟏% 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫-𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫-𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫 (𝐐𝟒 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟓: $𝟒.𝟐 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧)  ⇘ decelerating
New. The plan has holiday-quarter sales level with a year ago or slightly lower, after a slow, warm start to the season. In the last four quarters with a plan, sales averaged slightly under the middle of each range, so this one leaves little room.

𝐐𝟒 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧: 𝐀𝐩𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐱𝐢𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐥𝐲 𝟑𝟖.𝟎% 𝐭𝐨 𝟑𝟖.𝟑% (𝐐𝟒 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟓: 𝟑𝟖.𝟏%)  ⇘ decelerating
New. The plan has gross margin about level with last year's holiday quarter. That quarter usually carries the year's lowest margin, so the step down from the third quarter is seasonal.

𝐐𝟒 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐞 𝐚𝐬 % 𝐨𝐟 𝐧𝐞𝐭 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬: 𝐋𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐱𝐢𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐥𝐲 𝟏𝟎𝟎 𝐛𝐚𝐬𝐢𝐬 𝐩𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐬 (𝐐𝟒 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟓: 𝟑𝟐.𝟕%)  ⇒ stable
New. The company expects operating costs to take about 1 percentage point less of sales than a year ago. Together with the gross margin plan, that points to a holiday-quarter operating margin about 1 point above last year's, by our math.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐝𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐎𝐥𝐝 𝐍𝐚𝐯𝐲 𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐧 𝐚𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐢𝐭𝐬 𝐩𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐞 𝐜𝐮𝐭𝐬?
Gap Inc. lowered Old Navy prices and ran more discounts to steady sales, but it does not report profit by brand. A brand margin would show whether flat sales came with thinner profit at its largest chain.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐟𝐫𝐞𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐰 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐨𝐧𝐞-𝐨𝐟𝐟 𝐠𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐬?
By our math, tariff refunds and a legal settlement supplied nearly all free cash flow this year. Investors need the cash figure after tax on those items to judge whether buybacks at this pace can continue.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 $𝟗𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐨𝐫 𝐩𝐚𝐲𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐟𝐨𝐫?
The company nets a "commitment of appreciation" for certain vendors against its tariff refunds. It has not said whether the payment is contractual, when it falls due, or whether more such payments could follow.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐡𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐲 𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐧 𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐨𝐧 𝐧𝐞𝐰 𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐬?
Old Navy Sport, beauty, Gap bags and the Fanatics collection were all due this autumn. The release gives no sales for any of them, so readers cannot tell how much they add to the holiday-quarter plan.

𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐬𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐥𝐝 𝐀𝐭𝐡𝐥𝐞𝐭𝐚'𝐬 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐩 𝐟𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠?
Athleta's comparable sales have fallen for seven quarters, and a new chief executive is coming. The company has given no date for a turnaround, so readers cannot judge how long the brand will hold back group results.

The Curious Origins of the Dollar Sign
April 1, 2018
By Joshua D. Rothman
Civil War-era advertisement depicting the dollar sign as a snake, 1861 (Library of Congress)
Nobody knows for certain who invented the dollar sign. Rendered as the letter “S” struck through with one or two vertical lines, its use dates back at least to the late eighteenth century. Some have hypothesized it originated with the Pillars of Hercules appearing on Spanish coats of arms or that it derives from the intertwining of the letters “U” and “S,” standing either for “United States” or “units of silver,” but the likeliest explanation traces its lineage to the challenges of paying for the Revolutionary War. The oldest known example of the symbol that would come to serve as a stand-in for the might of American capitalism appears in the correspondence of an immigrant who worked to finance the Revolution, only to find himself largely abandoned in its aftermath by the nation he had helped bring into being.

Oliver Pollock was born in Ireland in 1737 and emigrated in 1760 to the town of Carlisle in what is now south-central Pennsylvania. Soon thereafter, he began working as a merchant based mostly in New Orleans, which was then in the process of becoming a Spanish city after the French lost the Louisiana Territory as an outcome of the Seven Years’ War. New Orleans struggled to support its rapidly growing population, even to the point of experiencing food shortages, and in the late 1760s Pollock earned the gratitude of Spanish officials by arranging for shipments of flour from Philadelphia that he then sold at a discount. Rewarded by the Governor-General of New Orleans with free trading rights throughout the Louisiana Territory, Pollock quickly became extraordinarily wealthy, mostly by trading among the ports of New Orleans, Havana, and other locales throughout the West Indies.

An early supporter of British colonial resistance to the policies of the home country, and always angling for ways to boost his fortune, Pollock was in an advantageous position to help the colonists when their protests became full-scale revolt. The American revolutionaries desperately needed money to pay for war against the British military, and while the French and Spanish governments offered financial assistance, Pollock both personally donated several hundred thousand Spanish pesos and organized a bond issue to raise funds in New Orleans. In 1777, Congress appointed Pollock as the official representative of the United States in that city, and most of the money Pollock contributed and raised went to finance the successful military campaign of George Rogers Clark in 1778 against British forces and their Indian allies in what are now Illinois and Indiana. In 1779, when Spain entered the Revolutionary War as an ally of France on the side of the colonists, Pollock became aide-de-camp for Bernardo de Gálvez, the Spanish governor of the Louisiana Territory, and in that capacity he helped muster forces and supplies instrumental to the Spanish capture of several British forts in the Mississippi Valley between 1779 and 1781.

The name "Deniz" is of Turkish origin, meaning "SEA" or "ocean." It is predominantly used as a feminine given name in Turkey, though it can also be used for males. The etymology of the name is rooted in the Turkish language, where "deniz" directly translates to the body of saltwater that covers a significant portion of the Earth's surface. The name reflects a connection to nature, particularly the vastness and beauty of the sea, which has been a crucial element in Turkish culture and geography, given Turkey's extensive coastline along the Mediterranean, Aegean, and Black Seas.

The name Nicaea derives from the Ancient Greek Νίκαια (Níkaia), which is formed from νίκη (níkē, meaning "victory") and the feminine suffix -ια (-ia).

The First Council of Nicaea[5] was a council of Christian bishops convened in the Bithynian city of Nicaea (now İznik, Turkey) by the Roman Emperor Constantine I, also known as the First Ecumenical Council. It met from May until the end of July 325.[6]

This ecumenical council was the first of many efforts to attain consensus in the church within the Roman Empire. Hosius of Corduba may have presided over its deliberations.[7][8] It was attended by at least 200 bishops, almost entirely from the eastern half of the Empire.[9] Its main accomplishments were the settlement of the Christological issue of the divine nature of God the Son and his relationship to God the Father,[3] the construction of the first part of the Nicene Creed, the mandating of uniform observance of the date of Easter,[10] and the promulgation of early canon law.[4][11]

History
1483–1990: early years
In 1483, the Franciscan religious Angelo Da Chivasso, founded the mount of piety (Italian: Monte di Pietà) of Genoa.[2][non-primary source needed] In 1846, a decree of Piedmont-Sardinia King Charles Albert of Sardinia created the Cassa di Risparmio di Genova,[2][non-primary source needed] which extended the basic financial services of the mount to encourage and protect small savings more widely.[citation needed] In the 19th century, the bank expanded into western Liguria, and in 1967, it became the Cassa di Risparmio di Genova e Imperia.[2][non-primary source needed] Imperia was the capital of the west-most province of Liguria region.

1991–1999
In 1991, due to Amato Law, the bank, as a statutory corporation, was split into Banca Carige S.p.A. and Fondazione Carige,[3] forming Gruppo Banca Carige in the same year. The bank absorbed Istituto di Credito Fondiario della Liguria and Mediocredito Ligure. In January 1995, Banca Carige entered into the Borsa Italiana as a listed company. In 1997, the Gruppo Banca Carige acquired some insurance companies.

2000–2013: Berneschi's Bank Management
In 2000, Carige Vita Nuova Assicurazioni was created from Basilese Vita Nuova, while in 2002, Carige Assicurazioni was founded from Levante Norditalia. In 2000, the Banca Carige Group acquired the Cassa di Risparmio di Savona and the Banca del Monte di Lucca. Between 2000 and 2002, Carige completed three further acquisitions of branches from other banks: 21 branches from Banco di Sicilia, 61 from Banca Intesa group, and 42 from the Capitalia Group in Piedmont, Lombardy, Veneto, Emilia–Romagna, Tuscany, Lazio, Marche, Umbria, Apulia, and Sicily. In 2004, the bank strengthened its position in Tuscany with the acquisition of the Cassa di Risparmio di Carrara and founded Carige Asset Management SGR for the management of financial products. In 2004, the bank acquired the private bank Banca Cesare Ponti. In 2008, two further major acquisitions were completed: 79 branches from the Intesa Sanpaolo Group in Aosta Valley, Piedmont, Lombardy, Veneto, and Sardinia, and another 38 branches from the UniCredit Group in Lazio, Sicily, Emilia–Romagna, Veneto, and Umbria.[4] In 2010, the bank acquired another 22 branches from Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena.[2][non-primary source needed]

In September 2013, the Bank of Italy (Italian central bank) blamed Carige for using accountancy tricks and being in a difficult situation due to derivatives the bank had bought from Deutsche Bank. Carige published a statement to explain the event.[5] The Bank of Italy demanded from Carige a new business plan by the end of October.[6] In 2013, the bank sold its asset management subsidiary to ARCA SGR for €101 million.[7]

2014–2019
In 2014, the bank sold its insurance subsidiaries Carige Assicurazioni and Carige Vita Nuova to investment funds managed by Apollo Global Management for €310 million (via Primavera Holdings S.r.l.).[8][9] However, in 2016 the new board of directors wanted to sue the old managers for mismanagement by selling the insurance companies, claiming it was actually harmful to the bank instead of gain.[10] However, the court rejected the lawsuit.[11]

In mid-2015, subsidiaries Cassa di Risparmio di Savona (with second-tier subsidiary Immobiliare Carisa), Cassa di Risparmio di Carrara, Columbus Carige Immobiliare were absorbed into Banca Carige.[12] In 2016 Banca Carige Italia was absorbed by Banca Carige.

Around 2015, Malacalza Investimenti replaced Fondazione Carige, as the largest shareholder of the bank.

The Banca Carige Chairman Giuseppe Tesauro resigned on 26 June 2018.[13][14] Vittorio Malacalza, representing the majority shareholder of the bank: Malacalza Investimenti, also resigned as a director in July.[15][16] In total, 8 directors, or the majority of the board excluding CEO Paolo Fiorentino, had resigned in mid-2018.[17][18][19][20][21] However, in the re-election of the whole board, Malacalza Investimenti, secured a majority of the new board for 7 seats, as well as hiring Fabio Innocenzi as the new CEO.[22]

The Bank of the Holy Spirit (Italian: Il Banco di Santo Spirito) was a bank founded by Pope Paul V on 13 December 1605. The bank was the first central bank in Europe (as the bank of the Papal States) at a level above city-states,[1] the first public deposit bank in Rome,[2] and the oldest continuously operating bank in Rome until its merger in 1992.[3]

First period (1605–1923)
Pope Paul V founded the Bank in 1605.
The Bank was founded by Pope Paul V in the Bench of S. Spirit building (which became known as the Palazzo del Banco di S. Spirito) on 13 December 1605.[4] The construction of the building was started in 1513 by Pope Leo X, on what became known as the "Street of the Banks."[5] The newly founded bank provided a new source of income for the Archhospital of Santo Spirito (founded 1201),[6] whose financial difficulties had been increasing throughout the 16th century, and in 1607 the bank began supervising the finances of the hospital, which owned the bank.[2]

From 20 February 1606 to 1923 the Bank of the Holy Spirit provided capital for churches and hospitals constructed in Rome, and other commercial purposes. The bank lent funds to several public works projects, including the Trajan aqueduct project (Begun 1608).[6]

In 1750, Pope Benedict XIV, known for his condemnation of usury: Vix pervenit (promulgated 1 November 1745), reorganized the Bank and restricted its lending activities. In 1786, the bank became one of the first to issue paper money during the pontificate of Pope Pius VI.[7] By the late 19th century, the bank was controlled by the state.[8]: 89 

The records of the Bank are extant in the Vatican Secret Archives, but not in Introitus et Exitus, the records of the Apostolic Camera.[9]

Second period (1923–1989)
In 1923, the Bank was reorganized as a joint-stock company. In 1935, the Istituto per la Ricostruzione Industriale (IRI) of the fascist Italian government gained a controlling interest in the bank.

In the 1930s, Neapolitan bank robbers attempting to dig into the underground vaults of the Bank accidentally discovered the skeletons of victims of an 1836 cholera epidemic, which after archeological excavation became known as the Fontanelle cemetery.[10]

Disappearance by merger (1989-1991)
In 1989–1991, the Banco di Santo Spirito merged with Cassa di Risparmio di Roma (est. 1836). In 1992, the resulting entity in turn merged with Banco di Roma (est. 1880) to form Banca di Roma, which itself merged with other banks in 2002 to form Capitalia. [11]

Heyman Hustle TV Roundtable Tackles Family Legacies with WWE Stars and O'Shea Jackson Jr.

Hosted by Jacob Heyman, son of Paul Heyman, the premiere featured WWE stars Cody Rhodes and Charlotte Flair plus actor O'Shea Jackson Jr., all children of famous fathers. They discussed pressures of family legacies, with Charlotte opening up about protecting her dad Ric Flair's impact and Cody sharing comparisons to Dusty Rhodes. Paul Heyman praised their candidness as executive producer, and fans called the hour-long talk genuine and therapeutic. The full episode is free on the Heyman Hustle YouTube channel. News

New Street Fighter Movie Opens to Mixed Reviews and Fan Buzz

Directed by Kitao Sakurai, the PG-13 film stars Andrew Koji as Ryu and Noah Centineo as Ken, reuniting for a World Warrior Tournament with Chun-Li. It boasts a wild cast including WWE's Roman Reigns as Akuma, Cody Rhodes as Guile, Jason Momoa as Blanka, and comedian Andrew Schulz as Dan Hibiki, who steals major screen time. Critics gave it a 28% on Rotten Tomatoes for its messy plot and uneven tone, though some praise its chaotic arcade vibe; box office projections hit $25-35 million domestic against an $82 million budget.
