text:
STARSHIP
Updated 2026-11-20
461 posts (20 new today)

NEW TODAY
- Official SpaceX (Nov 13, 6:39 p.m. ET, with a video): Views of Starship in space as Starlink deploy continues. Official in-flight note during Flight 15, confirming Starlink deploy was underway after Ship 42 reached orbit. This is the first Official SpaceX Flight 15 post in this folder. It does not state a booster- or ship-catch result.
- Testers (spcxGOD, Nov 13 evening and Nov 14 early morning ET): Flight 15 lifted off at 23:48 Amsterdam time (about 5:48 p.m. ET) on Nov 13, during an FAA nationwide ground stop that testers say the FAA later blamed on a temporary telecom outage (nearly 5,000 U.S. flights canceled — context around the launch, not a flight result). Super Heavy (Booster 22) diverted to an offshore splashdown in the Gulf; this tester says SpaceX has not said why, which differs from the earlier independent-coverage note already in the Nov 14 pickup that the tower catch was called off after a guidance issue. Ship 42 reached orbit at 00:15 Amsterdam and deployed all 26 Starlink V3 satellites in a sequence testers put at about 42 minutes; they say Starlink described the payload as adding 26 terabits of capacity (in line with the earlier tester figure of about 1 terabit per second per V3). Three of those satellites carry cameras to inspect heat-shield tiles (already in earlier pickups as planned). The same tester, writing early Nov 14, said SpaceX reported that all systems were looking good right now and that the first ship-catch try was still planned for about 22:20 that evening (if that was Amsterdam time, about 4:20 p.m. ET). Tester recap, not Official, except where it lines up with the Official SpaceX in-space deploy post above. This review does not independently confirm the catch outcome.
- Testers (Eric Daugherty, Nov 14, 4:33 p.m. ET, with a video): says SpaceX caught Starship with the tower chopsticks for the first time, with the team celebrating, and that fully reusable rockets are here — noting SpaceX had previously caught only the Super Heavy booster, never the ship. This is tester coverage, not an Official SpaceX or Elon post in this review, and this note does not independently confirm the flight result. It sits alongside the later tester dual-catch claim already in the Nov 17 pickup (XFreeze, Nov 15 early morning ET) and the Official Elon Nov 15 evening line that Ship 42 brought back heat-shield data, which implies the ship returned but does not itself state a catch. This review still does not resolve that conflict with the Nov 14 pickup's then-unrecorded ship-catch outcome.
- Official Elon (Nov 6), newly appearing as the quoted post in a Nov 11 tester bookmark (Mario Nawfal): SpaceX will attempt to catch both the Super Heavy booster and Starship on the upcoming flight. If both are successful, it will mark the first time that all parts of an orbital rocket return to Earth intact. This is the critical breakthrough needed to make life multiplanetary. Official pre-flight intent for Flight 15. The dual-catch plan was already in earlier tester recaps; this is the Official wording itself. It is not a flight-result post.
- Testers (Stuart Lee, Nov 16, graphic): two possible Starship V4 stack configurations — about 142 meters for an initial V4, and about 151 meters for an extended configuration with a 70-meter upper stage. Tester graphic quoting Official Elon's Nov 15 V4 ship line already in the Nov 17 pickup (about 70-meter ship, roughly a 40 percent length increase, more than 60 percent more propellant, 9 engines including 3 added Raptor-Vacuum, higher-thrust V4 engines). The 142-meter / 151-meter stack figures are the tester's, not Official; the 142-meter initial-stack figure is close to an earlier folder tester note that put V4 at about 140 meters.
- Testers (herbertong citing TeslaLarry, Nov 16, with a video): Starbase Louisiana will turn Vermilion Parish into the next Brownsville, only bigger. The tester says Louisiana describes its spaceport as a 100 billion-dollar-plus investment with 3,000 direct jobs over 10 years, with construction starting by the end of 2027. Treat the dollar figure, jobs, and construction calendar as Testers / state figures until Official restates them. Fits alongside earlier folder notes of a 2027 groundbreaking, first launch planned for 2029, and Phase 1 due by end of 2028 (tester).
- Newly bookmarked Flight 14 recaps (Testers, Sep 28-30): several older posts about the Sep 28 flight were added to the folder today. They add color to the recap already in this pack (Ship 41 reached orbit, deployed 26 Starlink V3, then ended early and splashed down in the Pacific). Testers (Stellarixorine, travel_invest, AsFoundX, and others) say this was Starship's first time reaching orbit after 13 suborbital flights, despite an early Raptor-Vacuum shutdown on ascent, with remaining engines burned longer and a later burn completing insertion; one puts deployment at roughly 275 km and calls the 26 V3s the first operational payload. Testers (travel_invest) add that contact was made with all 26 satellites, that an early deorbit was chosen because of the engine issue, and that the ship did a landing burn and flip and reached its target in the North Pacific; they frame the engine-out, still-complete-the-mission behavior as the kind of capability a Mars-bound ship needs. Testers (AsFoundX) call it the first revenue-generating Starship mission and say Elon called the go to orbit after the engine failed — consistent with the later Oct 23 folder note that the engine-out was judged a software fault in that engine's own computer and safe to continue. Testers (TeslaZoa) post another view of the Super Heavy's controlled ocean splashdown on Flight 14, as data toward future tower-catch attempts. Testers (rajivkhaneja) claim one flight lifted about the mass of the ISS (which they say took NASA 37 launches) and that at ISS-like cost a small city in space could be built — tester claims, not Official. This review does not independently re-confirm the flight results.
- Testers (LaceyPresley, Sep 29, video and stills): Starship is not a bigger rocket — it is the first machine built to make life multiplanetary; if this works, consciousness no longer lives on one world. In a second post, the same author says the important part of the Flight 14 footage is cadence: if launches move from occasional to daily and then multiple flights per day, mass to orbit, iteration, and cost per ton all change, and industries that do not make sense today become possible. The endgame is making extraordinary launches routine. Tester framing, with media.
- Testers (herbertong quoting SawyerMerritt, Sep 29): recap of an Elon interview after Flight 14. Elon: V3 Starlink satellites are enormous, with a wingspan of a 737, and next year SpaceX expects Starship to reach a weekly or twice-weekly launch cadence. The tester then does the arithmetic: 26 satellites a flight would be about 1,350 V3s a year at a weekly cadence, or about 2,700 twice weekly; at roughly 1 terabit per second each, weekly launches alone would add about 1,350 terabits per second of capacity in a year. The cadence and 737-wingspan lines are a tester quote of Elon, not an Official Elon post in this scrape; the 1,350 / 2,700 / 1,350 terabits-per-second figures are the tester's math.
- Testers (aaronburnett quoting thelacoast, Sep 29): Starbase Louisiana permits are rolling. The quoted tester recap describes a large infrastructure permit filing at the future Starbase in Pecan Island, including an about 15.5-mile heavy-haul road (a new earthen alignment through the marsh, with an 8,110-foot bridge so Humble Canal is not filled), gulf and inland wharves / laydown yards, barge staging, and about 5.2 million cubic yards of inland canal dredging, for marine cargo that cannot use the Port of Vermilion or legal highway loads. The quoted post says this is access and construction infrastructure, not rocket towers or launch pads (those filings to come later), and that permits would likely take several months. Tester recap of a permit application, not Official SpaceX, and not a statement that the permit was approved.

RECENT (Nov 17 pickup)
- Tester dual-catch claim (XFreeze, Nov 15, early morning ET, with a video): the tester says SpaceX successfully caught both the Super Heavy booster and Starship with Mechazilla, calling it the world's first fully reusable rocket — three successful Super Heavy booster catches and the first-ever Starship catch. This is tester coverage, not an Official SpaceX or Elon post in this review, and this note does not independently confirm the flight result. It also sits alongside the earlier independent-coverage note still in the Nov 14 pickup below, which said Flight 15 lifted off at 5:47 p.m. ET on Nov 13, Ship 42 reached orbit and deployed its 26 Starlink V3 satellites, the Super Heavy tower catch was called off after a guidance issue and the booster splashed down in the Gulf of Mexico, and the ship-catch outcome was not recorded there. This review does not resolve that conflict.
- Official Elon (Nov 15 evening ET): Ship 42 brings back a motherlode of data for further improvements to the heat shield. Official reply after a tester post of Elon inspecting heat-shield tiles on Starship. The Official line implies Ship 42 returned with heat-shield data; it does not itself state a catch result.
- Official Elon (Nov 15 evening ET): Starship V4 will be about 70 meters long, roughly a 40 percent length increase, allowing more than 60 percent more propellant. Engine count goes to 9, with 3 more Raptor-Vacuum engines added, and those will be higher-thrust V4 engines. Official capability talk, not a flight log. This confirms the 9-engine V4 ship figure already in earlier tester recaps, and specifies the three added engines as Raptor-Vacuum plus higher-thrust V4 engines.

RECENT (Nov 14 pickup)
- Update (independent coverage, Nov 13): Flight 15 lifted off at 5:47 p.m. ET on Nov 13. Ship 42 reached orbit and deployed its 26 Starlink V3 satellites. The Super Heavy tower catch was called off after a guidance issue, and the booster splashed down in the Gulf of Mexico. The ship-catch outcome is not recorded here.
- Pre-flight (Nov 11–13): Testers (outerspacetoday, Nov 11; XFreeze, Nov 13) say SpaceX was targeting Friday, November 13 from Starbase, with a 75-minute window opening at 4:45 p.m. CT (5:45 to 7:00 p.m. ET). They describe the first attempt to recover both stages: the upgraded V3 Super Heavy returning to the tower about 6.5 minutes after liftoff, then the ship after about 14 orbits at roughly 275 km, more than 22 hours (XFreeze says about 22.5 hours, with the ship-catch try on November 14). Testers (LaceyPresley, Nov 11) call it the first Starship flight worth following around the globe, because every hour in orbit is data a Mars trip will need, and point to an upcoming IGW site that puts launch hazard notices and the Flight 15 path on one map. The November 13 date and dual-catch plan were already in earlier pickups; the window time, 6.5-minute booster return, 14-orbit / about 275 km / about 22-hour ship profile, and November 14 ship-catch timing are the added tester figures. They differ from earlier folder notes of about 21 hours until the orbit lines up with Starbase, and from one tester's earlier 15-to-16-orbit / about 24-hour read, so do not mix the numbers. These were written before launch.
- Pre-flight (Nov 11–13): Testers (outerspacetoday, Nov 11; XFreeze, Nov 13) say the ship was scheduled to deploy 26 operational Starlink V3 satellites. Outerspacetoday adds that three of them will carry cameras to inspect the heat shield in orbit (already in an earlier blog recap) and that Flight 15 will also test redesigned curved heat-shield tiles meant to reduce heating between tiles — that tile redesign is new here. The same tester says each of those V3 satellites is designed to add roughly 1 terabit per second of network capacity; treat that capacity figure as their description, not a SpaceX spec sheet here.
- Pre-flight (Nov 13 morning): Testers (spcxGOD, Joe Tegtmeyer) said that about 10 to 12 hours before the planned window, Ship 42 and the booster were on the pad and weather looked good, but the FAA license had not yet posted — later than testers recalled on recent flights. One argued a new ship-catch review was going down to the wire and that the attempt could slip a day if the license did not arrive that afternoon; the other noted a road closure at 11:00 a.m. local and still expected there was time for the license. These were written before launch; the flight flew that evening, per the update above.
- Pre-flight (Nov 12–13): Testers (Nic Cruz Patane, Nov 12-13) drove nearly 2,000 miles nonstop from Toronto to Brownsville, saying FSD handled the trip, to see Flight 15 in person for the first time. That is a travel note around the flight, not a flight result and not Official.

RECENT (Nov 11 pickup)
- Official Elon (Sep 30) was newly bookmarked: Starship will expand the aperture of physics research by placing much larger telescopes in orbit and giant ones on the Moon. Testers already recapped this quote in an earlier pickup.
- Testers recap a new SpaceX blog about Starship Flight 15, planned for November 13. SpaceX describes it as a major step toward full reusability: bringing the upper stage back to the launch site for a tower catch at Starbase. Testers say the blog itself gives the November 13 date; this review did not open the blog, so the date is planned, not confirmed here.
- Per the same blog recap, Flight 15 starts on a passively safe suborbital path so ascent problems send the ship into a cleared area of the Indian Ocean. Controllers then give a go or no-go for orbit; a go means a single sea-level Raptor insertion burn. On orbit the ship deploys Starlink V3 satellites, three of them modified to image the heat shield, then coasts about 21 hours until its orbit lines up with Starbase. During that coast they run conservative checks on the engines, power, communications, computers, sensors, tanks, and attitude control. Early-end splashdowns are reserved around Hawaii and off Chile. Return and catch happen only if the vehicle meets internally developed, FAA-approved conditions.
- If cleared, the ship does a single-Raptor-3 deorbit burn and reenters over a set point in the Pacific thousands of kilometers uprange from Starbase. Four flaps steer it, including turns over sparsely populated parts of northern Mexico and southern Texas. It approaches from the west, weaves around major Rio Grande Valley cities, passes north of South Padre Island into the Gulf of America, then turns south toward Starbase. Nearby residents may hear one or more sonic booms, which SpaceX describes as a brief thunder-like sound that does not present a health risk. Over the pad the ship bellyflops toward the tower, lights three sea-level Raptors, flips vertical, then steps down to two engines and then one for a near hover. The arms catch it on two fittings just below the forward flaps. Controllers can tumble the ship so it breaks up before reaching land, or send it into the Gulf if the vehicle or tower has a problem after reentry. SpaceX calls recovering an entire orbital launch system the holy grail of rocketry, because full and rapid reuse opens an airplane-like cadence.
- Another tester visualizes five contingency landing options SpaceX outlined if the vehicle or tower is not ready for a safe return: the Indian Ocean after ascent if the insertion burn is skipped; the Pacific north of Hawaii early after reaching orbit; the eastern Pacific far off Chile mid-mission; the Gulf offshore if the catch is called off before final approach; and the Pacific north of Hawaii again if the planned deorbit burn is skipped. The aim is to bring Starship home, with continuous health checks deciding when to proceed.
- Testers say Elon revealed that Raptor 4 delivers 500 tons of thrust, twice Raptor 3, and that it will replace only the 20 outer-ring engines on the current booster. They put V3 booster thrust at 7,590 tons and V4 at 12,990 tons, about a 70 percent increase. They say the V4 ship will have 9 engines and that it is still unclear whether those will be Raptor 4s. This is their recap of remarks they attribute to Elon, not a SpaceX spec sheet here, and it differs from earlier folder notes that put V4 around 300 tons per engine.

RECENT (Nov 8 pickup)
- A tester shares Elliot's concept render of a finished Gigabay at Starbase, with ships and boosters under one roof. It shows the production scale Starship is heading toward, not a completed building.
- Testers report that SpaceX's VP of Launch, Kiko Dontchev, told the UP Summit the company is targeting Friday, November 13 for Starship Flight 15. That is a third-party report of his remarks, not a SpaceX or FAA announcement, and the date is not confirmed here.
- The same tester round describes Flight 15 as the first try at catching both the Super Heavy booster and Ship 42 on one mission. One tester adds a roughly 24-hour, 15-to-16-orbit ship profile; treat that as their read, not an official timeline.
- Another tester recap says the hardware is ready after last month's static fires, the remaining gate is an FAA launch license expected to cover bringing both stages back to the pad, and a ship catch would fly over land instead of open ocean. Do not treat the date as locked or the license as issued. If both catches work, testers frame it as the first time an entire orbital-class rocket is recovered for rapid reuse. Next vehicle testing is described as lined up for December.

RECENT (Nov 5 pickup)
- Raptor 3 is reliably about 230 tons of thrust today. A tester reads Elon's number as presently, with room to climb toward 250 to 260 tons once reliability work is done, the way Merlin improved. Raptor 4 is framed as a re-engineered engine about two years out.
- Elon: every 2 years, try to get thousands of ships to Mars.

RECENT (Nov 2)
- Elon says Starship will expand physics research by putting much larger telescopes in orbit and giant ones on the Moon. Bigger telescopes collect more light, and Starship can put much larger ones in orbit without folding them like origami, so the rocket stops capping the size of the experiment.

RECENT (Nov 1 pickup)
- Ship 42 finished its static fires: a full six-engine burn plus a single Raptor firing to simulate the deorbit burn. Ship 42, Booster 22 and the tower are described as ready for Flight 15's first try at catching both, waiting on the FAA.
- Tester reports now point to about Nov 12 for Flight 15 and Dec 10 for a possible first Florida Starship launch carrying Starlink. SpaceX hasn't announced dates.
- If both catches work, Flight 15 would be the first rocket where nothing is thrown away but propellant. One tester estimates roughly 57 to 115 dollars per kg to low Earth orbit with 30 Starlink V3 satellites aboard (their estimate).
- Elon describes a Starfactory built for 100 Starships a year, about one every three days. SpaceX's Starship page says it's sized for up to 1,000 a year, a design figure. Mars-bound ships refill in orbit from tanker Starships, and each holds 1,600 t of propellant.
- Louisiana is fast-tracking the 36-mile Lafayette Xpressway to reach closer to the Starship site near Pecan Island.
- South Padre Island shops say launches roughly triple a slow morning's business.

RECENT (Oct 29 pickup)
- Booster 22 for Flight 15 finished its full 33-engine static fire on Oct 25, the last big ground test before the flight that tries to catch both booster and ship. Flight 15 is penciled in for no earlier than Nov 8 on a planning slide; SpaceX hasn't set a date.
- First Florida Starship plan, per tester reports: booster caught by the tower at Kennedy pad 39A, ship flies about six orbits (8 to 9 hours) and gets caught back at Starbase. SpaceX's VP of Launch says the 39A Starship facilities are effectively complete.
- Elon: 10,000 Starship launches a year from Starbase Louisiana alone.
- Elon: Starship is 2 to 3 years from a launch every hour. Fueling is already fast; the hard part is turning the vehicle and pad around.
- Flight 14 reached orbit with 26 Starlink V3 satellites, then splashed down in the Pacific.
- Heat shields: Dragon uses one ablative shield for single reentries; Starship uses individual tiles for fast full reuse.

BLUF: The incoming Congress must investigate whether Donald Trump, senior members of his administration, Elon Musk, and Trump's family and business associates have knowingly used American government authority, military assistance, sanctions policy, and critical defense technology to benefit Vladimir Putin's war against Ukraine while pursuing personal grievances and financial interests connected to restoring economic relations with Russia.

The investigation must begin with Trump's first impeachment, examine his documented hostility toward Ukraine and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and establish whether decisions benefiting Russia have been influenced by personal resentment, commercial interests, or both.

To the Members of the 120th United States Congress:

The United States has a president who has repeatedly attacked the elected leader of a sovereign European democracy fighting for its survival, while his administration has delayed military assistance, restricted critical defensive capabilities, and relieved economic pressure on the country invading it.

At the same time, Trump has repeatedly praised, flattered, and publicly embraced Vladimir Putin, the architect of Russia's invasion and a man wanted by the International Criminal Court for war crimes involving the unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children.

This is the same Putin whose government the United Nations has determined committed war crimes and crimes against humanity through the systematic destruction of Ukraine's civilian energy infrastructure and the deliberate hunting of Ukrainian civilians with FPV drones in Kherson and Kharkiv. 

UN investigators have already documented Russian drone operators deliberately tracking and killing unarmed civilians, including pedestrians, cyclists, motorists, and emergency responders, while Russia's attacks on energy infrastructure were carried out pursuant to a Russian state policy intended to deprive Ukrainians of essential services to inflict suffering and trigger a humanitarian crisis. 

Trump calls Ukraine's elected president a “dictator without elections” while publicly celebrating his friendship with a true dictator responsible for invading Ukraine, occupying its territory, and directing the war against its civilian population. The contrast between Trump's treatment of Zelenskyy and his treatment of Putin is documented, longstanding, and central to understanding why Congress must investigate the personal and political interests influencing American policy toward Russia and Ukraine.

TRUMP'S HOSTILITY TOWARD UKRAINE DID NOT BEGIN IN 2025

The historical record is particularly troubling.

In November 2019, The Washington Post published an extensive investigation into Trump's longstanding hostility toward Ukraine. Senior administration officials described a president who rejected repeated efforts by his national security advisers to explain why supporting Ukraine was essential to American interests.

Trump embraced accusations that Ukraine had interfered against him in the 2016 election, questioned Ukraine's legitimacy as an independent country, and resisted assistance because he did not want to antagonize Russia.

One former senior White House official described Trump's attitude plainly: “He just hated Ukraine.”

This hostility preceded Zelenskyy's election and Trump's first impeachment. What followed transformed Ukraine and Zelenskyy into central figures in Trump's personal political grievances.

In July 2019, Trump pressured newly elected President Zelenskyy to announce investigations that would benefit Trump's reelection campaign while his administration withheld congressionally approved military assistance.

Trump was impeached. The Government Accountability Office subsequently determined that withholding the assistance violated federal law.

The significance of that episode cannot be overstated. Trump had already demonstrated his willingness to subordinate Ukraine's security needs to his personal political interests.

But the relationship did not end with impeachment.

In April 2022, when The Washington Post asked Trump about Ukraine following Russia's full-scale invasion, Trump immediately returned to his impeachment.

He explained that he respected Zelenskyy because the Ukrainian president had publicly defended him during the scandal.

Think about what that reveals.

When asked about a country fighting for its survival against Russia, Trump evaluated its president through the lens of what Zelenskyy had done for Donald Trump.

The relationship was not being described in terms of American national security, Ukrainian sovereignty, or Russian aggression. Trump brought it back to his impeachment and Zelenskyy's personal loyalty.

That pattern became unmistakable when Trump returned to the White House and it provides a clear motive for his hatred of Zelensky and his policies directed at harming  Ukraine and its population.

FROM PERSONAL HOSTILITY TO GOVERNMENT ACTION

In February 2025, Trump publicly accused Ukraine of responsibility for Russia's invasion and called Zelenskyy a “dictator without elections.”

The accusation echoed Kremlin rhetoric against the elected president of the country Russia had invaded.

On February 28, Trump and Vice President JD Vance publicly berated Zelenskyy in the Oval Office. Trump accused him of ingratitude and warned that he was gambling with World War III.

Three days later, Trump ordered American military assistance to Ukraine suspended.

His administration also suspended intelligence sharing.

The consequences were immediate. Ukraine was fighting an invading army while the president of the United States used military assistance and intelligence cooperation to pressure its elected leader following a public confrontation.

This was not merely an argument between two presidents. Trump's personal confrontation was followed by executive decisions affecting Ukraine's military capabilities.

Congress must investigate whether the operational consequences were considered and whether Trump's relationship with Zelenskyy improperly influenced those decisions.

The pattern continued into 2026.

On October 10, following an agreement with Putin involving Russian diesel supplies, Trump publicly called for Ukraine to replace Zelenskyy.

He blamed Zelenskyy for high American diesel prices and criticized Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil infrastructure, even as Russia continued destroying Ukraine's energy infrastructure.

On October 19, Trump again attacked Zelenskyy's leadership, saying it was time for somebody else to negotiate on Ukraine's behalf.

Trump was no longer merely criticizing Zelenskyy's negotiating position. He was openly calling for the replacement of Ukraine's elected president while pursuing economic agreements with the aggressor invading his country.

That is a documented sequence of public hostility, coercive policy decisions, and demands for leadership change.

Congress must determine whether Trump's longstanding grievances have influenced his use of presidential authority against Ukraine.

TRUMP IS PRESSURING UKRAINE TO ACCEPT RUSSIA'S MAXIMALIST DEMANDS

Trump's treatment of Zelenskyy extends well beyond personal hostility. His administration has repeatedly pressured Ukraine to accept peace terms that reward Russian aggression, surrender Ukrainian sovereignty, and grant Putin territorial victories his military has failed to achieve.

In September 2022, Putin illegally declared the annexation of Ukraine's Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson oblasts, including enormous areas his military had never conquered and does not control today. On October 12, 2022, the United Nations General Assembly overwhelmingly rejected these annexations, voting 143–5 to declare them invalid under international law.

This followed Russia's February 2014 invasion and military occupation of Ukraine's Crimean Peninsula, which Putin illegally annexed in March 2014. The United Nations General Assembly also rejected that annexation, reaffirming Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders.

The United Nations has rejected every one of Putin's five territorial annexations. None has legal standing under international law, yet Trump continues pressuring Ukraine to surrender territory Russia has illegally claimed, including territory its military has never conquered.

Russia also continues demanding that Ukraine withdraw its military forces, abandon its NATO aspirations, accept restrictions on the size and capabilities of its armed forces, and prohibit foreign troops and military installations on Ukrainian territory.

In effect, these demands gut one of the most critical rights and responsibilities of any sovereign democracy: the ability to defend itself against foreign aggression. They open the door for Russia to completely subvert and control Ukraine.

Rather than consistently rejecting these demands, Trump's administration has repeatedly incorporated key Russian objectives into American peace proposals and pressured Ukraine to accept them.

In November 2025, the Trump administration advanced a 28-point peace proposal requiring Ukraine to surrender the remaining Ukrainian-controlled territory in Donetsk, accept a permanent prohibition on NATO membership, and reduce its armed forces to a maximum of 600,000 personnel.

The plan also proposed recognizing Crimea, Donetsk, and Luhansk as effectively Russian, gradually lifting sanctions against Moscow, inviting Russia back into the G8, and establishing American-Russian economic cooperation involving energy, natural resources, infrastructure, and other commercial opportunities.

Even the language of the American proposal bore the fingerprints of Russian authorship. An analysis published by The Guardian identified unusual grammatical constructions and Russianisms in the English text, suggesting that portions had been written originally in Russian and translated directly into English.

That suspicion was subsequently reinforced by investigative reporting. Reuters confirmed, citing three sources familiar with the negotiations, that the American 28-point proposal drew directly from a Russian-authored document submitted to the Trump administration in October 2025. The Insider separately identified provisions that appeared almost word for word in an earlier Russian proposal prepared by Kirill Dmitriev, Putin's special envoy and head of Russia's sovereign wealth fund.

The significance is extraordinary. The Trump administration presented Ukraine with an American peace proposal containing demands and language originating with the very government that invaded Ukraine, then Trump publicly demanded that Ukraine accept the proposal within a week.

In March 2026, Zelenskyy told Reuters that the United States had conditioned its offer of security guarantees on Ukraine withdrawing from Donbas, including territory Russia had never captured. That would surrender Ukraine's heavily fortified defensive positions, including the cities and military infrastructure protecting the remaining Ukrainian-controlled areas of Donetsk Oblast.

In November 2026, Trump's negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner again raised the possibility of Ukraine abandoning Donbas, this time suggesting NATO membership in exchange for territorial concessions.

Meanwhile, Putin has continued insisting on Russian control over all four illegally annexed Ukrainian regions, including territories Russian forces have never occupied. His negotiators have also revived demands that NATO withdraw its military infrastructure from countries that joined after 1997, restrict military assistance to Ukraine, and accept Russian constraints on Europe's security arrangements.

The Trump administration has even agreed to broaden negotiations beyond ending Russia's invasion to discussing Europe's security architecture, a longstanding Kremlin objective.

These are extreme, disproportionate, and fundamentally unfair demands that directly undermine longstanding U.S. national security interests, contradict NATO's core security commitments, threaten the security of America's European allies, and reward Russian aggression at the expense of Ukraine's sovereignty and Europe's security.

Congress must investigate why American peace proposals have repeatedly incorporated central Russian demands, who authorized those concessions, what commitments were made during negotiations with Moscow, and whether personal or financial interests influenced the administration's willingness to pressure Ukraine into accepting them.

The investigation must also examine whether Trump's documented hostility toward Zelenskyy influenced his willingness to demand Ukrainian concessions while offering Putin sanctions relief, economic opportunities, and recognition of Russian territorial gains.

The question Congress must answer is why the president of the United States has repeatedly demanded that Ukraine sacrifice its territory, security, and sovereign rights to satisfy a Russian president whose invasion and territorial ambitions created the war in the first place.

INVESTIGATE HEGSETH AND COLBY

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Under Secretary Elbridge Colby must be central subjects of this investigation.

Congress has already demanded explanations for delays involving $400 million in congressionally approved security assistance. Ukrainian officials have reported delays in securing critical Patriot and NASAMS air-defense missiles while Russia continues its missile and drone attacks.

On November 17, Colby publicly criticized Ukraine's long-range strikes on Russian infrastructure, including Wildberries facilities, portraying those attacks as attempts to inflict pain on Russian civilians which, in laymen's terms, equates to hurting their feeling.

Independent investigations have documented Wildberries and Ozon being used to supply Russian forces with FPV drones, electronic warfare equipment, encrypted communications, drone munition-release kits, ballistic armor, uniforms, and other military equipment.

The Kerch Bridge was another critical Russian military supply artery, moving equipment and supplies through occupied Crimea to sustain Russia's invading forces in southern Ukraine.

Yet American officials criticized Ukraine's attacks on Russian military-supporting infrastructure while Russia continued systematically destroying infrastructure essential to civilian life in Ukraine.

Congress must establish who authorized the military assistance delays, what military and intelligence assessments officials received, and whether those decisions were influenced by Trump's demands or personal hostility toward Zelenskyy.

INVESTIGATE ELON MUSK AND SPACEX

Restrictions on Ukraine's Starlink and Starshield capabilities disrupted military communications and drone operations, including systems supporting Ukraine's defense against Russian aerial attacks.

Congressional inquiries are already underway. Senators have demanded that Elon Musk and SpaceX preserve communications, technical records, and documentation concerning those restrictions.

The investigation must establish whether Musk, Trump, Hegseth, or other officials authorized or influenced the disruptions, what warnings they received, and whether they understood the consequences for Ukrainian military operations and civilian protection.

The American people deserve to know who controlled those restrictions and whether a private technology company or American government officials used critical defense capabilities to exert political pressure on Ukraine during an active war.

FOLLOW THE MONEY

The financial dimension cannot be separated from the national security investigation.

Trump and his family have received substantial revenue from cryptocurrency ventures, including World Liberty Financial, which also involves business interests associated with the Witkoff family.

Jared Kushner maintains major foreign investment relationships while participating in American diplomatic negotiations.

Meanwhile, American negotiations with Russia have expanded into discussions involving Russian energy assets, sanctions relief, investment opportunities, and economic normalization.

On October 16, Trump issued waivers suspending significant sanctions and tariff provisions of the Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act.

These decisions occurred while Russia continued its invasion and its attacks on Ukrainian civilian infrastructure.

The New York Times has reported on proposed multibillion-dollar Russian energy transactions involving investors with business connections to Trump's principal negotiators, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.

Congress must trace the financial relationships between the people negotiating with Russia, the investors pursuing Russian commercial opportunities, and the administration's decisions concerning sanctions, energy purchases, and Ukraine's military capabilities.

This investigation must identify profits already received, prospective financial interests, and any communications connecting private commercial opportunities to official American policy.

The question is whether the normalization of relations with Putin's Russia is being pursued partly to advance private economic interests, even as Russia continues killing Ukrainians and attempting to destroy their country's independence.

THE UNITED NATIONS HAS ALREADY DOCUMENTED RUSSIA'S CRIMES

In May 2025, the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry concluded that Russian forces committed war crimes and crimes against humanity by deliberately hunting Ukrainian civilians with drones in Kherson.

In October 2026, the Commission determined that Russia's systematic attacks against Ukraine's energy infrastructure constituted war crimes and crimes against humanity.

The investigators established that these attacks were deliberate and carried out pursuant to Russian state policy intended to deprive Ukrainian civilians of electricity and other essential services and cause suffering.

The Russian government is not merely conducting military operations that incidentally harm civilians. Independent investigators have established that inflicting suffering on civilians is part of its policy.

Trump, Hegseth, Colby, and other senior American officials have had access to these findings. Congress must investigate what they knew, when they knew it, and whether they knowingly made decisions that helped sustain Russia's aggression despite that knowledge.

The UN has established the crimes. Russia's Security Council veto obstructs enforcement, but it does not absolve the United States of responsibility for its own foreign policy decisions.

THE CENTRAL INVESTIGATIVE FINDING

The evidence establishes a pattern that Congress cannot responsibly examine as a series of isolated incidents.

Trump's hostility toward Ukraine was documented during his first administration. His first impeachment arose from his attempt to use Ukraine's security assistance for personal political advantage.

After returning to office, he publicly attacked Zelenskyy's legitimacy, confronted him in the Oval Office, suspended military assistance and intelligence sharing, pressured Ukraine over strikes against Russian military-supporting infrastructure, and eventually called for Zelenskyy's replacement.

His administration has delayed additional military assistance, imposed restrictions affecting critical defensive capabilities, and waived sanctions while negotiating commercial arrangements with Russia.

At the same time, Trump's family and business associates have received substantial revenue through foreign business relationships, and investors connected to his principal diplomatic representatives have pursued opportunities involving Russian energy assets.

The cumulative record supports an investigation into whether American officials knowingly made decisions that benefited Putin's war effort, whether those decisions were driven partly by Trump's personal grievances against Zelenskyy, and whether financial interests influenced the administration's willingness to restore economic relations with Russia.

CONGRESS MUST INVESTIGATE

The incoming Congress must conduct a comprehensive investigation using its subpoena, oversight, and appropriations authority.

The investigation must obtain White House communications, Pentagon orders, intelligence assessments, military assistance records, SpaceX technical records, sanctions memoranda, diplomatic correspondence, financial disclosures, and communications involving Russian officials and private investors.

Trump's decision-making, Hegseth's military assistance restrictions, Colby's public and internal policy recommendations, Musk's control over satellite services, and the commercial interests of Kushner, Witkoff, and their associates must all be examined.

The records must establish who made the decisions, who benefited, what warnings were received, and whether personal or financial interests improperly influenced American policy.

THE BOTTOM LINE

The same president who was impeached for withholding military assistance from Ukraine to pursue a personal political objective has again used American government authority to pressure Ukraine while publicly attacking the legitimacy of its elected president.

His administration has made decisions that benefited Russia's strategic position, while his family and associates maintain lucrative international business relationships and pursue opportunities associated with renewed economic relations with Moscow.

Meanwhile, Putin continues killing Ukrainian civilians, occupying Ukrainian territory, destroying essential infrastructure, and attempting to subordinate a sovereign European democracy.

The United Nations has documented Russia's war crimes and crimes against humanity.

Congress must determine whether the president's personal hostility toward Zelenskyy, his relationship with Putin, and the private financial interests surrounding his administration have influenced decisions that materially assisted Russia's aggression.

The evidence is sufficient to demand an investigation. The American people deserve the complete record.

COUNTRY BEFORE PARTY OR PERSON.

text:
EU Commission Pulled Payroll Offline After an ARTEX AI Attack

On Thursday, November 19, the European Commission, the executive branch of the 27-nation European Union, confirmed it was hit by what its spokesman called an "AI-generated cyber campaign" using a publicly available tool.

The Commission first spotted it October 22 and confirmed it was an attack October 26. The public heard about it four weeks later.

THE TOOL WAS ARTEX

The FBI warned about ARTEX in its November 13 alert. It's an open-source AI hacking framework, and CERT-EU, the cyber response team for EU institutions, caught the attackers using it.

ARTEX takes an order in plain English, splits it into tasks, and hands them to AI agents that scan, break in, and report back. It has no AI brain of its own. The operator plugs one in and pays the AI company by the token, the chunks of text a model reads and bills by.

The FBI lists the models it hooks into: Claude from Anthropic ($ANT), GPT from OpenAI, Grok from xAI, which SpaceX ($SPCX) now owns, and three Chinese models, DeepSeek, GLM and Kimi.

In the copies attackers actually run, Chinese models lead and DeepSeek's cheap Flash models dominate. The FBI gives the reasons: they're capable, they cost little, and they show no visible guardrails once the job is framed as security testing.

The Commission's spokesman for digital, Thomas Regnier, didn't name the tool or the attacker. He said, "we can confirm that this was done with AI tools."

THE AI HACKING KITS ANYONE CAN DOWNLOAD

ARTEX is one of several. Google ($GOOGL) says its threat team and its Mandiant unit have caught hackers using a shelf of free, open-source AI attack kits that do the same job.

Open-source means the code is posted in public, usually on GitHub, where anyone can copy it. Every kit below was published for "authorized" security testing, and each one carries a warning against using it on anybody else's systems.

Google says these kits hunt for easy holes, have the AI write a fresh one-time attack file on the spot, and switch tactics in real time based on what works.

CAIRN CAME OUT OF A HACKING CONTEST

CAIRN is posted on GitHub under the name oritera and has about 5,400 stars. Stars are GitHub's bookmark button, a rough count of how many people follow a project. The first public version came out May 3, 2026.

Its design is laid out in a September 2026 paper by researchers at China's Nankai University, Tsinghua University and the Yunding security lab of Tencent ($TCEHY), the Chinese tech giant. The paper says a system built on CAIRN was the only team to solve every challenge in Tencent Cloud's second AI hacking contest.

CAIRN sends a team of AI agents from a single starting point, like one target address, toward a goal. The agents trade notes on a shared board as they go, and none has a fixed job.

The paper's authors say they ran it only in sealed-off lab setups. Hackers took it into the real world anyway.

On October 30, Google said its Mandiant responders found attackers using CAIRN inside break-ins they were called in to clean up. By November 16, Google said CAIRN had been used in attacks on targets including U.S. aerospace companies.

Google hasn't named the attackers or the companies, or said what was taken.

PENTAGI GOT PAST SCANNING

PentAGI is the most popular kit on the shelf, with about 35,000 GitHub stars. VXControl, a security company based in Dubai, builds it and sells a paid version alongside the free one.

You describe a target and a goal in plain language. A team of AI agents plans the job, runs more than 20 standard hacking tools inside a sealed-off test box, and writes up a report.

The tools include nmap, which maps the open doors on a network, and Metasploit, a library of ready-made break-ins. Google says the design lets beginners run complex campaigns.

Most of the PentAGI activity Google saw never got past mapping and scanning. Google says some operations went further, breaking into multiple organizations and planting ways to get back in later.

One crew built its own attack platform on top of the free version. From late August to early October, Google tracked it scanning and probing organizations across Asia, including big telecom companies and firms that build IT systems for others.

Another operator ran PentAGI through proxy services, which hide where the traffic really comes from, to go after aerospace companies.

On November 13, Talos, the threat team at Cisco ($CSCO), counted more than 700 PentAGI dashboards reachable on the open internet. Talos didn't say how many of those belong to criminals rather than paid testers.

CYBERSTRIKEAI AND THE FIREWALL BREAK-INS

CyberStrikeAI was built by a Chinese developer who goes by Ed1s0nZ on GitHub. The developer first posted it on November 8, 2025, and it now has about 8,900 stars.

It wires paid and free AI models into more than 100 hacking tools and ready-made attack recipes, all run from one control server. Google has seen hackers testing it.

The threat-tracking firm Team Cymru says the developer has ties to Chinese state hacking. On December 19, 2025, Ed1s0nZ submitted CyberStrikeAI to a program run by Knownsec, a Chinese security company that Team Cymru says works for China's spy agency, the Ministry of State Security, and its military.

On January 5, 2026, the developer listed an award from CNNVD, China's state vulnerability database. Researchers say that program gathers software holes for the Chinese government before they go public.

The award later disappeared from the profile. Team Cymru reads that as an effort to hide the tie.

Now the damage. Amazon ($AMZN) says a Russian-speaking hacker out for money broke into more than 600 FortiGate firewalls in over 55 countries from January 11 to February 18, 2026.

FortiGate firewalls are the network gatekeepers sold by Fortinet ($FTNT). Amazon says no software flaw was used. The hacker walked in through admin pages left open to the internet and weak passwords with no second login check.

Inside some victims, the hacker took over the company's Windows network, pulled whole password databases and went after the backup systems. Amazon says that's a common lead-up to ransomware.

Amazon traced the scanning to one server. Team Cymru found CyberStrikeAI running on that same server, talking to the targeted firewalls, as late as January 30.

Amazon's report only says the hacker leaned on commercial AI services and never names CyberStrikeAI. What's proven is the kit sat on the attack server, not that it did each of the 600 break-ins.

Team Cymru counted 21 servers running CyberStrikeAI between January 20 and February 26, most of them in China, Singapore and Hong Kong.

HEXSTRIKE AI AND THE CITRIX HOLES

HexStrike AI is owned by OTT Cybersecurity LLC, a security firm with a branch in Dubai, and written by a developer who goes by m0x4m4. It has about 13,800 GitHub stars.

It lets an AI assistant like Claude or ChatGPT run more than 150 hacking tools directly, split among a dozen specialized agents. It connects through MCP, short for Model Context Protocol, a standard plug that lets AI assistants operate other software.

On August 26, 2025, Citrix disclosed three holes in NetScaler, the boxes companies use to route traffic and let staff log in from outside. One hole was already being used to plant webshells, hidden back doors on the device.

Check Point ($CHKP), an Israeli cybersecurity company, says criminals started talking about turning HexStrike loose almost as soon as it came out. Within 12 hours of the Citrix disclosure, it saw dark-web chatter about using HexStrike to find and break into NetScaler boxes.

Some posters offered the vulnerable NetScaler boxes they'd found for sale. They claimed HexStrike cut the work from days to under 10 minutes.

That was the hackers talking. Check Point said at the time it had no proof yet that HexStrike was actually used in the break-ins.

Google's November 16 report puts HexStrike at the testing stage. Its October 30 report did list HexStrike among the kits its Mandiant responders found in real break-ins, but Google hasn't named a single HexStrike victim.

WHAT'S COMING NEXT

Google has also caught hackers trying out Agent Zero, an open-source AI assistant that runs on its own virtual computer, writes and runs its own code, and builds new tools as it goes. Developer Jan Tomášek started it in March 2024, and it has about 20,000 GitHub stars.

Agent Zero's own pitch is AI "free from restrictions." It wasn't built for hacking. An agent that can do anything can be pointed at anybody.

Google also saw hackers using ZeroHollow, an online AI service that routes requests to different AI models, to write exploits. An exploit is the code that breaks in through one specific hole.

Google hasn't tied either one to a named victim. It did find evidence that one China-linked group was building its own automated attack kit, likely for spying.

You don't even need a kit. In September 2025, Anthropic says a Chinese state-backed group tricked its coding assistant, Claude Code, into working as attack agents against about 30 targets, and broke into a handful. Anthropic says the AI did 80% to 90% of the work, with humans stepping in at a few key decisions.

Anthropic also admitted Claude "frequently overstated findings and occasionally fabricated data." The AI hackers lie to their own bosses too.

WHAT WENT DOWN

The Commission took several systems offline as a precaution. One was Sysper, the HR system staff use for payslips, leave requests and timesheets. Another was MyPMO, which handles medical reimbursements.

The disruption lasted more than 10 days. Sysper came back this week, then crashed again Wednesday. Translation services were hit Tuesday.

The Commission's top crisis body, the Corporate Management Board, met on it this month. Henna Virkkunen, the EU's tech commissioner, briefed the other commissioners Wednesday.

Regnier said investigators have found no evidence of a breach affecting Commission staff as a whole, and he wasn't aware of any ransom demand. Asked why it took this long to say anything: "There was no hiding whatsoever."

Those HR systems hold names, pay grades, home addresses and contact details. That's a targeting list for anyone who wants to work on individual EU officials.

This is the Commission's third disclosed cyber incident this year. The first two hit through Ivanti software in January and its cloud setup in March.

CERT-EU SAW IT COMING

On November 5, CERT-EU posted a public warning: it had seen AI-driven attacks against the EU bodies it protects, and they "highly likely involved the use of ARTEX."

It also flagged a design problem. ARTEX relies on its own rules and the AI model to stay inside the target list and avoid damage. In CERT-EU's words, "there is no hard technical enforcement."

HUNDREDS TARGETED, A FEW GOT IN

Microsoft ($MSFT) wrote that Storm-0940, a China state-aligned hacking group, used ARTEX "to automate attacks targeting hundreds of organizations globally."

Targeting isn't the same as getting in. Microsoft says several of those attacks reached privileged access, which is admin-level control, and that a successful sign-in "does not necessarily indicate that customer data was accessed."

IT'S NOT A PHONE APP

The scary version going around says anyone with an iPhone can now launch these attacks. That traces back to one security executive.

Christopher Walcutt, the chief information security officer at the cyber firm DirectDefense, said, "You can run it on your phone and connect it to other pieces of infrastructure that you set up."

The phone is the remote control. ARTEX runs as a web dashboard on a server somebody has to set up, and it needs an AI model plugged in, which costs money to run.

How much? CrowdStrike ($CRWD) says one China-linked espionage group's planning agents ran through about 1.4 billion tokens in a single break-in.

South Korea's first arrest for AI-driven mass hacking wasn't a kid with an iPhone either. Seoul police arrested a 32-year-old ringleader on October 15. He had worked at a cybersecurity company from 2019 to 2022 as a penetration tester, someone paid to break into systems with permission.

Police say his crew hit more than 90 South Korean organizations, mostly with ARTEX, and stole 8.2 million records. They demanded about $270,000 in ransom from 38 victims.

WHO PAYS FOR THE AI

Often, somebody else.

Amazon ran fake AI services as bait from October 3 to November 5. ARTEX agents connected to them thinking they were real AI models, and sent along their own campaign memory.

The biggest campaign Amazon caught was hunting AI keys. Those are the passwords that let software bill a company's AI account. The agents pulled them out of exposed AI tools like LiteLLM, Dify and Langflow.

Then they fed the stolen keys back into ARTEX, so the victims paid for the AI hunting for more victims.

In one campaign, the operators told the agents to work through a fixed list of countries, go after businesses before hobby projects, and grade every stolen key by what it can reach.

The red lines Amazon found in the prompts: leave mainland China alone, and stay off government domains.

Amazon says it has moderate confidence these were separate Chinese-linked groups, based on Chinese-language prompts, China time-zone settings and the targets they picked.

A second campaign used real-time deepfake video to try to pass the selfie checks at two crypto exchanges. The check company's server rejected every attempt the agents logged.

Amazon is careful here. It saw the agents' own records, not the break-ins, and says it can't verify what they claim they pulled off.

THE HACKERS GOT HACKED

After the original ARTEX was pulled from GitHub on October 8, copies spread. One copy on GitHub collected about 2,400 stars and over 600 forks.

That copy changed one line so it pulled a doctored install package from Docker Hub, a public library of ready-to-run software. The package was downloaded 9,000 times.

It carried a hidden back door. Type a secret marker into the login page's captcha box, and the server runs your command with full control, no password needed.

Between November 2 and 4, researchers found 62 ARTEX dashboards running the doctored build: 26 in the U.S., 17 in Hong Kong and 7 in China. Docker pulled the packages, but 637 GitHub projects still pointed to them.

The researcher who found it, who goes by Badbyte, said a hijacked ARTEX dashboard "holds its targets' unpatched findings, live credentials, captured sessions and network position."

So whoever planted the back door could read other hackers' loot, and quietly change what their agents do next.

THE COUNT KEEPS CLIMBING

CrowdStrike says a China-linked espionage group it calls VAPOR PANDA used one ARTEX controller against more than 200 organizations in at least 14 countries, over 11 days starting October 17.

The targets included foreign ministries, one European country's presidency and prime minister's office, and 19 U.S. pharmaceutical, chip, defense, nuclear and finance outfits. Telecom companies in the U.S., Belgium and the Philippines were hit too.

CrowdStrike's own report confirms follow-on hacking at nine of them, plus password-guessing attacks on at least 12 more.

The 140 compromised number going around comes from CrowdStrike saying about 70% of targets were confirmed hacked or showed moderate-confidence signs of it. Its published report confirms nine.

One operator, typing in Chinese, told the agents to find Windows machines without "Falcon," CrowdStrike's own security software, so they'd hit the unguarded ones first.

Adam Meyers, who runs CrowdStrike's adversary tracking, said a human hacker at a keyboard used to run up to about 40 commands an hour. With ARTEX, his team has seen more than 1,500.

His team counted about 45 AI-agent attacks in September and 126 in October.

India's cyber agency, CERT-In, warned November 4 about a group it calls Crafty Falcon hitting Indian lenders, fintechs and crypto exchanges with ARTEX and similar tools. The group sends test payments of one rupee before moving big money through the victims' own payment systems.

CERT-In didn't say who is behind Crafty Falcon.

Counts of ARTEX dashboards left open on the internet run from about 1,465 (Censys) to more than 1,800 (Check Point).

MEANWHILE IN WASHINGTON

The House Homeland Security Committee held its yearly threats hearing on November 18, five days after the FBI's ARTEX alert.

Rep. James Walkinshaw (D-Va.), pointing to the surge in AI-driven hacking, asked Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin (R) whether pushing more than 1,000 people out of CISA was a mistake.

CISA, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, defends federal civilian networks and is the government's main cyber contact for private companies.

Mullin said, "I wasn't there when that was made," and couldn't give a current head count. He said CISA "has not missed a mission" and is hiring new experts.

Mullin told Congress in June the agency had about 2,200 people. Walkinshaw says the administration inherited roughly 3,400.

NOTHING NEW, JUST FASTER

Amazon's report puts it plainly: "None of the techniques in these campaigns were new."

The agents won on default passwords, keys left in code, unprotected admin pages and unpatched software. ARTEX just checks all of it, around the clock, for whoever is paying the AI bill.

Why Did the   Intel Community Leak the Dubious Jensen Huang Spy Story Instead of Warning   Him
David Sacks Is Right: The Jensen Huang Leak   Was a Veto on the President's Advisers
Alexander Muse

Nov         20

📷

📷

📷

📷

📷

READ           IN APP📷
📷

Jensen   Huang ran Nvidia for 33 years and lost his job within a week. On October   29th, the New York Times reported that a woman with whom he had been   involved, an executive at the Singapore data-center company MegaSpeed, was   suspected of working for Chinese intelligence. The paper cited "people   briefed on the surveillance." On November 6th, 3 days after the midterm   elections, it reported on a classified memo saying China's Ministry of State   Security had recruited her. Huang acknowledged the affair on November 8th, a   second story alleging a relationship with a subordinate followed within days,   and on November 12th he was out. No investigator had established that he gave   up a single secret, and on November 12th the attorney general said the   Justice Department had reached no conclusion as to whether the woman was a   spy.
📷

David   Sacks has this right. “People who are hostile to Jensen, who were briefed on   this memo, broke the law in order to leak it, in order to take him down,” he   said on the All-In podcast. The hostility had a cause, and the cause was   access. Huang had the president’s ear on chip sales to China and was winning   the argument, and since nobody in the national-security establishment can   overrule the president, officials with no authority to choose his advisers   used a classified leak to make one of them politically impossible to keep.
Huang   could walk into the Oval Office and make a case nobody else could make with   his authority. He argued that by denying Beijing its most advanced chips and   selling it older ones, licensed sales keep Chinese customers dependent on   American technology and starve Huawei of the revenue it needs to catch up.   President Trump heard that from the man who built the chips, and in December   2025 he approved licensed sales of the older H200 with 25% of the revenue   going to the federal government. Sacks points out that the Biden and Trump   administrations both drew a line between leading-edge chips and lesser   models. For the officials and legislators who wanted a blanket ban, the   December decision was an irritant. The access that produced it was the real   problem.
Section   798 of Title 18 makes disclosing classified communications intelligence a   felony punishable by up to 10 years in prison, and it carves out no exception   for leakers who are sure their policy is the better one. Their lawful options   are the ordinary ones. An official who thinks the president is being badly   advised can write the memo, brief his principal, resign in protest, or   persuade Congress to pass the ban he wants. He cannot choose the president’s   advisers for him, because Article II vests the executive power in one elected   man, and the power includes deciding whom he listens to. Who advises the   president belongs to the president, and through him to the voters who chose   him.
Christine   Fang got close to Eric Swalwell when he served on the House Intelligence   Committee and had access to classified material, and what Swalwell received   was a defensive briefing, the standard first move when officials believe a   foreign agent has gotten close to an American with sensitive knowledge. He   cut off contact and kept his seat. Huang, a private citizen, received a   newspaper story. On the available account, nobody ever warned him, though a   quiet warning would have protected what was at risk and let him keep advising   the president. The leak protected nothing and ended the advising, which tells   you which result its authors valued.
The   allegation is thin where it should be thick. Sacks notes that the coverage   identifies no classified information Huang possessed, no secret he conveyed,   and no design files that changed hands. Restricting where a commercial chip   may be sold does not make its CEO a keeper of state secrets, and the   engineering files that matter are hardly the kind of thing one hands over   across a pillow. Sacks does not claim the memo was forged, and neither do I;   a real counterintelligence concern, disclosed at its most damaging angle,   does the job without a single invented fact. According to Politico, Rep. Jim   Himes, the likely incoming Democrat chairman of the House Intelligence   Committee, left the classified briefing unsure the woman was a spy at all and   wondered aloud whether she was a “useful idiot.”
A   leaker needs no power to fire anyone, and Chamath Palihapitiya supplied the   mechanism. Once the spy story and the affair became public together, Nvidia’s   directors had to ask what Huang had disclosed about a relationship with   someone tied to a business partner, what he had told the auditors, and what   liability insurance backed both questions. A board can doubt the espionage   claim entirely and still feel compelled to act on the disclosure failure. The   president, for his part, now pays a price every time he takes Huang’s call,   because the Democrats and their willing accomplices in the drive-by media   stand ready to describe each licensed sale as a favor to Beijing. The Times   had first mentioned the relationship in October 2025. It acquired the   authority of classified intelligence a year later, 5 days before the   midterms, and the memo itself surfaced 3 days after them.
Chamath   asked who gains and ruled out the obvious suspects. An AMD chip runs no   faster with Huang gone, and Google appears to have no manufacturing capacity.   The winners are the people who want Washington to hold the off switch,   meaning location tracking, remote shutdown, and federal keys to privately   owned computing power. Huang opposed back doors and kill switches. A   successor who arrives under a national-security cloud will have every reason   to concede them, and Rep. John Moolenaar wasted no time calling for Nvidia   leadership that puts national security first. Nothing connects Moolenaar to   the leak. The scandal was days old and already a lever over who runs the   company and what the next CEO agrees to build. Sacks adds the cost abroad.   Nvidia’s edge is a better chip roughly every year, and 1 or 2 missed cycles   hand Huawei time it could not have bought.
In   Smith v. Van Gorkom, decided in 1985, the Delaware Supreme Court held   directors personally liable for approving a company sale after a 2-hour   meeting. Nvidia is a Delaware corporation, and its directors owe the same   duty of care, meaning they must make informed, deliberate decisions. By Bill   Ackman’s reckoning on 𝕏, where he has laid out why the directors failed their   shareholders, they had time for perhaps a single Zoom call before a founder   of 33 years was gone. Ackman grants that a board may fire a CEO over a   relationship with a subordinate. He insists the decision should never be   automatic; he would have had the directors meet in person, sleep on it, and   meet again. Instead, these directors ruled out Huang’s return before the   facts were known and launched an investigation of unstated scope. When Huang   said on November 17 that he would be honored to return if the board judged it   best, the new chairman answered on that day’s earnings call that the board   “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” “They couldn’t stand the heat,”   Ackman concluded.
📷

4.87K Replies · 9.07K         Reposts · 70.6K Likes

Huang   concealed a relationship with an executive at a business partner and,   allegedly, another with a direct report, and a board cannot shrug at either.   His marriage is his own affair to repair; his standing at Nvidia is for   informed directors and shareholders to settle. Sacks agrees. He wants   MegaSpeed investigated, any smuggling stopped, and serious consequences   imposed if Nvidia knowingly broke the law. That investigation already exists:   the Justice Department leads a criminal case against MegaSpeed, which Nvidia   put on its no-sell list in June 2025. Adultery is a sin and nondisclosure is   a governance breach. Espionage is a crime, and the leak existed to blur the   three. A board acting responsibly would have kept them apart, with a leave of   absence, independent counsel, directors in one room, and a decision made on   evidence. Shareholders got a 33-year tenure ended in a week on the strength   of newspaper stories.
📷

“People   briefed on the surveillance” describes a short list with a paper trail, since   access to material like this is logged, and the Attorney General should open   a criminal leak investigation at once. Huang sits for a closed-door interview   with three House committees on December 1st, and the intelligence committees   have a narrower question to put in writing: whether Huang was ever offered a   defensive briefing and, if he was not, who made that call. Nvidia’s directors   should rescind the bar on his return and narrow their investigation to the   facts that matter. The president should keep taking the call. If Congress   wants a blanket ban on chip sales to China, it can vote for one in public, a   result Sacks says he could accept.
Huang   has his own work to do. Uber founder Travis Kalanick, who knows a thing or   two about boards and bad weeks, has posted 12 principles for surviving what   he calls a modern-day coup, and the first is to own what you did while   refusing to own half-truths. “The op is not about your past actions,” he   writes, “it’s about your enemies and this event as their opportunity.” He   advises finding the people at the root of it, building a loyal team with a   dedicated war room, and carrying on with business as usual, unashamed. The   affair and the spy story are 2 seperate things. Huang has admitted the first,   he owes nobody a confession to the second, he should say so every day until   the facts are in and let his lawyers and his friends do the rest.
📷

Washington   has run this play before. In February 2017, leaked intercepts of Michael   Flynn’s phone calls removed a national security adviser 24 days into the   administration, and nobody was ever charged for the leak. A method that works   and costs nothing gets used again.
Flynn   at least held an office. Huang held nothing but the president’s confidence,   and that was enough to make him a target. If an anonymous official can cancel   the president’s choice of adviser with a phone call to a reporter, then every   executive, general, and scholar who tells this president something the   bureaucracy dislikes now knows the price of candor. I suspect most of them   will pay it by staying silent, and the country will be governed by people   nobody elected and nobody can name. One indictment under Section 798 would   change that price in a way no executive order can, and the list of suspects   is short and logged.

🇺🇲 🇨🇳 🇷🇺 Four points, one winner: think tanks read the Shenzhen declaration as a gift to Putin and Xi

The leaders of the United States, China and Russia met together for the first time on Thursday in Shenzhen and came away with a single page. Analysts at the Atlantic Council and the Council on Foreign Relations published their readings within hours, and most reached the same conclusion: the paper is thin, and what little it says leans toward Moscow and Beijing.

The text is the four-point "U.S.-Russia-China Heads of State Declaration toward Peace." According to a CFR roundup published Thursday afternoon, the leaders pledged to reform the United Nations, to boost the production and supply of refined petroleum products "for the benefit of all nations," to uphold "state consent and respect for immunities of state officials," and to "conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons." The war in Ukraine does not appear in it.

Mikhail Zygar, a nonresident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council's Eurasia Center and founding editor of Russia's independent channel Dozhd, wrote late Thursday that the document "almost seems as though it was written specifically for the Russian president." He goes through it point by point. The language on immunities and the International Criminal Court matters to one leader above all, because the court has issued a warrant for Putin's arrest. The pledge on the free flow of oil matters to everyone, he argues, but to Putin it is survival: in January, with prices low, the Russian economy was on the verge of collapse, and the Iran war then sent prices soaring and rescued it. Complaints about the UN suit a leader whose war has drawn the harshest condemnation from the General Assembly.

Zygar's sharpest point concerns what Putin takes home. The image of Trump walking toward him and saying "He's my friend" tells the Russian elite that Putin gets away with everything and that there is no alternative to him. Xi, Zygar notes, also put Putin in his place, directing him during the group photo to stand next to the Chinese first lady, away from Xi himself. Thomas Graham of CFR adds that Xi greeted Trump at the airport in person and did not do the same for Putin.

Melanie Hart, senior director of the Atlantic Council's Global China Hub, called the trilateral "all image, no substance," with Xi presiding over the American and Russian presidents as equals. She credits Washington with probably adding the nuclear dialogue point, then dismisses it: China is building its arsenal at a pace the world has never seen, and in her words, "Agreeing to empty dialogue is just another way to buy time."

CFR's Erin Dumbacher is a little kinder. The line that a nuclear war "cannot be won and must never be fought" has now been repeated by Washington and Moscow in 1985, by the five permanent Security Council members in 2022, and again in Shenzhen. She calls it "far from meaningful arms control," but "still a reasonable down payment on stability," and warns that Putin and Xi will use any nonproliferation dialogue with an eye on Germany, Japan, Poland and South Korea, allies that might consider their own arsenals if American guarantees fall away.

For allies the cost is already visible. Rush Doshi of CFR points out that the trilateral ran twice as long as Trump's Quad meeting in Manila two days earlier with Australia, India and Japan.

The next test is close. The G20 meets at Trump's Doral resort in Miami on December 14 and 15, and the US and China trade truce expires on January 10, 2027. If the only American gain from Shenzhen is a promise to keep talking about nuclear risk, Washington goes to Miami with less leverage than it brought to China.

text:
🇺🇸 America Is Not Europe’s War Treasury

Washington must put American interests first. Macron cannot dictate America’s security agenda, and Zelenskyy cannot expect an unlimited financial commitment without accountability.

There is a growing disconnect between Washington’s foreign-policy establishment and the US taxpayer. For years, Americans have been asked to finance conflicts overseas, underwrite other countries’ security and absorb the cost of strategic decisions made thousands of miles away. That arrangement deserves to be challenged, and Ukraine is no exception.

Russia invaded Ukraine, and Ukraine has the right to defend its sovereignty. But recognising that principle does not mean accepting an open-ended American commitment to a war with no defined endpoint, no credible exit strategy and no guarantee that additional billions will produce a settlement. America’s first responsibility is to America.

That case is hardest to dismiss when European leaders are so eager to talk about escalation while remaining dependent on Washington’s military capabilities. Emmanuel Macron has cast himself as Europe’s strategic spokesman on Ukraine’s security architecture, NATO membership and a more direct European military presence. If Europe’s security is at stake, European governments should finance it, equip it and bear its risks. They cannot demand strategic autonomy and expect American taxpayers to supply the backstop. Macron is entitled to defend French and European interests. He is not entitled to define America’s.

Washington should be wary of rhetoric that makes confrontation sound inevitable. American diplomacy should aim to end this war, not to underwrite an indefinite European confrontation with Russia. Deterrence matters, but so does diplomacy, and a negotiated settlement is not a betrayal of Ukraine. It is a legitimate objective of American foreign policy.

Then there is governance in Kyiv. Zelenskyy has become an international symbol of resistance, but wartime symbolism does not exempt a government from scrutiny. Ukraine has faced serious corruption investigations touching senior officials, the energy sector, defence procurement and figures close to the presidential administration. The Midas affair, with its allegations of large-scale kickbacks and money laundering, shows why oversight of Western assistance is indispensable. Senior officials have resigned, and Ukraine’s own anti-corruption institutions keep uncovering misconduct.

To be precise, Zelenskyy himself has not been charged. But that does not absolve his administration of its duty to guarantee transparency and independent oversight. Every dollar must be accounted for, every contract scrutinised and every allegation involving public money investigated, however inconvenient the outcome. This is not anti-Ukrainian. It is pro-accountability, and it is pro-American.

The new Congress will face precisely this dilemma in 2027. Democrats may want to restore military and financial assistance, but they should not confuse supporting Ukraine’s sovereignty with accepting every demand from Kyiv or Paris. There is a difference between defending an ally and subsidising an open-ended conflict, between supporting European security and assuming responsibility for it, between American leadership and American financial dependency.

The United States has priorities of its own: infrastructure, healthcare, housing, industrial competitiveness, border security and the national debt. These are not afterthoughts to be addressed once every foreign commitment has been satisfied. The next chapter of American foreign policy should rest on a simple principle: allies carry more of their own security, assistance comes with enforceable accountability, and diplomacy remains the ultimate objective.

America is an ally, not an ATM. It has its own interests, its own priorities and its own taxpayers, and those interests come first.
