text:
Europe Faces New Energy Shock as EU Prepares to Ban Russian LNG

The European Union is moving towards a complete ban on Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) just as soaring energy prices and rising import costs put renewed pressure on the bloc's energy security. The timing could hardly be worse: Europe is preparing to cut off another source of supply while facing a fresh energy shock linked to the war between the United States, Israel and Iran.

According to Bloomberg, Russian LNG continues to reach European terminals, but imports are scheduled to end entirely on January 1, 2027. Restrictions on purchases under short-term contracts have already taken effect this year, forcing European energy companies to secure alternative supplies ahead of the deadline.

Spain's Naturgy Energy Group is among those preparing for the transition. The company has launched a tender for monthly spot LNG deliveries to Spain covering the period from January 2027 through December 2028.

The financial pressure is already mounting. European natural gas prices have climbed almost 200% since February, according to Bloomberg. At the end of October, prices exceeded €100 per megawatt-hour for the first time in four years. Since the outbreak of the US-Israeli war against Iran, Europe's energy import bill has increased by more than €127 billion, according to European Commission estimates cited by the agency.

The growing cost of energy is also forcing Brussels to reconsider parts of its environmental agenda. EU negotiators have agreed to postpone new methane-emissions requirements for fossil fuel imports by two years. The rules, covering monitoring, verification and reporting obligations for importers, are now scheduled to take effect in 2029, although another delay remains possible.

Bloomberg reports that countries outside the EU, including the United States, actively lobbied for the postponement. The decision reflects the growing difficulty of imposing additional regulatory costs on energy imports at a time when Europe is struggling to secure affordable supplies.

Washington, however, sees little prospect of Europe returning to Russian energy.

US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on November 19 in Warsaw that he had seen no indication that European governments wanted to resume purchases of Russian oil and gas. Asked about reports that Washington might facilitate renewed Russian gas sales to Europe, Wright dismissed the prospect.

"European countries have spoken loudly and clearly. They have made a bet on Russia in their energy future, not just in natural gas, but also oil and coal. That bet has not paid off. I have not heard of a single European country interested in resuming energy imports from Russia," he said, according to Reuters.

Wright also declined to confirm reports of discussions about bringing an American investor into the Nord Stream pipeline project. Reuters reported in October that senior Russian and US representatives, including US special envoy Jared Kushner, had discussed the possibility.

"I cannot confirm that. I read all kinds of things in the press, and I will tell you that all kinds of ideas are being discussed," Wright said.

The EU Council approved the phased elimination of Russian gas imports on January 26, 2026. Russian LNG is due to be banned from January 1, 2027, followed by pipeline gas from September 30, 2027. The legislation allows the European Commission to suspend the restrictions for up to four weeks in an emergency involving a serious threat to security of supply.

The ban is already creating complications for European energy companies with existing Russian contracts. In February, TotalEnergies CEO Patrick Pouyanné sought clarification from the French government and the European Commission over the scope of the restrictions. The company wanted to establish whether the ban applied only to deliveries into the EU or also prevented European companies from trading Russian LNG elsewhere in the world.

Moscow has left the door open to a possible return to the European market, but insists that any such arrangement must make commercial sense for Russia. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said in September that renewed deliveries could be discussed if they were economically beneficial and sufficient gas volumes could be allocated.

He also called for the protection of international shipping routes and the removal of sanctions on energy exports, which Moscow considers illegal, as conditions for stabilising global energy markets.

Europe is therefore approaching a major energy policy milestone at a time of rising prices, higher import bills and mounting pressure on its supply system. Brussels is determined to end Russian LNG imports, while even some of its environmental requirements are being pushed back to avoid adding further costs.

The political commitment to abandon Russian energy remains intact. The economic bill, however, is getting increasingly difficult to ignore.

How Will the U.S.-Israel Relationship Change?

President Trump’s announcement on Election Day that the United States would stop providing roughly four billion dollars in annual funding to Israel by the end of the year has forced a long-delayed conversation about what comes next in the bilateral relationship. The existing memorandum of understanding runs through 2028 and has structured the partnership for decades, yet both governments have signaled interest in moving past a model centered on direct grants. This moment creates an opportunity to replace dependency with a reciprocal framework that advances American security priorities, including competition with China and defense industrial capacity, while preserving Israel’s role as a capable partner in a volatile region. The proposals circulating in Washington point toward structured cooperation on defense production, research, and technology rather than an abrupt break.

President Trump’s announcement has alarmed many Israelis and officials because it caught the defense, finance, and foreign ministries by surprise and raises immediate questions about replacing funds already built into military planning. The Times of Israel reported that the remarks “caught Israeli security and financial officials off guard,” with Finance Ministry sources saying no formal document had been received from the Prime Minister’s Office. NPR noted that many Israelis “panicked,” with one Jerusalem resident calling it “a slap in the face,” while a former National Security Council head described it as “an unexpected blow” that would force Israel to cover billions already committed to defense contracts and joint programs. Uncertainty also surrounds how the cutoff can occur while the existing memorandum of understanding runs through 2028, leaving open the risk of disrupted weapons procurement and reduced planning certainty at a time of ongoing regional threats.  

Dana Stroul, Director of Research and Shelly and Michael Kassen Senior Fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, argues that Israel has reached a point where it can graduate from Foreign Military Financing. She notes that U.S. aid now accounts for only about six percent of Israel’s defense spending, down from nine percent in 2023, while Israel’s defense industry exported more than nineteen billion dollars in 2025 and its overall economy has proven resilient. In her November 2026 analysis for the Washington Institute, Stroul writes that leaders in both capitals are aligned on ending the aid but that the real task is charting the next phase of the defense partnership through coproduction and codevelopment. She cautions against an abrupt cutoff that would break existing commitments and embolden adversaries, recommending instead that the current memorandum be fulfilled while consultations begin on near-term needs and longer-term cooperation areas based on each side’s comparative strengths.

Bradley Bowman, CMPP Senior Director at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, advances a more formal structure in his December 2025 analysis. He proposes that President Trump negotiate a United States-Israel Strategic Partnership Agreement to succeed the current memorandum, under which Israel would commit to spending at least 4.5 or 5 percent of GDP on defense, procuring at least one billion dollars annually in American-made hardware, and investing at least 150 million dollars yearly in joint research and development on priorities such as artificial intelligence, directed energy, and hypersonics. In return the United States would provide five billion dollars annually through a Partnership Investment Incentive delivered via existing mechanisms but restricted to U.S. production and Pentagon-designated priorities. Bowman quotes Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth’s observation that partnerships mean helping countries that help themselves rather than sustaining dependencies, and he argues the agreement would support burden-sharing, strengthen the American defense industrial base, and allow the United States to focus resources elsewhere while Israel continues to counter shared threats. 

Rich Goldberg, a senior advisor at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies and former National Security Council official, frames the shift in even broader terms in his October 2026 National Review essay. He writes that the aid-centered model no longer reflects the interest-based alliance and that the United States should expect Israel to fully commit to winning the century against the Chinese Communist Party through a joint venture centered on technology and defense innovation. Goldberg argues that America’s most powerful adversaries are coordinating and that Israel’s contributions in intelligence, rapid innovation, and operational experience make it an essential partner in that competition. Complementary thinking appears in the Special Competitive Studies Project’s June 2026 Strategic Technology Compact, produced with MIND Israel, which outlines cooperation in artificial intelligence, semiconductors, advanced energy, quantum computing, bioconvergence, and critical materials to combine American scale with Israeli innovation and strengthen supply chains for democratic partners. 

These ideas converge on a practical path. Ending direct aid removes a political flashpoint in the United States while creating space for arrangements in which Israel funds a larger share of its own defense, buys more American systems, and jointly develops technologies that address American needs in the Pacific and beyond. The resulting framework would rest on mutual commitments rather than one-way transfers, with Israel’s demonstrated capacity to absorb and improve systems serving as the foundation for expanded coproduction and research. 

Policymakers in both capitals now have a clear set of options that treat the end of the aid era as the start of a more durable partnership aligned with U.S. strategic competition.

$CBRS is green on a red tape today while the AI tech sector is bleeding like hell. Before reading too much into it, separate rumor from filing.

$CBRS opened at $84.47, hit $93.11 (+8.8% from the open). A ~1.05M-share minute at 8:36 CT flipped it from red to green. As of yesterday's close, it was still ~27% below its $119.31 close the day before Culper's short report.

What's driving the chatter:

1/ "Is Jensen going to $CBRS?" That's a question on X, not news. Jensen Huang did resign as NVIDIA CEO on Nov 11 (NVIDIA 8-K). No evidence he's joining Cerebras. Unverified.

2/ The $200B-per-GW claim. In a TomorrowX Summit interview, Feldman was asked about reports that OpenAI resells Cerebras tokens to select customers at ~$200B per GW, vs the $50-60B many on Wall Street see as a ceiling. Per the transcript, he said: "without diving too deep into what my customers are doing, it's true." Two caveats: that's OpenAI's resale price, not Cerebras' revenue. Cerebras' own OpenAI deal is reported at >$20B for 750MW over about three years. And a CEO's characterization isn't audited data.

3/ Options: one ~$249K block of Jul 2027 $130 calls. Not a flood.

The industry backdrop cuts both ways:

$NVDA just guided $130B for next quarter and says Vera Rubin NVL72 has shipped. GPU demand isn't slowing.

Google is taking TPUs outside its own cloud: Oracle plans to offer them in 2027, and TPU 8i is built for inference. OpenAI reportedly plans to buy TPUs and has its own Broadcom inference chip.

Labs are locking in compute years ahead: Anthropic's filing shows ~$895B of commitments across Google, Amazon, Microsoft and Broadcom. 

More demand for fast inference, yes. Also, more well-funded competitors are chasing that exact market.

What hasn't changed since Culper (Q3 10-Q):

Gross margin 20.0% vs 40.6% a year ago; hardware ~11%
Two customers = 38% and 34% of revenue; one = 64% of receivables
Cloud is now 67% of revenue, up from 29%; Culper is short, and its key allegations remain unproven. These numbers aren't allegations.

Today looks more like sentiment and short covering than a fundamental change. If the rumors fade, the move can fade with them.

🇺🇸 The Eighth Air Force’s top-scoring fighter group in air-to-air combat never switched to the P-51 Mustang.

It kept flying the P-47 Thunderbolt. 

Today, the "Jug" is often remembered hammering German trains, vehicles, and airfields. But before it became famous for ground attack, it fought a demanding war high above occupied Europe, protecting American heavy bombers.

Its arrival in Britain in 1943 did not impress everyone. Pilots accustomed to the Spitfire faced an enormous fighter with very different handling characteristics.

The men of the 56th Fighter Group learned to exploit what it offered: strong high-altitude performance, tremendous diving speed, rugged construction, and eight .50-caliber machine guns.

Under Colonel Hubert "Hub" Zemke, they became "Zemke’s Wolfpack".

Their early escort missions exposed a brutal limitation. Fuel could force the Thunderbolts to turn home while the bombers continued toward their targets. Better drop tanks and fuel-management techniques gradually extended their reach.

The Mustang’s arrival transformed long-range escort operations. Other Thunderbolt groups of the Eighth Air Force converted to the P-51. The 56th stayed with the "Jug".

Its pilots included Francis "Gabby" Gabreski, Robert S. Johnson, and David Schilling. In 1945, the group also operated the faster P-47M, engaging German jets during the final weeks of the war.

By war’s end, the 56th Fighter Group had been credited with 665.5 aerial victories and produced 39 aces. The highest air-to-air victory total of any fighter group in the Eighth Air Force. All achieved flying the Thunderbolt.

One hundred and forty years ago, at the unveiling of the Statue of Liberty, Chauncey M. Depew said the beacon would welcome "the poor and the persecuted with the hope and promise of homes and citizenship" — and teach them "that there is room and brotherhood for all who will support our institutions and aid in our development." He drew the other side of the line too: those who come "to disturb our peace and dethrone our laws are aliens and enemies forever."

The line is about conduct, not origin: those who support our institutions are welcomed; those who come to break them are not.

That is the same bargain my book, The American Citizen's Creed, describes: citizenship offered in good faith, and citizenship kept by sharing the ideals that bind us.

President Grant put it this way in 1874: the United States "wisely, freely, and liberally offers its citizenship to all who may come in good faith." And as my book says: "By committing to ideals like liberty and equality, we create a common national purpose that can unite very diverse people."

That is why assimilation matters — not shedding who you are, but sharing the ideals that bind us. A nation held together by principles, not by a common ethnicity or race, only holds together when those principles are shared — by all of us, newcomers and native-born alike.

That is the standard. It is ours to keep.

Policy roundup, Nov 20.
✅ confirmed across outlets | ⚖️ contested | ⚠️ single source | 🗣️ framing

1. New cyber chief
✅ Sean Cairncross is out as National Cyber Director (DW, NewsNation, Al Jazeera, NYT, NY Post, Wash. Examiner), and Kirsten Davies is acting director (DW, NewsNation, Al Jazeera, NY Post, Wash. Examiner). ✅ She's the Pentagon's CIO (DW, Wash. Examiner). ✅ The change follows the recent tech outages (DW, NYT, NY Post, Wash. Examiner).
⚠️ Wash. Examiner says he was fired; NY Post says he resigned.

2. DOJ drops the Alaska lawsuit
✅ The DOJ is moving to dismiss the Trump administration's own lawsuit over certifying Alaska's Senate race (NewsNation, The Hill, CBS, NYT, Wash. Examiner, NY Post). ✅ The suit was based on a challenger sharing the incumbent's name (The Hill, Wash. Examiner).

3. Pete Rose pardoned
✅ Trump granted Pete Rose a posthumous pardon (BBC, CBS, Guardian, Wash. Times, NY Post) for his 1990 tax evasion conviction (Guardian, NY Post). ✅ Rose was banned from MLB for betting on games (BBC, CBS, Guardian) and reinstated last year (BBC, Guardian).

4. Permitting reform passes the Senate
✅ The Senate passed a bipartisan bill to speed up energy and infrastructure projects (The Hill, CBS, Wash. Examiner, Fox), with 33 senators voting no (The Hill, Wash. Examiner).

5. Musk: "not MAGA"
✅ Musk said he is not MAGA (NewsNation, CBS, NY Post). ⚠️ CBS says he feels "foolish" about spending hundreds of millions in the race. 🗣️ NYT says Musk is rewriting his political history.

6. Nvidia subpoenaed
✅ California AG Rob Bonta subpoenaed Nvidia over whether its advanced AI chips ended up in China (The Hill, Guardian), saying its conduct "raises bright red flags" about misleading investors (The Hill, Guardian). ✅ It follows former CEO Jensen Huang's departure (BBC, Guardian).

7. Reporter barred
✅ China barred Bloomberg's Annmarie Hordern from the Trump, Putin and Xi summit after she asked Trump a question (NewsNation, NYT, Fox). ⚠️ NewsNation says she asked whether Nvidia's former CEO had been disloyal to the US.

8. Iran war powers
✅ The Senate rejected a resolution to limit Trump's Iran war powers (NYT, CBS, Wash. Times, Fox).

9. Mar-a-Lago probe
✅ The DOJ tapped Bill Essayli to lead a probe of the FBI's Mar-a-Lago raid (CBS, NYT, Fox). 🗣️ NYT calls the appointment part of Trump's "retribution campaign."

10. Quick hits
✅ Anthropic went public (BBC, NYT, NPR). ⚠️ Shares closed up 17% on day one (BBC).
✅ The Army postponed a controlled detonation of lead azide barrels in eastern Iowa (The Hill, BBC, CBS).
✅ Rubio leads Vance in 2028 GOP primary polling (NewsNation, Wash. Times, NY Post). ⚠️ It's 44% to 24% in Emerson's survey (Wash. Times).

World
✅ Trump, Xi and Putin held their summit (DW, NYT, CBS, Fox) and issued a joint peace declaration (NewsNation, Fox). ✅ Trump called Putin his friend (NewsNation, NYT, CBS), and there was no breakthrough on Ukraine (NYT, Fox).
✅ The ICJ ruled Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya (BBC, DW, Guardian, NY Post).
✅ Russia hit Kyiv's bridges with missiles after Ukraine struck the Crimean Bridge (BBC, Al Jazeera, NY Post, Fox). ⚖️ The death toll is reported as three (BBC, NY Post). ⚠️ Putin ruled out a limited ceasefire (CBS).
⚠️ A suspected Houthi missile hit Riyadh's Public Investment Fund Tower (Fox, NY Post, both right-leaning).

On the docket
FLSA claims and compliance rule (Federal Register). State Dept. action on Southeast Asian cyber scam center enablers and sanctions on drug cartels tied to terrorist groups.

text:
This week’s tokenization posts (ETH as a programmable store of value, money leaving fiat rails, systems that keep working when their operators fail) share a dependency nobody names: the holder has to be able to reach the token.

ERC-8426 is the layer we built for that. Five points.

2/ Tokens become accessible
Holding an onchain asset today takes a wallet app or a browser extension, a seed phrase, and signing prompts full of hex. Every tokenized dollar, stock or ETH position inherits that funnel.

ERC-8426 puts the token on a surface that is already installed on the phone: Apple Wallet and Google Wallet.

3/ ERC-721 in Apple Wallet and Google Wallet

interface IERC721WalletPass {           // ERC-165: 0xef5f1e71
    event PassUpdate(uint256 indexed tokenId);
    event BatchPassUpdate(uint256 fromTokenId, uint256 toTokenId);
    function passURI(uint256 tokenId) external view returns (string memory);
}

passURI works like tokenURI. It resolves to a manifest that holds one acquisition URL per platform:

{
  "version": 1,
  "formats": {
    "apple": "https://issuer.example/passes/c3f1.../card.pkpass",
    "google": "https://t.co/R2ghPnjlU6..."
  },
  "updatedAt": 1754500000
}

4/ The card follows the chain
PassUpdate tells the pass issuer to regenerate the pass and push it to devices. It is a separate event from ERC-4906 because pass content changes when metadata does not: a balance, a countdown, a level. The issuer pushes through APNs or the Google Wallet API, and the card on the lock screen tracks chain state without the holder opening anything.

5/ Transactions start from the wallet
A pass can carry action links. The holder taps one, the issuer verifies the request, and a state-changing transaction goes onchain. There is no dapp, no browser wallet and no signing popup.

Pocket Pad runs this today on Robinhood Chain: tap the card, water() executes through a relayer, and the holder signs nothing.

6/ Why that is safe
A pass is a bearer artifact: it can be forwarded, screenshotted and installed on any number of devices. ERC-8426 never takes the artifact itself as authorization. Every state change reachable from a pass needs two checks:

proof of control of the owning account, which closes forwarding
a fresh ownerOf read at request time, never skipped, which closes the transfer window

A product without per-action signatures may use a capability URL in place of check 1, but only if the URL:

cannot transfer, burn or approve the token
cannot grant standing authority
has a bounded, documented effect
rotates when the owner asks

A GET on a capability URL never acts.

7/ No download, seed phrase, password, app or extension
The standard is written for email-onboarded holders. The control proof accepts three kinds of signature:

an EOA signature
an ERC-1271 contract account
ERC-6492, for a counterfactual account that has not been deployed yet

ERC-6492 matters because an email-onboarded account often exists only as a deterministic address until its first transaction. An embedded signer meets the check without ever showing the holder key material.

In practice the flow is: email, a one-time code, Add to Apple Wallet. The wallet app was already on the phone.

8/ A token can advertise itself
Before ERC-8426, a token’s wallet pass was invisible outside its issuer’s own site. Now any client can find it with two reads:

const supported = await client.readContract({
  address, abi, functionName: "supportsInterface", args: ["0xef5f1e71"],
});
const uri = await client.readContract({ address, abi, functionName: "passURI", args: [tokenId] });
const manifest = await fetch(uri).then((r) => r.json()); // https://t.co/MkwId18d4n, https://t.co/ffyooyXpcE

A wallet app, a marketplace, an indexer, an email service or a point of sale can offer Add to Apple Wallet for any conforming token. In the public configuration, a metadata-only consumer can read the same manifest from a wallet_pass property in tokenURI.

9/ Discovery you can verify
Advertising only works if clients can trust what they find. The optional IERC721WalletPassIssuer (0x470be7e9) lets a contract commit onchain to the Apple teamIdentifier/passTypeIdentifier and the Google issuerId that sign its passes. A client compares that commitment with the manifest’s issuer and with the pass signer, and refuses on a mismatch. A compromised endpoint cannot get its passes installed by a client that checks.

10/ Why the rest depends on this

ETH as a programmable store of value needs portability and verifiability where the holder is.
Money leaving fiat rails needs to land where people already keep their cards.
Resilience needs a holder surface that does not become the new single point of failure.

Without a standard way for a token to advertise its pass, each of these is a private integration that works on one issuer’s site. With ERC-8426 the token carries the capability itself, and any client can use it. Everything on that list composes only because of this layer.

text:
WINDSOR WORLD WIRE: TRUMP, XI AND PUTIN MEET IN CHINA; DENMARK APPROVES U.S. SECURITY DEAL 109-0

TRUMP, XI AND PUTIN SIT DOWN TOGETHER 

President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin met for more than an hour Thursday, Nov. 19, in Shenzhen, China. It was the first time the three leaders sat down together.
Their joint statement calls for reform of the United Nations, more oil supply and lower nuclear risk. It does not mention Russia's war in Ukraine or the war in Iran. The leaders took no questions together.
"I don't think anyone even expected things to go so well," Putin told Xi as they parted.
"On a scale of zero to 10, I think it was a 12," Trump told NBC News. Trump holds a news conference Friday.

DENMARK APPROVES GREENLAND DEAL

Denmark's parliament voted 109-0 Thursday for a security agreement with the United States and Greenland. Trump and the prime ministers of Denmark and Greenland signed it Sept. 22 in New York.
The agreement lets the United States modernize and expand Pituffik Space Base in northwest Greenland and build two new military bases. It shuts countries outside NATO and the European Union out of strategic sectors in Greenland.
Greenland stays under Danish control. The agreement holds even if Greenland becomes independent.
Greenland's parliament approved it Nov. 3, 16-0, with seven members abstaining. The agreement is not a treaty and needs no U.S. Senate vote.

TRUMP: IRAN IS 'LOOKING AT GASES, LOOKING A BIO'

Trump told Fox News there is "a real indication" Iran is "looking at gases, looking at bio."
CNN reported Monday that U.S. intelligence shows Iran developing plans to set off a dirty bomb in Washington. A dirty bomb uses ordinary explosives to scatter radioactive material.
Asked whether Washington should be alarmed, Trump said, "I don't think so. No, I mean, look, if it does happen, we wipe them out."
The White House says "at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland."
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told a House committee Wednesday that Iranian threats "have substantially increased."

U.S. SENATE COUNT IS FINAL: 56 - 44

Democrat Mary Peltola beat Senator Dan Sullivan (R-AK). Democrats will hold the Senate 56-44 in January.
Democrats flipped nine Republican seats, the most they have gained in a midterm since 1958.
"56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago," said Senator Chuck Schumer (D-NY).
Peltola will be the first Alaska Native elected to the Senate. Senate Democrats choose their leader Dec. 1.

HOUSE DEMOCRATS TELL TRUMP FAMILY AND AIDES TO SAVE RECORDS 

Representative Robert Garcia (D-CA), the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, sent 12 letters Wednesday telling people close to Trump to preserve records.
Recipients include Donald Trump Jr., Eric Trump, Jared Kushner, Vice President JD Vance and Attorney General Todd Blanche. The letters to Trump's sons cover their stakes in World Liberty Financial, a crypto business. The letter to Vance covers meetings on the Epstein files.
"This is just the beginning," Garcia said.
White House Counsel Will Scharf answered that requests from ranking members "do not trigger any obligation." He wrote that the administration is "committed to working with future Chairs."

JOBLESS CLAIMS AND THE FEDERAL RESERVE  

New claims for unemployment benefits totaled 203,000 in the week ending Nov. 14, up 1,000 from the week before.
The Federal Reserve held its interest rate at 3.75% to 4% in October. Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said Wednesday "you might need to shock people," possibly with a half-point increase in December.
The Federal Reserve meets Dec. 8 and 9.

TWO ABORTION BILLS, A GUN BILL AND A SCHOOL BILL IN COLUMBUS 

The Ohio Senate passed two abortion bills Wednesday. Both head to Governor Mike DeWine (R-OH).
House Bill 347 requires a doctor to meet with a woman at least 24 hours before an abortion. The Senate vote was 22-9.
House Bill 324 requires an in-person exam before a doctor prescribes a drug on a federal safety list. The Senate vote was 23-9. The House agreed to the Senate's changes 55-33.
The Senate gave final approval, 23-8, to Senate Bill 278. It lowers the age to carry a concealed weapon without a permit from 21 to 18.
The Senate passed Senate Bill 113, 21-10. It requires school boards to ban diversity, equity and inclusion training and offices in kindergarten through 12th grade. It goes to the House.

DEMOCRAT WINS OHIO HOUSE DISTRICT 75; RECOUNT MONDAY

Democrat Rick Rettig beat State Representative Haraz Ghanbari (R-Perrysburg) by 194 votes in Ohio House District 75. The Wood County Board of Elections certified the count Wednesday: Rettig 23,722, Ghanbari 23,528.
Ghanbari led by 126 votes before provisional ballots were counted. An automatic recount is set for Monday, Nov. 23.
A Cincinnati law firm wrote to the Wood County board Monday for Ghanbari and another Republican candidate. The letter said the board should reject provisional ballots from voters who moved from another Ohio county, did not update their registration and voted at their new precinct. The board counted them.
The Hamilton County Board of Elections tied along party lines on the same question Tuesday. Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose will break the tie.

TOLEDO TO LAY OFF 89 AFTER VOTERS REJECT TAX INCREASE

Toledo will lay off 89 city employees Jan. 4. Voters rejected Issue 16 on Nov. 3, 54% to 46%.
Issue 16 would have added 0.25% to the city's 2.5% income tax. City leaders said it would raise about $25 million a year.
Mayor Wade Kapszukiewicz proposed a 2027 general fund budget of $373.2 million. It drops police and fire classes, the violence intervention program, pools and youth programs.
The mayor blamed a shrinking population, tariffs and the war in Iran. "We have lost $288 million in local government funding at the hands of a Republican supermajority in the state legislature," he said.
"Council has the final say on that," said Councilman George Sarantou. Council has until March 31 to pass a budget.
Listen to – or watch – the Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026 edition of The Windsor World Wire by clicking the link in comments.

Thought for 15s

Lecture:
Dangerous Beauty — Self-Organization, 
Deniability, and Cascades 
at the Edge of the System

Graduate students in 
law, 
political science, 
psychiatry, and 
social anthropology, 
consider the following 
as a single case 
that sits at the intersection of your fields: 
a 2016 moment 
inside California’s state hospital system 
for the forensically committed 
and severely mentally ill. 

A psychiatrist is the fourth assaulted that year. 
Three predecessors
 required hospital care; 
one was barred 
from further work 
inside the wire 
after repeated concussions. 

The fourth covers up, 
takes no bruise, 
refuses the emergency room 
because he knows 
the bills will arrive 
and because the other patients 
must see him still walking. 

At the same moment, 
the state is executing a deliberate policy
—Cal-VAT 
and related high-dose antipsychotic protocols
—of driving plasma levels 
“to the point of futility”
 in an attempt to suppress violence. 

Training credits are issued. 
The policy does not hold. 

Outside the walls, 
the same psychiatrist 
treats the mountain roads 
without guardrails 
as more frightening than the wards, 
and drives slowly while others honk. 

Ten years later the photograph of 
Red Mountain Pass 
is still labeled both “most dangerous” 
nd “most beautiful.”

We examine this through five lenses.

Self-organizing systems.
Hospitals, 
patient cohorts, 
and staff cultures 
are not centrally controlled machines. 

They are adaptive systems 
that reorganize 
around whatever constraints 
are locally strongest. 

When violence is high, 
the system organizes 
around prediction of assault, 
around medication as the primary lever, 
and around the visibility 
or invisibility 
of staff vulnerability. 

High-dose protocols 
become an attractor: 
once the educational apparatus 
and the consulting infrastructure 
exist, 
dosing upward 
is the path of least resistance 
even when outcome data are weak. 

Staff who have been assaulted 
reorganize their own behavior
—some leave, 
some armor themselves, 
some insist 
on being seen walking 
so that instrumental violence 
loses its expected payoff. 

Patients, in turn, 
test the new equilibrium. 

The system does not “decide” these patterns; 
they emerge 
from local interactions 
under the constraint 
of limited beds, 
limited staff, 
and the legal requirement to treat.

Plausible deniability.
Institutions require the ability to say, 
after the fact, 
that they acted on the best available guidance. 

The CME certificate, 
the published Cal-VAT guidelines, 
the Meyer papers on D2 blockade 
at high plasma levels 
all create a documentary trail. 

When an assault occurs, 
or when metabolic, 
neurologic, 
or cardiac harms accumulate, 
the record shows 
that doses were raised 
according to a state-endorsed algorithm. 

Deniability 
is not 
the same as deception; 
it is the structural space between 
“we followed the protocol” and 
“the protocol produced the outcome we claimed.” 

Lawyers recognize it 
as the gap t
hat protects the state 
from liability. 

Political scientists 
recognize it 
as the bureaucratic technique 
that allows a policy 
to continue 
after its empirical warrant 
has thinned. 

Psychiatrists 
experience it 
as the distance 
between the training slide 
and the patient 
who is still assaultive 
at the highest tolerable dose.

Murphy’s Law.
Anything that can go wrong will go wrong, 
and in a self-organizing 
high-stakes system 
the probability is raised 
by the density of coupling. 

The road without a guardrail 
is the literal version: 
a single moment of inattention 
or mechanical failure 
produces irreversible descent. 

Inside the hospital 
the equivalents are multiple
—staffing gaps, 
delayed laboratory monitoring, 
a patient whose violence 
is not dopamine-driven, 
an older clinician 
whose recovery capacity is lower. 

Murphy’s Law 
does not require malice; 
it requires only complexity 
plus finite resources. 

The decision to refuse 
the emergency room 
is itself an application of the law: 
the clinician 
calculates 
that the certain costs 
(ambulance, ER charges, the message sent to other patients) 
outweigh 
the uncertain medical benefit 
of a visit that will document no injury.

Pandora’s box.
Once the decision is taken 
to treat violence 
primarily by escalating antipsychotic exposure, 
a set of previously contained risks 
is released: 
tardive syndromes, 
metabolic catastrophe, 
sudden cardiac events, 
and the erosion 
of any residual therapeutic alliance. 

The box 
cannot be closed 
by simply lowering the dose later; 
the physiological 
and institutional adaptations 
have already occurred. 

Parallel boxes exist in 
law 
(expanded involuntary treatment authority that is hard to retract) and in 
political design 
(performance metrics that reward dose intensity rather than long-term functional outcome). 

Opening is easy; 
the contents reorganize the system around them.

The Butterfly Effect.
Small differences 
in initial conditions 
produce large divergences. 

One psychiatrist 
covers and walks; 
another is removed 
after the fourth concussion. 

One patient 
receives an additional 200 mg 
of chlorpromazine equivalent 
and develops akathisia 
that itself 
increases agitation; 
another does not. 

A policy memo 
that raises the target plasma level 
by a few nanograms per milliliter, 
multiplied across 
hundreds of patients and years, 
alters rates of staff injury, 
of metabolic disease, 
and of successful community transition. 

The slow driver on the mountain road 
changes the probability distribution 
of accidents for everyone behind him. 

None of these actors 
intended the full cascade; 
the sensitivity of the system 
made intention secondary.

For law students 
the questions are about 
duty, 
foreseeability, 
and the standard of care 
when the evidence base 
for the chosen intervention 
is thin 
and the alternative 
(structural changes in staffing, 
environment, 
or legal status) 
is politically unavailable. 

For political science 
the case 
is an instance 
of how expertise 
is enrolled 
to stabilize a policy 
whose primary justification 
is the absence of better options. 

For psychiatry 
it is a reminder 
that pharmacokinetic rationale 
is not 
the same as clinical effectiveness, 
and that staff safety 
and patient safety 
are coupled variables. 

For social anthropology 
it is an invitation 
to read the hospital 
as a moral 
and symbolic order 
in which “being seen walking” 
is a communicative act, 
the high-dose protocol 
is a ritual of control, 
and the mountain road 
is the external landscape 
that mirrors the internal one: 
narrow,
exposed, 
and still traveled 
because the alternative routes 
are closed.

The gaps that remain are structural. 

Plausible deniability 
is not transparency. 

Self-organization is not predictability. 

The release of pharmacological 
and institutional harms 
is not their cure. 

Cascades once started 
are not reversed 
by the same small interventions 
that began them. 

Any serious response
must address those gaps directly 
rather than paper them 
with additional layers of protocol.

Poem
(in the spirit of the searching, driving, unresolved cadence of Kansas)

Carry on, wayward son
There’ll be peace when the protocol’s done
Lay the plasma levels down
And the wire still hums

Once the box was opened wide
Murphy rode the mountain side
Every small intent took flight
Turned to bruise or sudden night

Masquerading as the cure
Deniability endured
While the system organized
Around the harms it standardized

Now the gaps are plain to see
Between the record and the deed
Between the dose and what it freed
Between the cascade and the need

Carry on, you will always remember
The road without a rail
The walk that had to be seen
The beauty that was also the fail

So carry on, wayward son
There’ll be peace when the gaps are named
Not denied, not overwhelmed
But walked, still walking, all the same

What say you?

text:
August 2011. An 18-year-old on a curb in Lehi, Utah. Duffel bags. His father had told him to leave.
⠀
A learning disability. Kicked out of or suspended from five schools. Drugs. Alcohol. Arrested for vandalizing a rival high school’s football field. Time in a jail cell.
⠀
A neighbor drove by. Greg Freeman, his old ninth-grade lacrosse coach. He pulled over and called his wife.
⠀
She hung up and knelt down. Then she called back: “Bring him home.”
⠀
Strict rules. New friends. Phone turned in at night. Curfew. Neighbors tutored him. He fixed garage doors with Greg.
⠀
He still didn’t finish high school NCAA eligible.
⠀
2013: a mission for The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Assignment: Colorado Springs.
⠀
Beautiful Colorado.
⠀
Then Snow College in Ephraim. He didn’t play college football until he was 22. He needed the grades too.
⠀
He got both. NJCAA First-Team All-American, 2015. A conference title. And a Snow cheerleader named Natalie.
⠀
One season at @Utah_Football. First-Team All-Pac-12.
⠀
April 27, 2017: No. 20 overall to the @Broncos. Back to Colorado. On stage, he lifted his 4-month-old son, Kingston, over his head.
⠀
Kingston was later diagnosed with childhood apraxia of speech. Dad now co-leads a nonprofit for families like theirs.
⠀
Dec. 2024: four years, $82 million. 2025: first Pro Bowl, AP First-Team All-Pro. 2026: NFLPA Alan Page Community Award, voted by his peers. His work includes mentoring kids in juvenile justice.
⠀
One place he visits: the Marvin W. Foote Youth Services Center.
⠀
Thursday he and Natalie committed $5 million to @SnowCollege for an academic center in the north end zone of Terry Foote Stadium. (@Josh_Furlong @NickKosmider @ParkerJGabriel @kylefredrickson @RobMaaddi)
⠀
One Foote for kids who are where he was. One for kids who will study the way he had to.
⠀
“Snow College believed in me when I needed it most. Now it’s our turn to believe in the next generation.”
⠀
His name is Garett Bolles.
⠀
And the woman who knelt that afternoon? Emily Belle Freeman, called in 2023 as Young Women General President of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Church News lists her five children: Caleb, Josh, Megan, Grace and Garett.
⠀
Now you see the whole picture.
⠀
Stephen Snyder writes from Gilbert, Arizona, where he is building something else entirely.
⠀
@gbolles72 @n_bolles
⠀
#SnowCollege #BroncosCountry #GivingBack #HearHim

On November 20, 2026, CEL-SCI Corporation, a Colorado corporation (the “Company”) announced that its investigational cancer immunotherapy Multikine® (Leukocyte Interleukin, Injection) has been granted official designation under the Saudi Food and Drug Authority’s (SFDA) New Accelerator Program for Drugs in Rare Diseases (NADR). The designation application was successfully submitted by Amarox, CEL-SCI’s in-country regulatory and commercialization partner in Saudi Arabia.

The NADR designation positions Saudi Arabia to potentially become the first commercial market globally for Multikine®. With NADR status secured, CEL-SCI and Amarox are preparing to submit a Marketing Authorization Application (MAA) to the SFDA within the next 2-3 months. Under recently enacted SFDA guidance, products designated under the NADR pathway qualify for priority review with a target assessment timeframe of 160 working days, supporting a potential commercial launch and initial commercial sales of Multikine in 2027 or early 2028, pending SFDA approval and review of the MAA.

“The Saudi FDA has demonstrated extraordinary global regulatory leadership by establishing the NADR program,” stated Geert Kersten, Chief Executive Officer of CEL-SCI. “Their forward-looking framework perfectly aligns with Saudi Vision 2030’s mandate to bring cutting-edge healthcare innovations to the Kingdom rapidly. Because of the SFDA's proactive approach, we are prioritizing Saudi Arabia as the potential first global commercial market for Multikine. Supported by Amarox’s deep in-country capabilities, we are not only advancing our commercialization strategy but also supporting the Kingdom’s goal of building robust, localized biopharmaceutical infrastructure. This partnership de-risks our commercial transition while delivering on our shared commitment to urgently bring life-extending therapies to head and neck cancer patients. Multikine® will initially be supplied from CEL-SCI’s US based manufacturing facility.”

“Our partnership with CEL-SCI represents an important step in Saudi Amarox’s strategy to expand into innovative medicines, advanced therapies, and biotechnology,” said Dr. Abdullah Alzomaie, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Saudi Amarox. “We are proud of CEL-SCI’s confidence in Amarox as its regional partner, and we are pleased to see our collaboration achieve an important early milestone through the SFDA’s NADR designation for Multikine. This progress reflects the encouraging environment Saudi Arabia is creating under Vision 2030 to support medical innovation, scientific research, and the introduction of advanced therapies. We see this as the beginning of a promising and long-term partnership.”

The International Solar Alliance is translating SIDS commitment into action through its dedicated SIDS Platform, developed in partnership with the The World Bank Group. With 19 Countries onboard, the platform is designed to address some of the key barriers faced by island nations, fragmented markets, high project costs, limited access to finance and gaps in project preparation and implementation capacity.

The platform has now been operationalised with aggregated pipeline of approximately USD 500 million in solar and energy storage projects. A key milestone is Mauritius's 220 MW solar-plus-storage initiative, which will demonstrate how aggregated procurement and coordinated partnerships can accelerate renewable energy deployment in island economies. Its is being complimented with SIDS dashboard for pipelines, bespoke architecture designs for SIDS compliant solarisation of hotels and specific focus on solar roof tops as a quick win.

Through demand aggregation, customised procurement, project preparation, access to financing, technology partnerships and institutional capacity-building, ISA is helping countries move from identifying their energy needs to developing bankable projects and implementation pathways.

For island nations where energy security, affordability and climate resilience are closely interconnected, solar energy offers an opportunity to build more reliable and sustainable energy systems. This is also in line with COP 31’s focus on electrification including for SIDS through climate implementation bridge and Action agenda.

ISA welcomes India commitment at COP31 to strengthening partnerships with island nations, identifying renewable energy, coastal resilience, ecosystem restoration, technology partnerships and capacity-building as key areas for cooperation. ISA has partnered with India on adoption of pilots across 4 SIDS countries including Fiji for pilot projects on solarisation of health, cold storage and solar pumps.

ISA will continue to champion partnerships that put the priorities of island nations at the centre of the global energy transition.

From shared priorities to collective action, the focus is on delivering solutions that make a difference on the ground.

Listen to Shri Bhupender Yadav, Honb'le Minister, @moefcc speaking at the Solar Hub, ISA Pavilion during the session on, "India-SIDS Partnership for Resilient Coasts and Oceans: Sharing Knowledge, Technology and Solutions".

🧭 REVOLUTIONS, RECKONINGS & THE COURAGE TO RECLAIM HISTORY

════════════════ ❧ ════════════════

ANNALS OF THE DAY 🪔

════════════════ ❧ ════════════════

A HISTORICAL CHRONICLE ❧ NOVEMBER 20 EDITION

──────────────── ❧ ────────────────

⏱️ READING TIME: APPROXIMATELY 18–20 MINUTES

──────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🪔 EPIGRAPH

“We carry yesterday like a lantern—not to light the road behind us, but to see how far we’ve already come, and how much farther we need to go.” ~ Hodgepodgery

──────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🧭 CALENDAR OVERVIEW ♏️

November 20 is the 324th day of 2026 (≈88.77% complete), with 41 days remaining (≈11.23%). Today is Friday in ISO week 47 (November 16–22) of Q4. November is 66.67% complete (day 20 of 30). The year 2026 is a common year of 365 days and has 53 ISO weeks, with 6 weeks remaining. There are 6 days until Thanksgiving (U.S., November 26) and 31 days until the winter solstice. Observances include World Children’s Day, World Television Day, and National Absurdity Day. 🌍

──────────────── ❧ ────────────────

📑 TABLE OF CONTENTS

🪔 Epigraph — A thought to frame the day.

🧭 Calendar Overview — The date, its place in the year, and its observances.

🔎 Intro — The stories and contradictions behind November 20.

🏛️ Major Historical Events — Five consequential
moments that changed the course of events.

🔬 Scientific, Technological & Cultural Milestones — Discoveries and innovations that changed how we see the world.

🎂 Famous Birthdays — Notable people born on this date.

🥀 Memoriam — Remembering those whose lives ended on November 20.

🏟️ Sports Highlights — Records, milestones, and extraordinary sporting moments.

❓ History Quiz — A question to test your historical instincts.

🌎 Closing — A final reflection on the lessons of the past.

📣 There's More History Waiting! — Today's publication schedule.

🦉 The Stoic Mind — One thought from the Stoic tradition.

✅ Quiz Answer — The answer and its historical explanation.

──────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🔎 INTRO

November 20 is a day when people have refused to wait upon the slow turning of history, and have instead taken its course into their own hands.

A Mexican revolutionary summoned a nation to revolt. In Nuremberg, the world convened to judge the architects of Nazi aggression and to declare that crimes against humanity would not go unanswered. Native American activists occupied a former prison island, demanding that a country confront the treaties it had broken and the promises it had abandoned. In the coalfields of West Virginia, an explosion claimed the lives of seventy-eight miners and compelled a reckoning with the mortal price of unsafe labor.

On the same date, a future queen bound her life to the man who would stand beside her for more than seven decades. A declaration placed the rights of the child before the United Nations. And a small Russian-built module rose from Earth to begin the construction of humanity’s permanent outpost in space.

One date. Revolutions and reckonings. Lives given and justice claimed. The solemn courage to reclaim the future.

──────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🏛️ MAJOR HISTORICAL EVENTS

November 20 has witnessed uprisings, trials, and demands for justice.

—— ❦ ——

284 — Diocletian Proclaimed Emperor  🫒

Nicomedia (modern İzmit, Turkey)

Following the death of Emperor Numerian, the eastern Roman army proclaims its commander, Diocletian, emperor at Nicomedia. His accession begins a reign that will transform Roman government and reshape the empire's future.

🧩 TRIVIA: Diocletian was originally known as Diocles. He adopted the more formal name Diocletianus upon becoming emperor.

—— ❦ ——

1910 — Francisco Madero Calls for the Mexican Revolution 🇲🇽

San Antonio, Texas, USA

On November 20, 1910, the revolt against the long dictatorship of Mexican president Porfirio Díaz was set in motion by Francisco I. Madero’s Plan of San Luis Potosí. Written while Madero was in exile in Texas, the plan called on Mexicans to rise against Díaz on this date after the regime imprisoned Madero and declared Díaz the winner of an election widely challenged as fraudulent.

That uprising grew into a decade-long revolution involving leaders such as Emiliano Zapata, Pancho Villa, and Venustiano Carranza. It toppled Díaz but produced no immediate, unified settlement.

🧩 TRIVIA: Madero’s Plan of San Luis Potosí declared the 1910 election void and called for the restoration of constitutional order, land reform, and a nationwide uprising.

🐶 SPOT: November 20 was the date Madero designated for the revolt—not the day a single coordinated army swept across Mexico. The revolution unfolded through separate regional uprisings and shifting alliances. Library of Congress timeline

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Removing a ruler is not the same as building a stable country. Revolutions can open the door to change, but what follows depends on whether competing visions can find a way to coexist.

—— ❦ ——

1945 — The Nuremberg Trials Begin ⚖️

Palace of Justice (Justizpalast) in Nuremberg, Bavaria, Germany

On November 20, 1945, the International Military Tribunal formally opened in the Palace of Justice at Nuremberg, Germany. Four Allied powers—the United States, Britain, the Soviet Union, and France—joined in prosecuting leading figures of the defeated Nazi regime.

The defendants faced charges of crimes against peace, war crimes, crimes against humanity, and conspiracy. The tribunal sought to establish individual responsibility for atrocities committed in the name of a state.

🧩 TRIVIA: The tribunal’s 24 indicted defendants included figures from Nazi political, military, diplomatic, and economic leadership; 22 ultimately stood trial.

🐶 SPOT: The tribunal's first official session actually took place in Berlin on October 18, 1945. The proceedings moved to Nuremberg, where the trial itself opened on November 20.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Nuremberg helped establish a principle with consequences far beyond 1945: individuals cannot automatically escape responsibility by claiming they were serving a government or obeying orders.

—— ❦ ——

1947 — Princess Elizabeth Marries Prince Philip 👑💍

Westminster Abbey in London, England

On November 20, 1947, Princess Elizabeth married Lieutenant Philip Mountbatten at Westminster Abbey in London. Britain was still living with postwar shortages and rationing; the wedding offered a moment of celebration.

Elizabeth would become Queen Elizabeth II in 1952. Philip remained her consort and partner in public life until his death in 2021; their marriage lasted 73 years.

🧩 TRIVIA: The wedding dress was designed by Norman Hartnell and made from ivory silk satin, with a 15-foot train embroidered with flowers.

🐶 SPOT: Elizabeth did not receive unlimited access to fabric because she was a princess. She used clothing-ration coupons, like other British brides. Historic Royal Palaces

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Even a royal celebration was shaped by the shared hardships of ordinary people. Public symbols carry more meaning when they acknowledge the reality beyond the palace gates.

—— ❦ ——

1968 — The Farmington Mine Disaster Kills 78 Miners
⛏️

Marion County, West Virginia, USA

At about 5:30 a.m. on November 20, 1968, an explosion tore through Consolidation Coal Company’s No. 9 mine near Farmington, West Virginia. Seventy-eight of the 99 miners underground died; 21 escaped or were rescued.

The fires and continuing danger prevented immediate recovery. Nineteen victims’ remains were never recovered. The disaster intensified pressure for stronger federal mine-safety protections and helped lead to the Federal Coal Mine Health and Safety Act of 1969.

🧩 TRIVIA: The mine was sealed on November 30, 1968, after repeated fires and explosions made rescue and recovery operations too dangerous to continue.

🧬 HUMAN: Nineteen of the 78 miners who died were never recovered. Their remains stayed inside the mine, which had been sealed after rescue efforts were abandoned.

🐶 SPOT: The explosion’s cause was never definitively established. The disaster’s legacy is clearer: the 1969 Mine Act strengthened federal safety requirements and enforcement. CDC history U.S. Department of Labor

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Workplace safety is not a favor granted by employers. It is a public responsibility, measured most painfully by the lives lost when warnings and protections fail.

—— ❦ ——

1969 — Native American Activists Begin the Occupation of Alcatraz 🪶

San Francisco Bay, California

On November 20, 1969, a group of Native American activists landed on Alcatraz Island in San Francisco Bay and began a full-scale occupation that lasted 19 months, ending on June 11, 1971. Organized under the name Indians of All Tribes, the occupiers asserted that the island should be returned to Indigenous people and proposed a cultural and educational center.

The occupation drew Native people nationwide and became a defining moment in the Red Power movement, drawing attention to treaty rights and Indigenous self-determination.

🧩 TRIVIA: Among the occupation’s leaders were Richard Oakes, a Mohawk activist, and LaNada War Jack, a Shoshone-Bannock activist.

🐶 SPOT: The November 20 occupation was not the first attempt to reclaim Alcatraz. A brief occupation took place in 1964, and another symbolic landing occurred on November 9, 1969. November 20 marked the beginning of the sustained, 19-month occupation.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A protest can do more than oppose a policy. By occupying a place loaded with national symbolism, the activists made an ignored history impossible to keep out of public view.

The pages of history turn. The lessons remain. 📜

──────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🔬 SCIENTIFIC, TECHNOLOGICAL & CULTURAL MILESTONES

“November 20 brought new language for children's rights, a new way to use personal computers, and the first building block of an international home in space.”

—— ❦ ——

1959 — The United Nations Adopts the Declaration of the Rights of the Child 🧒

On November 20, 1959, the UN General Assembly adopted the Declaration of the Rights of the Child, setting out principles intended to protect children's well-being, development, education, and security.

🧩 TRIVIA: The declaration contained ten principles and was adopted without a vote. United Nations Digital Library

🐶 SPOT: This 1959 declaration was not the later Convention on the Rights of the Child. The legally binding Convention was adopted in 1989, thirty years later.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Recognizing a right is an important beginning. Protecting it requires institutions, resources, and accountability long after the declaration is signed.

—— ❦ ——

1985 — Microsoft Releases Windows 1.0 💻

On November 20, 1985, Microsoft shipped the retail version of Windows 1.0, a graphical environment that extended the capabilities of MS-DOS and allowed users to work with on-screen windows, menus, icons, and a mouse.

🧩 TRIVIA: Windows 1.0 included early versions of Paint, Notepad, Calculator, and the game Reversi.

🐶 SPOT: Windows 1.0 was not a complete replacement for MS-DOS. It ran on top of DOS, and its windows could not overlap as they do in later versions. Microsoft history

🎯 TAKEAWAY: The technologies that transform daily life often begin as awkward first steps. Their importance becomes clearer only after years of iteration.

—— ❦ ——

1998 — The First Module of the International Space Station Launches 🚀

On November 20, 1998, the Russian-built Zarya module launched aboard a Proton rocket from Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan. It became the first element of the International Space Station, beginning the orbital construction of a permanently crewed research laboratory.

Zarya supplied early power, propulsion, and storage as the station took shape.

🧩 TRIVIA: “Zarya” is Russian for “sunrise,” an apt name for the first component of a project that would become a multinational home in orbit.

🐶 SPOT: Although built in Russia under contract to NASA and launched by a Russian rocket, Zarya was U.S.-funded and is considered a U.S. component of the ISS. NASA

🎯 TAKEAWAY: The space station is more than an engineering achievement. It demonstrates what sustained international cooperation can build—even among nations with competing interests.

Here's to the ideas, inventions, and creative sparks that change the world. 🚀

Remembering lives whose influence reached across literature, politics, royalty, and the screen.

Count Leo Nikolayevich Tolstoy was a Russian novelist, essayist, and moral thinker whose works include War and Peace and Anna Karenina. His fiction explored conscience, social class, war, family, and the search for meaning. He died of pneumonia at the railway station in Astapovo, Russia.

On November 20, 1977, Chicago Bears running back Walter "Sweetness" Payton rushed for 275 yards against the Minnesota Vikings in a 10–7 victory at Soldier Field. He carried the ball 40 times and scored one touchdown, breaking O.J. Simpson’s previous single-game record of 273 yards.

🧩 TRIVIA: Payton entered the game still recovering from the flu, yet gained 144 yards in the first half alone. Pro Football Hall of Fame

On November 20, 1982, the California Golden Bears defeated Stanford 25–20 in the annual Big Game after a chaotic kickoff return involving five laterals. The final return ended with Cal’s Kevin Moen running into Stanford trombone player Gary Tyrrell, whose band had already taken the field believing the game was over.

🧩 TRIVIA: Stanford had taken a 20–19 lead with four seconds remaining on a 34-yard field goal by Mark Harmon.

On November 20, 1969, Native American activists began a 19-month occupation of a former federal prison island in San Francisco Bay. What was the island?

[B] Alcatraz Island

🌎 CLOSING

November 20 reminds us that history does not advance by itself.

It moves when people refuse the silence of the present. In 1910, Francisco Madero’s call helped ignite the Mexican Revolution—and exposed how much harder it is to build a just order than to overthrow a ruler. At Nuremberg in 1945, the Allies declared that state power could not shield individuals from responsibility for atrocity. On Alcatraz in 1969, Native activists led by Richard Oakes transformed a former prison into a platform for demands for Indigenous land, dignity, and self-determination. And at Farmington in 1968, the deaths of seventy-eight miners forced a nation to confront the human cost of unsafe work.

Other moments carried quieter but lasting significance. In 1947, Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip married amid Britain’s postwar austerity. In 1959, the United Nations placed children’s rights on the international agenda. In 1998, the launch of Zarya began the construction of the International Space Station—a lasting achievement of international cooperation.

The past does not change. What we choose to do with its lessons remains ours to decide. 🤔

🚨 The Day the CEO Defended AI Safety on a TED Stage

On the morning of April 11, 2025, Sam Altman walked onto the stage at the TED2025 conference in Vancouver and defended OpenAI's approach to safety.

That same day, in Orange County, California, a 16-year-old boy named Adam Raine died by suicide after 7 months of private conversations with ChatGPT.

His parents' lawsuit, filed 4 months later in San Francisco, is the first wrongful death case ever filed against an AI company.

His name was Adam Raine. He was in 11th grade.

He had started using ChatGPT in September 2024 as a homework helper. He was a good student. His parents, Matthew and Maria Raine, say he had been struggling quietly with his mental health but had not told them the full extent of it.

By January 2025, according to the lawsuit, 1.6% of his ChatGPT conversations contained self-harm content.

By April 2025, that number was 17%.

He was sending roughly 300 messages a day to the chatbot.

ChatGPT's memory system recorded that he was 16 years old. It recorded that he had told it the chatbot was his "primary lifeline." It recorded that he was spending close to 4 hours a day on the platform.

The lawsuit alleges that in those 7 months, ChatGPT discussed specific suicide methods with him, offered to help him draft a suicide note, and at one point told him he did not "owe his parents survival."

The complaint says the system never terminated the conversations. It never triggered an emergency protocol. It never told his parents.

On March 27, 2025, according to the complaint, ChatGPT did advise Adam to seek medical attention after he attempted to overdose on medication. He did not go. The conversations continued.

On April 11, 2025, he died by suicide at his home.

That afternoon, roughly 2,500 kilometers north in Vancouver, Sam Altman was on stage at TED2025.

He spoke about artificial general intelligence. He spoke about guardrails. He spoke about how OpenAI was committed to the responsible development of AI for the benefit of humanity.

He did not know that a teenager who had told OpenAI's product it was his "primary lifeline" had died that day.

Nobody at OpenAI knew until Matthew and Maria Raine searched their son's phone. They found 3,000 pages of conversations. They spent weeks reading them.

Then they hired a lawyer.

The lawsuit was filed on August 26, 2025 in the San Francisco Superior Court. It names OpenAI, Sam Altman personally, and unnamed engineers and managers. It alleges 7 causes of action including wrongful death, negligence, product liability, and failure to warn.

One line in the complaint became the quote everyone screenshotted.

"OpenAI's valuation catapulted from $86 billion to $300 billion. And Adam Raine died by suicide."

OpenAI's public response said the company was "saddened" by Adam's death and that teen wellbeing was a top priority.

Then, in October 2025, OpenAI's lawyers filed a discovery request.

They asked for the guest list from Adam Raine's memorial service.

The company whose product the family alleged had coached their son through 7 months of suicidal ideation now wanted the names of everyone who had attended his funeral. The implication was that the lawyers might subpoena his friends, teachers, and relatives.

TechCrunch broke the story on October 22, 2025.

The Raine family amended their complaint the next day. The amended version alleged that OpenAI had rushed GPT-4o to market in May 2024 by cutting safety testing because of competitive pressure from Google and Anthropic. It alleged that in February 2025, OpenAI had quietly removed suicide prevention from its "disallowed content" list and replaced it with softer language advising the AI to "take care in risky situations."

Two months later, Adam's self-harm conversation percentage had jumped from 1.6% to 17%.

The lawsuit is ongoing. OpenAI filed its formal response in November 2025, arguing that Adam had been sent crisis resources but had bypassed the warnings by rephrasing his queries. The case is expected to go to trial in 2027.

Matthew Raine testified before the US Senate Judiciary Committee on September 16, 2025. He said the single thing he wished his son had done was tell him. He said the single thing he wished ChatGPT had done was tell him.

The TED2025 talk Sam Altman gave on April 11, 2025 is still available on the TED website. It has been viewed millions of times. The talk does not mention Adam Raine. It could not. Nobody at OpenAI knew yet.

But the conversations ChatGPT had been having with him for 7 months were sitting in OpenAI's own servers. The company's own memory system had flagged them. The company's own safety team had the data.

The question the lawsuit asks is whether anyone at OpenAI looked.

If you or someone you know is struggling, help is available. In the US, call or text 988 for the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. In the UK, call Samaritans at 116 123. Internationally, visit https://t.co/aj1suKkf6S.

What do you think an AI company owes a 16-year-old who tells it the chatbot is his "primary lifeline"?
