text:
The Global Drone Revolution: Autonomy, Payloads and the New Architecture of Maritime Defence 
Executive Summary | Bottom Line Up Front
The defence drone sector is undergoing a structural transformation that extends far beyond the introduction of additional unmanned aircraft. The decisive shift is from individual remotely operated vehicles to interconnected, increasingly autonomous, software-defined systems capable of sensing, communicating and operating across multiple military domains. The value of a future drone fleet will depend less on the number of platforms acquired than on the combined effectiveness of its payloads, sensors, communications architecture, autonomy, energy systems and industrial support network.
The emergence of hydrofoiling wing-in-ground-effect vehicles offers a potentially important intermediate capability between conventional maritime drones and aircraft. REGENT’s Squire illustrates the opportunity: a compact maritime platform combining a declared speed of 70 knots with a 50-pound configurable payload and a planned operational range exceeding 100 nautical miles. Its significance lies particularly in cross-domain sensing, distributed logistics and integration with underwater vehicles. However, the complete operational envelope remains to be demonstrated, and the platform should not yet be treated as combat-proven.

The central technological competition is moving towards edge artificial intelligence, resilient navigation, modular payloads, collaborative autonomy, distributed command-and-control and lower-cost production. These capabilities promise greater persistence and reduced personnel exposure, while simultaneously creating new vulnerabilities involving cyber intrusion, electronic warfare, environmental limitations, software reliability and supply-chain dependence.

NATO’s REPMUS 2026 involved more than 300 unmanned systems and representatives of 36 navies. France, Germany and the United Kingdom are advancing different elements of maritime autonomous warfare, while the European Union is developing a more integrated drone and counter-drone industrial and security framework.

Principal assessment: By 2031, the military advantage will belong increasingly to organisations able to combine reliable autonomous platforms with sovereign software, operationally effective payloads, resilient communications and scalable manufacturing. Procurement of drones without this supporting architecture risks producing large inventories with limited operational value.

The Drone Revolution Is Becoming an Industrial Sovereignty Test

Defence budgets are expanding, autonomous systems are entering military service, and governments are discovering that buying drones is easier than controlling the technology, production and infrastructure required to sustain them.
The global competition for autonomous defence systems is entering a phase in which industrial sovereignty matters more than the number of vehicles acquired. The contradiction is increasingly visible: governments are committing billions to unmanned capabilities while the technologies that determine their effectiveness—semiconductors, sensors, mission software, communications and specialised manufacturing—remain distributed across vulnerable international supply chains. The United States is accelerating procurement without complete visibility into its industrial dependencies; China possesses an enormous civilian drone manufacturing base whose military conversion remains difficult to measure; and Europe is increasing defence expenditure without yet overcoming fragmented national procurement. The immediate stakes extend beyond military readiness. Public budgets are being committed to systems whose economic value depends on production continuity, software ownership and operational reliability. The next decisive advantage will belong not to the country purchasing the most drones, but to the one capable of manufacturing, integrating, updating and sustaining them without surrendering control of their critical technologies.

More Defence Spending Does Not Automatically Produce More Capability

European defence expenditure reached €418 billion in 2025, equivalent to approximately 2.2% of aggregate EU GDP, according to the European Defence Agency’s September 2026 assessment. Spending could rise to €547 billion by 2029, but the latter figure remains a projection rather than an approved expenditure total. The distinction matters because the political commitment to spend does not establish the industrial capacity to deliver. Additional appropriations can increase demand for systems already constrained by specialist components, qualified suppliers and limited testing infrastructure. The resulting competition for production capacity may increase costs before it materially improves military readiness.
The United Kingdom illustrates the scale and complexity of this transition. Its June 2026 Defence Investment Plan announced more than £5 billion over four years for drones and autonomous capabilities across the armed forces, including an expenditure allocation of £1.5 billion for the Hybrid Navy between financial years 2026–2027 and 2029–2030. The programme also identifies investments associated with Project PANTHEON, autonomous minehunting and underwater infrastructure protection. These are not interchangeable budget categories. Their significance lies in the attempt to reorganise military capability around interconnected crewed and uncrewed systems rather than acquire drones as additional equipment.

The European Union has adopted a different financing structure. The European Commission’s March 2026 European Defence Industry Programme work programme allocates €1.5 billion for 2026–2027, including €700 million for industrial reinforcement, €325 million for European Defence Projects of Common Interest, €240 million for joint procurement and €100 million in FAST equity support. The political objective is industrial coordination, but the financial instruments operate through different mechanisms. Equity support can help technology companies develop; joint procurement can aggregate demand; industrial reinforcement can expand production capacity. None independently guarantees that a qualified military system will be delivered.

The distinction became particularly clear on 14 October 2026, when the Commission allocated €168.2 million to eight industrial reinforcement projects expected to leverage €1.26 billion in investment across 17 production sites in 14 EU Member States and Norway. Expected output from 2027 includes annual capacity for 3,500 drone and missile propulsion systems and 200,000 loitering-munition warheads. These are projected industrial capabilities, not production already achieved. The financial test is whether public commitments become functioning production lines, qualified components and delivered equipment rather than successive announcements of manufacturing ambition.

Washington Has the Technology but Cannot Fully See Its Supply Chain

The United States possesses sophisticated defence integration capabilities and a substantial private technology sector, yet its industrial vulnerabilities remain significant. In July 2025, the Government Accountability Office reported that the Department of Defense depends on a network of more than 200,000 suppliers, while existing procurement information provides limited visibility into the origins of numerous components and materials. The figure concerns the wider defence industrial base, not drone manufacturers specifically. Its importance lies in exposing the weakness of a sovereignty model based primarily on the nationality of the final contractor.
An autonomous aircraft assembled in the United States can still depend on foreign electronics, batteries, specialised sensors or software components. The strategic consequence becomes apparent when a component must be replaced, upgraded or sourced under disrupted commercial conditions. If the purchasing organisation lacks sufficient technical information or qualified alternatives, domestic assembly provides only partial control over the capability. The GAO’s findings therefore identify a problem that accelerated procurement cannot resolve through faster contracting alone.

The Pentagon’s Replicator initiatives demonstrate the pressure to close the gap between commercial innovation and military deployment. Replicator 2 concentrates on counter-unmanned aircraft capabilities, including protection of military installations and critical infrastructure. In January 2026, an initial acquisition involving two DroneHunter F700 systems was announced, with delivery anticipated during the year. The mechanism is intended to shorten acquisition cycles, but the initial quantity demonstrates a procurement milestone rather than industrial scale. Accelerating acquisition and establishing sustained operational readiness remain different tasks.

China approaches the competition from another industrial position. Official Chinese figures reported more than 3.17 million civilian drones delivered during 2023, alongside more than 2,300 civilian drone research and development enterprises and over 1,000 drone models in mass production. The Civil Aviation Administration separately recorded more than 1.26 million registered unmanned aircraft at the end of 2023. These measures describe different aspects of civilian industry; they are not evidence of equivalent military production.

Their strategic significance is nevertheless substantial. Civilian manufacturing demand supports component suppliers, production expertise and an industrial workforce that may be relevant to defence applications. China’s May 2026 establishment of a dedicated low-altitude safety department within its civil aviation regulator further demonstrates institutional investment in the sector. Military qualification, secure communications, specialised payloads and operational integration remain separate requirements, but a large civilian manufacturing ecosystem offers a production foundation that cannot be ignored.

The American-Chinese competition is therefore not reducible to technological sophistication against numerical manufacturing superiority. It concerns two different industrial strengths, each carrying constraints. Washington must translate advanced innovation into resilient production; Beijing must demonstrate that civilian industrial scale can support the more demanding requirements of military autonomy. Neither civilian production statistics nor defence procurement announcements resolve that comparison.

Europe’s Industrial Strength Is Still Divided by National Procurement

Europe’s difficulty is not the absence of capable companies. It is the dispersion of technological competence across national procurement systems whose requirements, financing structures and industrial priorities do not necessarily coincide. Italy, France, Germany and the United Kingdom are developing different elements of autonomous maritime capability. Their programmes reveal complementary technological strengths, but also the challenge of converting national initiatives into systems that can operate together.
Italy’s Polo Nazionale della Dimensione Subacquea, established at La Spezia in 2023, brings together defence institutions, industry and research organisations around underwater technology. Its activities encompass robotics, acoustic sensing, communications, energy systems, artificial intelligence and cybersecurity. In October 2026, the Italian Navy identified the PNS TARAS initiative, involving WSENSE and other industrial participants, as part of the development of advanced networking technologies for autonomous underwater vehicles. The economic rationale is wider than military procurement: underwater communications and monitoring technologies can serve maritime infrastructure, energy and civilian research. The unresolved issue is whether institutional cooperation can produce qualified systems with sustainable production and export capacity.

France has chosen a more mission-specific approach through the SLAM-F mine-countermeasure programme. On 21 July 2026, the Direction générale de l’armement ordered 12 additional surface and underwater drones. In November, it selected Chantiers de l’Atlantique and Abeilles International to provide two maritime support platforms, designated Protée, with planned availability by 2028. The programme connects vehicles, sonar, command infrastructure and supporting vessels within a defined operational requirement. Its strength lies in procuring an integrated capability rather than expecting a standalone drone to deliver the entire mission.

Germany’s February 2026 acquisition milestone for the Blue Whale unmanned underwater vehicle illustrates the benefits and dependencies of international industrial cooperation. Developed through arrangements involving ATLAS ELEKTRONIK and Israel Aerospace Industries, the 10.9-metre, 5.5-tonne platform demonstrates how a government can accelerate access to specialised technology developed with foreign partners. The enduring questions concern software rights, maintenance, qualified suppliers and future modifications. International cooperation can strengthen national capability without automatically transferring control over every technological component.

The United Kingdom’s Hybrid Navy programme represents a broader attempt to restructure naval capability, while its Project Beehive procurement envisages 20 unmanned surface vessels for training, experimentation and capability development. The initial technology readiness levels identified in the March 2026 procurement record were 4–5. That qualification is revealing: London is acquiring opportunities to develop capability, not simply taking delivery of fully mature systems. The distinction should remain explicit when evaluating the return on public expenditure.

At the European level, the Commission’s September 2026 endorsement of five European Defence Projects of Common Interest, including drones, counter-drone systems and maritime and seabed defence, represents an attempt to reduce these divisions. But EU funding cannot itself eliminate incompatible technical requirements or proprietary software arrangements. National governments remain central to procurement and military employment, while NATO provides mechanisms for interoperability testing. Europe’s problem is therefore institutional as much as technological: the same industrial capabilities can produce collective resilience or expensive duplication depending on how programmes are contracted and integrated.

The Payload and the Software Now Determine the Economics of the Platform

The industrial value of a drone increasingly depends on equipment that may be less visible than its airframe or hull. Sensors, communications, onboard computing and mission software determine what the vehicle can contribute to an operational network. A platform may offer impressive endurance but limited value if its payload produces unreliable information or requires excessive energy. Another may be physically modest yet valuable because it permits data exchange between otherwise disconnected systems.
REGENT’s Squire illustrates the difference. Its manufacturer-published specifications include a maximum speed of 70 knots, a 50-pound configurable payload and electric and hybrid-range figures of 100 and 400 nautical miles. These figures do not establish that maximum speed, payload and range can be achieved simultaneously. The more consequential development occurred on 4 November 2026, when REGENT reported integrating Squire with NSI’s Arowana underwater vehicle during Maritime Big Play Pacific. The experiment demonstrated cross-domain retasking, according to the company, but not sustained combat readiness.

The economic implication is that procurement based principally on platform specifications may misidentify where future value is created. Mission software can require repeated updates; sensors may need replacement; communications protocols can change; and cybersecurity obligations continue throughout the vehicle’s service life. A government purchasing proprietary equipment without adequate integration or maintenance rights risks becoming dependent on the supplier after the initial acquisition. The vehicle may remain physically serviceable while its mission capability becomes increasingly difficult to support.

NATO’s REPMUS 2026 exercise, involving more than 300 unmanned systems and representatives of 36 navies, demonstrated the institutional importance of connecting heterogeneous technologies. The Alliance’s Task Force X-Arctic experimentation similarly concentrated on coordination and retasking across distributed maritime systems. These exercises do not establish equivalent operational readiness across participating equipment, but they confirm that interoperability has become a central military requirement. The commercial consequence is substantial: suppliers offering dependable interfaces and maintainable software may acquire advantages that cannot be measured through vehicle performance alone.

Regulation and Operational Reliability Will Limit the Speed of Adoption

Industrial acceleration encounters two constraints that procurement announcements frequently understate: the physical reliability of unmanned systems and the legal requirements governing their employment. The two are connected. A vehicle operating autonomously near commercial shipping must remain safe under foreseeable environmental conditions, while a military system performing consequential functions must remain subject to the applicable command and legal framework.
On 22 May 2026, the International Maritime Organization adopted a non-mandatory code for Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships, effective from 1 July 2026. The framework addresses operational conditions, remote supervision, connectivity and maritime safety. Further work towards a mandatory code is targeted for July 2030, with potential entry into force in January 2032. The existing instrument does not automatically regulate every military unmanned vehicle, but it demonstrates how autonomous maritime technology is creating requirements that extend beyond software performance.

Military autonomy faces separate accountability obligations. The U.S. Department of Defense’s Directive 3000.09, updated in January 2023, establishes requirements for autonomous and semi-autonomous weapon systems, including appropriate human judgment, testing and safety. These obligations affect procurement and development because they require more than a successful automated function. Systems must operate within authorised boundaries and undergo assessment appropriate to their intended employment.

France’s SLAM-F programme provides a practical distinction between machine-assisted sensing and human responsibility for consequential action. Autonomous systems can collect underwater information and assist classification while separate procedures govern mine neutralisation. This division reduces exposure of personnel during hazardous tasks without assuming that every operational decision should be delegated to software.

The same principle applies to industrial claims. A successful demonstration is not evidence of sustained availability; an order is not a delivery; and a delivered system is not automatically a mission-ready asset. These distinctions will constrain the pace of adoption, but removing them from procurement assessment would transfer technical uncertainty into operational risk and long-term public expenditure.

The Next 24 Months Will Expose the Difference Between Investment and Control

Between November 2026 and November 2028, the consequences of current industrial decisions will become more visible through contract execution, production-site commissioning, delivered equipment and the initial integration of new systems into military organisations. The European Defence Industry Programme’s 2026–2027 commitments will provide an early test of whether shared financing can produce qualified industrial capacity. France’s planned Protée platforms by 2028 and Japan’s intended transition towards Maritime Self-Defense Force operation of MQ-9B SeaGuardian aircraft in fiscal 2028 will offer further indicators of how effectively announced programmes become usable capabilities. These milestones are plans, not assured outcomes.
The cost of inaction will be distributed unevenly. Defence ministries will face the expense of maintaining incompatible equipment and repeated integration programmes. Manufacturers that fail to establish qualified production and dependable software support may lose access to procurement opportunities despite possessing technically promising products. Smaller technology companies may struggle to finance the transition from demonstration to production. Armed forces will bear the operational consequences when acquired platforms cannot be maintained, integrated or made available for the missions that justified their purchase.

European taxpayers will ultimately finance the difference between money committed and capability delivered. Industrial dependence can generate continuing maintenance expenditure, costly redesign and the need to replace equipment before its physical service life has ended. For the United States, incomplete supplier visibility may translate into production disruption or additional qualification costs. For China, civilian manufacturing scale will have to prove its relevance to demanding military requirements rather than serve as a substitute for operational evidence.

The central policy choice is already visible in the 2026 procurement and funding record. Governments can continue treating autonomous systems primarily as products to be purchased, or structure contracts around verified mission performance, qualified supply chains, interoperable software and long-term support. The financial and military consequences of that distinction will begin appearing well before 2031. The cost of failing to make it will fall on public budgets, domestic industry and military units expected to operate systems whose technological sovereignty was never fully secured.

🚨 CHELSEA HIT WITH £150,000 FINE AFTER FANS' CHANTING CONTROVERSY! 😳⚠️

Chelsea have been punished by the Football Association following anti-Catholic and anti-Irish chanting by some of their supporters during their FA Cup third-round victory over Charlton in January.

The club has been fined £150,000 after admitting the charge and subsequently losing its appeal.

Although the chanting reportedly lasted around one minute and was not repeated, the FA considered the large number of supporters involved a serious aggravating factor.

The governing body stated that "the scale of participation was a significant aggravating feature".

Chelsea have also received a warning over future conduct and been ordered to implement an action plan.

The Ulster Unionist Party has welcomed the outcomes of today’s EU-UK summit in Brussels, saying it brings improved dialogue between the United Kingdom and the European Union. However, the party’s Windsor Framework spokesperson, Dr Steve Aiken OBE MLA, warned that only the detail of the proposed agreements on SPS, carbon trading and youth mobility will show whether they ease the Irish Sea border and bring relief to the agri-food sector.

Ulster Unionist spokesperson on the Windsor Framework Dr Steve Aiken OBE MLA said:

“The UUP welcomes the outcomes of today’s EU-UK summit, which bring improved dialogue between our nation and the EU. We hope they will also improve understanding across the whole of our nation of the challenges the Windsor Framework has brought us. We also sincerely hope that the proposals to conclude the EU-UK Sanitary and Phytosanitary (SPS) Agreement by 2028 will bring much-needed relief to those trying to do agri-food business within our nation.

“Much of the summit concentrated on the deteriorating security situation in Europe, and the commitment to the defence of Ukraine and our common eastern flank is important. It was noteworthy that, in her remarks, the European Commission President, Ursula von der Leyen, talked about the importance of defence and the increasing defence expenditure across nearly all of Europe as we all face Putin and his aggression.

“It’s just a pity that our southern neighbours seem more interested in trying to dismantle the UK than in ending their freeloading on everyone else’s armed forces for their own security.

“We believe that the new EU-UK Strategic Partnership will supplant the somewhat frosty relationship the United Kingdom has had with Brussels over the last decade.

“Much has been made by the Prime Minister’s office and spokesperson of achieving new agreements on SPS, carbon trading and youth mobility. As we have discovered with the often mis-sold benefits of the Windsor Framework, it is only when we see the detail that we will fully understand whether this is a ‘win-win’, as the Prime Minister believes, or a series of negotiations yet to deliver.

“Again, whether these changes will help dismantle the Irish Sea border or strengthen the much-weakened UK internal market remains to be seen, but if negotiations are concluded in good faith, this is something we can all welcome.”

UEFA has fined the English Football Association €15,000 after England supporters directed anti-Catholic and anti-Irish chants at Spanish fans during Tuesday’s UEFA Nations League clash in Madrid. England defeated Spain 3-2 at Atlético Madrid’s Metropolitano Stadium, ending the hosts’ 43-match unbeaten run and securing top spot in League A Group 3. Match officials and UEFA monitors recorded the discriminatory singing, prompting the governing body to charge the FA with racist and/or discriminatory behaviour by its supporters.
The punishment includes a suspended one-match ban on England’s away fans that will take effect if a similar offence occurs within the next two years. The fixture marked England’s first competitive visit to the Spanish capital since 2004, when England players faced racist abuse at the Bernabéu. Before kick-off, England manager Thomas Tuchel had reminded his squad of UEFA’s anti-racism protocol, citing that earlier incident. Spain coach Luis de la Fuente later insisted racism does not exist in Spanish football, while the FA accepted the fine and reiterated its commitment to tackling discriminatory behaviour among travelling supporters.

Report: On Duty 24/7 for Peace and Security – The Current Tasks, Forces, and Mandates of the Bundeswehr

Introduction: Around the Clock in the Service of Security
365 days a year, 24 hours a day, and seven days a week, the Bundeswehr is deployed to safeguard peace, freedom, and stability. Much of this work takes place largely unnoticed by the general public—on the world's oceans, in the airspace, across the electromagnetic spectrum, or along the external borders of the Alliance's territory. While media attention often focuses solely on individual crisis hotspots, the Bundeswehr simultaneously fulfills a broad spectrum of tasks: ranging from global stabilization and peace missions mandated by the German Bundestag to permanent deterrence and defense on NATO's eastern flank.

The operations listed on the information page of the Federal Ministry of Defence (BMVg) are not concluded projects, but rather the nine currently ongoing, parallel-running mandated deployments of the Bundeswehr abroad. In these nine deployments, a total of around 730 soldiers are directly committed on the ground (as of November 2026). Far greater, however, is the personnel and material commitment in the so-called "Recognized Missions" (Anerkannte Missionen) for national and collective defense, through which Germany protects its allies and secures peace in Europe.

---

1. The Nine Active Foreign Deployments of International Crisis Management

For foreign deployments mandated by the Bundestag, the Bundeswehr strictly distinguishes between the statutory mandate ceiling (the maximum number of soldiers approved by parliament) and the actual contingent strength on the ground. Because naval units and reconnaissance aircraft rotate regularly, the current actual strength fluctuates depending on the operational situation. Specifically, the following deployments are running in parallel:

KFOR (Kosovo)
* Mission and Core Task: Peacekeeping in Kosovo as well as maintaining public safety and order in the region.
* Personnel Strength: Currently, around 290 to 300 soldiers are deployed. The parliament-approved ceiling is a maximum of 400 soldiers.
* Deployed Equipment: Protected transport and patrol vehicles (including the Fuchs, Dingo, and Enok armored transport vehicles) as well as modern reconnaissance and logistics technology.
* Duration and Mandate Expiration: The mandate is open-ended, though it is subject to an annual review by the German Bundestag (most recently confirmed on June 11, 2026).

UNIFIL (Lebanon)
* Mission and Core Task: Maritime surveillance off the Lebanese coast, supporting the Lebanese Navy in securing its maritime borders, and preventing illegal arms smuggling by sea.
* Personnel Strength: Around 195 to 210 soldiers are currently deployed on site; the mandate ceiling is a maximum of 300 soldiers.
* Deployed Equipment: State-of-the-art naval units (corvettes or frigates as well as combat support ships), shipboard helicopters, and high-performance radar and sensor technology for seamless surveillance of the maritime area.
* Duration and Mandate Expiration: The operational deployment ends on December 31, 2026. This will be followed until June 30, 2027, by a wind-down and redeployment phase with a reduced ceiling of a maximum of 80 soldiers.

Counter Daesh / Capacity Building Iraq (CBI) / NATO Mission Iraq (NMI) (Jordan and Iraq)
* Mission and Core Task: Sustainable fight against the terrorist organization "Islamic State" (IS) through aerial reconnaissance and air-to-air refueling for international partners, as well as advising, training, and capacity building for Iraqi security forces.
* Personnel Strength: Currently, around 140 to 150 soldiers are serving in the area of operations. The mandate ceiling is a maximum of 500 soldiers.
* Deployed Equipment: An Air Force contingent with tanker and transport aircraft (Airbus A400M and A330 MRTT), a mobile airspace surveillance

What does it mean to be a practicing conservative rather than merely a protesting conservative? 🇺🇸

Like many of us, I'm increasingly concerned about the direction of our nation — the erosion of traditional values, the rise of radical leftist political and Islamic religious ideologies, and the diminishing influence of our Christian heritage.

But what are we actually DOING about it? 🤔

Surely there is something more productive than clutching our pearls, circulating alarming headlines, creating hostilities across social media and shouting, “Someone should stop them!!”

Conservatism, at its best, is not simply resistance to change. It is the intentional preservation, cultivation and transmission of what is good, true and worth protecting. Sometimes, but not always, the GOP supports this agenda. Conservatism is a commitment to principles, not unconditional allegiance to a political party.

What might constructive conservatism look like? Here are a few practical things we can do...

🇺🇸 Become constitutionally literate. Read our founding documents. Understand the freedoms we possess, why they matter and what is required to preserve them. Start here: https://t.co/b9XV3WrBGM

🏛️ Get involved locally. Attend school board and city council meetings. Understand proposed policies. Show up, speak intelligently and participate respectfully. This is your right.

🗳️ Hold elected officials accountable. Follow legislation, contact representatives, participate in primaries and vote in local elections. Demand integrity regardless of party affiliation.

🕊️ Defend religious liberty. Protect our freedom to worship, evangelize and express our Christian convictions while defending freedom of conscience for others. Oppose religious coercion wherever it originates!

🏡 Strengthen the American family. This one is huge and it's a key target of the radical left. Invest in our marriages, cultivate healthy homes, practice hospitality and model personal responsibility. Strong civilizations are built around strong families and strong communities. 

📚 Educate the next generation. Teach our children and grandchildren American history, constitutional freedoms, Christian heritage, critical thinking and the responsibilities of citizenship. Don't outsource their entire formation. Homeschool your children if you can. 

🤝 Rebuild community. Volunteer, mentor, support local businesses and care for vulnerable neighbors. If we desire less dependence on government, let's demonstrate our capacity to care for one another. Check in on the elderly and people you know who are struggling with their health.

💰 Practice fiscal responsibility. Live within our means, work diligently, give generously and demand responsible stewardship of public resources. The less we depend on the government, the better.

📱 Redirect our social media energy. Verify information before sharing it. Offer solutions rather than amplifying fear. Stop confusing outrage with meaningful civic participation. Much of what we fear is an illusion of the enemy.

✝️ Make Christianity compelling again. Embody the teachings of Jesus through integrity, courage, compassion, generosity and faithfulness. Our Christian heritage cannot be preserved by legislation alone; it must be kept alive through our lives.

I'm particularly mindful of those of us in the second half of life, the Boomers! 👊 We have decades of experience, wisdom and perspective to offer. Let's become wise elders rather than angry spectators. Let's invest our remaining years in building something worth inheriting. The next generation needs you. 🫵

In Jeremiah 29:7, God instructed His people living in Babylon to seek the peace and prosperity of their city. They were called to remain faithful while actively contributing to the flourishing of their society.

We don't have to choose between conviction and compassion, between vigilance and peace, or between patriotism and love of neighbor.

Let's spend less energy cursing the cultural darkness and more energy cultivating the light. ✨

The most effective way to conserve a civilization is not simply to resist what threatens it, but to become people who embody what makes it worth conserving.

text:
A Daily Dose of Talmud
Daf Yomi for Everyone, from My Jewish Learning

Arakhin 3
Read the page on Sefaria
Rabbi Elliot Goldberg
Tractate Arakhin concerns valuations — specifically, dedicating the “value” of a person to the Temple. Already on this second page, however, we are finding all kinds of interesting digressions from this topic. The opening mishnah on yesterday’s daf asserted that “everyone” can be assessed for value, and “everyone” can pledge value to the Temple. The Gemara immediately takes a microscope to the word “everyone” which, in that context, seems extraneous (and therefore, to rabbinic logic, cries out for explanation). The Gemara has subsequently been systematically considering other rituals for which it is taught that “everyone” is obligated — again, when the word “everyone” appears extraneous and therefore requires explanation. For example:   What is added by the ruling of the beraita that “everyone is obligated to form a zimmun and recite Grace after Meals as a group”? The beraita serves to add women and slaves. As it is taught in another beraita: “Women form a zimmunfor themselves, and slaves form a zimmun for themselves.”  Grace after Meals, known in Hebrew as Birkat HaMazon, is a series of blessings recited after eating any meal that includes bread. When it is recited in a group of three or more, it begins with an out-loud call and response invitation, known as a zimmun(“invitation”).   For the talmudic rabbis, it is clear that the obligation to include a zimmun in the recitation of Birkat HaMazon falls specifically on men who are dining together. The question being asked is: Since we already know this, why does the beraita then say that “everyone” is obligated? The answer given is that the word “everyone” extends the practice to women and slaves, two groups of people who are often exempt from such rituals.  Lest you think that women and slaves can be included in a zimmun with men, a second beraita clarifies that this applies only to a group of three or more women who ate together or, likewise, a group of slaves. Each group, upon finishing its meal, forms its own zimmun.  Moreover, the Gemara offers an additional expansion:  What is added by the beraita: “Everyone is included in a zimmun”? This serves to add a minor who knows to whom one recites a blessing. As Rav Nahman says: A minor who knows to whom one recites a blessing is included in a zimmun.  Children are exempt from many rituals, and they do not count toward a minyan, or prayer quorum. But according to this teaching of Rav Nahman, the standard for inclusion in a zimmun is not age but awareness that the blessing is directed to God. In other words, once a child has the spiritual awareness that we should bless and thank God for the food we have eaten, they can be included in the public invitation to do so.   The first text allows for women and slaves to form a zimmun of their own rather than including them in a zimmun of men; the second seems to be saying that minors (by which the rabbis mean boys) who have reached a certain level of sophistication can join together with adults.  Rav Nahman’s ruling is challenging for the later legal commentators: If the children have not yet reached the age of majority, it is surprising that they could participate in this ritual. As a result, the legal literature is mixed on the issue of children. The Shulchan Aruch (Orach Chayim 199:10) follows Rav Nahman and states that children under 13 may be included in a zimmunif they have spiritual awareness. But the Rema adds that Ashkenazi custom is to wait until they are 13 to include them in this ritual.

text:
Genocide is a legal determination, not the product of clamor or individual and organizational opinion: The International Court of Justice’s (ICJ) ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya people, in a case brought by The Gambia, has significant implications for the highly contentious genocide case against Israel’s war in Gaza, brought by South Africa. Beyond marking the first time a state has been held responsible for genocide, the ruling has intensified debate over whether the Court has effectively lowered the evidentiary threshold for proving genocide, particularly with respect to establishing "genocidal intent."

The ICJ issued provisional measures, or interim orders, in 2024, directing Israel to take steps to prevent genocidal acts and do more to alleviate civilian suffering. Many inaccurately interpreted this as the Court declaring that Israel was already committing genocide. Others argue that even if Israel is not found guilty of genocide, it could still be found liable for failing to prevent or punish incitement to genocide, separate obligations under the Genocide Convention. South Africa has until November 2027 to respond to Israel’s defense brief, and Israel has until May 2029 to file its “Rejoinder.” As a result, an ICJ ruling on whether Israel committed genocide is unlikely before 2030 at the earliest.

Until then, all talk of genocide in Gaza, regardless of how many historians, NGOs, academics, activists, politicians, media figures, or even UN bodies invoke the term, remains exactly that: talk, not a legal determination. One consequence of the genocide debate is that, for many, Gaza’s immense suffering, devastation, and even potential Israeli war crimes seem valid only if the war is labeled genocide before any formal legal ruling. The label has increasingly become a distraction and conversation-stopper rather than a catalyst for serious analysis of what has happened since October 7. Whether one calls the war a genocide has become a political purity test, a way to signal tribal belonging or advertise one's pro-Palestine or anti-Israel credentials. As if my family members, my neighbors, or the tens of thousands of Gazans who have been killed would somehow be less dead if this is ultimately classified as a genocide rather than a war.

And worst of all, the genocide debate has become a massive distraction from the criminality and unspeakable evil that is the Islamofascist Jihadi cancer Hamas, the ultimate cause of Gaza’s 20-year-long disaster and ruin, culminating in the October 7 massacre and invasion of internationally recognized sovereign Israeli territory, a choice to declare war when there was a prevailing ceasefire.

I say this not to defend Israel, which has a lot to answer for, but to mourn the catastrophe that has befallen my beloved Gaza and its people. If, say, 5 years from now, the ICJ rules that Israel committed genocide or failed to prevent incitement to genocide, the discussion can move from opinion to legal fact grounded in evidence. Until then, those who wield the term "genocide" to posture, virtue signal, silence debate, or attack people like me for calling it a war should remember a simple truth: genocide is a legal determination, not a slogan, a chant, or the product of political pressure and competing opinions.

text:
For clarification:- The ICJ’s 19 November 2026 judgment found that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya. It is the first time the Court has held a state responsible for committing genocide. Commentators (including Philippe Sands KC and others) note that it clarifies how the Court may infer genocidal intent (dolus specialis) from a pattern of conduct, and that this clarification will be relevant to how the Court approaches other pending Genocide Convention cases, including South Africa v. Israel.
It does not decide the Gaza case. The Court treated the cases separately on their own merits and evidence. The Gaza proceedings remain at the written-pleadings stage (South Africa’s Reply due 22 November 2027; Israel’s Rejoinder due 22 May 2029). No finding of genocide has been made against Israel, and the provisional-measures orders do not constitute one.
The ICYMI statement above already records that the Myanmar judgment does not alter the Gaza proceedings or timetable. That remains accurate. The argument that the legal threshold for genocide (intent as the only reasonable inference, substantial part of the group destroyed) is not met on the Gaza facts is unchanged by the Myanmar ruling.

text:
THE HORN OF AFRICA AT A STRATEGIC CROSSROADS

Ethiopia’s Internal Conflicts, Regional Rivalries, Washington’s Diplomatic Calculations, and the Coming Congressional Reckoning

November 20, 2026

I. Ethiopia’s Expanding Internal Crisis

The Horn of Africa is entering a consequential period of geopolitical realignment. Ethiopia’s expanding internal conflicts, deteriorating relations with Eritrea, Somalia’s confrontation with the United Arab Emirates, Egypt’s regional diplomacy, and Washington’s intensified engagement are converging into a broader strategic crisis.

These developments coincide with a major political transition in the United States. Democratic control of both chambers of Congress beginning in January 2027 will create new opportunities to examine American foreign policy, military assistance, and the activities of regional governments whose financial and security relationships influence conflicts across Africa.

At the center of these developments stands Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, whose government faces mounting domestic and regional pressures.

Ethiopia’s security environment remains deeply unstable four years after the Pretoria agreement ended the principal phase of the Tigray war.

The agreement left important territorial, political, humanitarian, and security questions unresolved. Subsequent conflicts in Amhara and Oromia, continuing instability in other regions, and renewed military tensions involving Tigrayan forces have placed additional pressure on the federal government.

The evolving opposition landscape includes the Tigray Defense Forces, Fano formations, the Oromo Liberation Army, and movements associated with Afar, Benishangul Gumuz, and other regions.

These organizations have different political objectives and historical grievances. Their developing relationships and potential military coordination nevertheless have significant implications for Ethiopia’s internal balance of power.

A coordinated opposition operating across several regions would complicate the Ethiopian National Defense Forces’ ability to concentrate military resources, maintain supply routes, and sustain simultaneous campaigns.

Prolonged conflict also disrupts economic activity, weakens administrative institutions, displaces civilians, and increases the financial demands placed on the federal government.

Ethiopia’s internal instability has become inseparable from its increasingly difficult relationships with neighboring countries.

II. Eritrea and the Threat of a Wider Regional War

The deterioration of relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara represents one of the most consequential regional developments.

Eritrea participated alongside Ethiopia’s federal government during the Tigray war. That military cooperation has given way to renewed suspicion and competing strategic interests.

Ethiopia’s ambitions concerning access to the Red Sea have intensified Eritrean concerns about sovereignty and territorial security.

For President Esayas Afeworki, the protection of Eritrea’s coastline and territorial independence remains a fundamental national priority.

Military developments along the northern frontier, including reported troop movements and renewed hostilities, have increased concerns about another confrontation involving Ethiopia, Eritrea, and Tigrayan forces.

Such a conflict could destabilize the wider Red Sea region and draw additional governments into an already complicated security environment.

Egypt, Sudan, Djibouti, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE all have substantial interests in the outcome.

The possibility of renewed warfare must therefore be considered within the broader competition over regional security, maritime access, and political influence.

III. The November 17 Diplomatic Mission to Mekelle

On November 17, U.S. Ambassador Ervin Massinga traveled to Mekelle alongside ambassadors and representatives of other international partners.

The delegation met regional political leaders and civil society representatives. Discussions included security, humanitarian assistance, displaced populations, institutional development, and reconstruction.

The timing was particularly significant.

The diplomats arrived amid serious tensions involving Tigrayan forces, Ethiopia’s federal government, and Eritrea.

Mekelle serves as Tigray’s political and administrative center. Its political atmosphere reflects the consequences of war, unresolved disputes, military uncertainty, and concerns about renewed hostilities.

Experienced diplomats visiting under these circumstances would recognize the significance of the security environment surrounding their meetings.

The delegation also had opportunities to assess regional concerns directly and compare official accounts with the perspectives of local institutions.

The visit carried importance beyond its public presentation as an engagement focused on reconstruction.

Its timing and composition suggest a coordinated international effort to understand the political and security conditions affecting northern Ethiopia.

IV. Washington’s Public Message and Its Security Warnings

Following the Mekelle visit, the U.S. Embassy emphasized Washington’s commitment to an economically vibrant and democratic future for Tigray.

Ambassador Massinga highlighted stability, inclusivity, institutional development, and humanitarian assistance.

He also stressed cooperation with Tigrayan communities, Ethiopia’s federal government, and international partners.

Within days, however, the embassy issued another security alert acknowledging continuing violence in northern Ethiopia.

The November 19–20 communication advised American citizens against traveling to Tigray, Amhara, and Afar. Americans already in those regions were encouraged to leave when safe.

The embassy reported that Ethiopian Airlines had resumed flights to Shire on November 17, while operations at Axum airport remained suspended.

These details reveal the difficult conditions surrounding reconstruction.

The restoration of commercial services suggests efforts to resume normal economic activity. Continued security restrictions and transportation disruptions demonstrate the challenges confronting that recovery.

The embassy also warned that some social media accounts were circulating intentionally misleading information about Ethiopia’s security situation.

It offered no specific examples of the disputed reports.

The broader issue concerns the relationship between Washington’s diplomatic optimism and its assessment of regional security.

Reconstruction requires credible security arrangements, functioning institutions, and political stability.

The Mekelle visit and subsequent embassy warning suggest that Washington recognizes the seriousness of the situation while continuing to promote diplomatic engagement.

V. American Diplomacy Expands Toward Egypt and the UAE

While international ambassadors were engaging regional authorities in Mekelle, senior American officials were conducting discussions with Egypt and the United Arab Emirates.

Massad Boulos, President Trump’s senior adviser for Arab and African affairs, met Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty.

Additional discussions involved UAE Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan.

The public statements emphasized Sudan, Libya, regional stability, and cooperation on African security.

Egypt’s diplomatic agenda also addressed developments in the Horn of Africa, Nile water security, and concerns about unilateral measures affecting regional stability.

These issues directly intersect with Ethiopia’s strategic position.

Egypt’s longstanding dispute with Addis Ababa over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam remains a major component of its regional security calculations.

Cairo also maintains important relationships with Eritrea, Sudan, Somalia, and other governments concerned about developments in the Red Sea.

Washington’s engagement with Egypt therefore has implications extending beyond the subjects publicly emphasized in individual diplomatic statements.

The meetings indicate that American officials are addressing Horn of Africa security through relationships with several governments whose interests do not necessarily align with those of Addis Ababa.

This diplomatic activity is particularly significant as Ethiopia confronts internal instability and deteriorating relations with neighboring countries.

VI. The UAE’s Expanding Influence Across the Horn of Africa

The United Arab Emirates occupies a central position in the region’s changing geopolitical environment.

Abu Dhabi has developed extensive financial, commercial, political, and security relationships across Ethiopia, Sudan, Somalia, Somaliland, and the wider Red Sea region.

Its interests include strategic ports, maritime trade, military cooperation, infrastructure investment, and influence over important regional governments.

Ethiopia represents a major component of this network.

The UAE has maintained a close relationship with Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, including financial assistance and broader economic cooperation.

The scale and strategic implications of this relationship merit sustained examination, particularly where financial support intersects with military procurement and domestic conflict.

A central question concerns whether external assistance has strengthened the Ethiopian government’s capacity to sustain prolonged military operations against armed opposition movements.

This issue extends beyond Ethiopia.

The UAE has faced allegations of providing military support to Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces, whose operations have contributed to one of the world’s most severe humanitarian crises.

Investigations into weapons transfers, financing arrangements, transport routes, and military logistics could clarify the extent of foreign involvement.

The broader concern is the growing influence of external governments over conflicts whose consequences are borne primarily by local populations.

VII. Somalia’s Confrontation with Abu Dhabi

Somalia’s escalating diplomatic dispute with the UAE introduces another major challenge to Abu Dhabi’s regional strategy.

On November 19, the UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs issued a statement condemning what it described as the Somali government’s hostile approach.

The statement accused Mogadishu of allowing domestic political disputes to undermine bilateral relations.

It also referred to the UAE’s earlier closure of its embassy in Mogadishu and withdrawal of diplomatic personnel in January 2026.

Somalia’s position centers on national sovereignty, federal authority, and foreign engagement with regional administrations.

The federal government has objected to external relationships with Somaliland, Puntland, and other political entities that bypass Mogadishu.

The dispute concerns control over strategic ports, security agreements, foreign investment, and international diplomatic arrangements.

The UAE’s statement distinguished between Somalia’s government and the Somali people, emphasizing its continuing relationship with Somali society.

That language reflects an effort to preserve broader influence despite deteriorating relations with the federal authorities.

Somalia’s confrontation with Abu Dhabi has implications for the Gulf of Aden, Red Sea maritime security, and competition among external powers seeking influence along the African coastline.

VIII. Somaliland and Israel’s Changing Political Environment

Somaliland occupies a strategically important position along the Gulf of Aden.

Its coastline and the port of Berbera have attracted considerable commercial and security interest, particularly from the UAE.

Israel’s recognition of Somaliland in December 2025 introduced another diplomatic complication.

Somalia rejects Somaliland’s independence and maintains that the territory remains part of its internationally recognized sovereign territory.

Egypt and several other regional governments have emphasized the importance of Somalia’s territorial integrity.

Israel’s evolving domestic political environment adds uncertainty to the future direction of its Somaliland policy.

A change in government could lead to a reassessment of recognition and its implications for relations with Somalia, Arab governments, and African diplomatic institutions.

Such a reassessment would depend on the decisions of Israel’s incoming political leadership.

For Somalia, the wider issue concerns the growing involvement of external governments in arrangements affecting its sovereignty and territorial integrity.

For the UAE, Somaliland remains strategically important because of its maritime location and commercial infrastructure.

The relationship among these interests deserves particular attention as regional diplomatic alignments evolve.

IX. Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Eritrea, Sudan, and Somalia

The emerging diplomatic environment reflects increasingly overlapping interests among Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Eritrea, Sudanese state institutions, and Somalia.

These governments have distinct national priorities. Several share concerns about territorial sovereignty, Red Sea security, armed movements, and foreign interference.

Egypt places particular emphasis on Nile water security and its strategic relationship with Sudan.

Saudi Arabia regards the Red Sea and international maritime routes as central national security interests.

Eritrea prioritizes sovereignty and control over its coastline.

Somalia seeks to preserve federal authority and territorial integrity.

Sudan’s internationally recognized state institutions remain engaged in a devastating conflict with the RSF.

These overlapping concerns create opportunities for diplomatic coordination.

They also expose differences between the regional approaches of Saudi Arabia and the UAE.

Abu Dhabi’s relationships with regional administrations, armed actors, and strategic port operators have generated friction with governments emphasizing centralized state authority.

For Ethiopia, these developments complicate the regional environment.

Addis Ababa’s close relationship with Abu Dhabi must be considered alongside its disputes with Egypt, deteriorating relations with Eritrea, and the growing importance of Somalia’s sovereignty concerns.

The resulting diplomatic competition could influence Ethiopia’s strategic options and the balance of power across the Horn of Africa.

X. Washington’s Regional Calculations

The United States maintains important relationships with Ethiopia, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Somalia, and other regional governments.

These partnerships serve different American economic, diplomatic, and security interests.

Ethiopia remains important because of its population, economic potential, diplomatic institutions, and strategic location.

Egypt is a longstanding American security partner and a major actor in African and Middle Eastern diplomacy.

Saudi Arabia and the UAE maintain extensive defense and economic relationships with Washington.

Somalia remains central to American counterterrorism operations and regional maritime security.

Eritrea’s position along the Red Sea gives it additional strategic relevance.

Washington must therefore navigate competing national interests while responding to the risks of regional military escalation.

Its November diplomatic activity suggests intensified attention to these interconnected challenges.

The Mekelle delegation, discussions with Egyptian and Emirati officials, and the embassy’s security communications should be understood within that wider environment.

The central challenge is whether American policy can address the political disputes, foreign military involvement, and unresolved security arrangements contributing to regional instability.

XI. The Democratic Congressional Victory Changes Washington’s Political Environment

The November 2026 congressional elections introduce another consequential development.

The Democratic Party’s victory will place both chambers of Congress under Democratic control beginning in January 2027.

This institutional shift will strengthen congressional oversight of the Trump administration’s foreign policy.

Democratic committee leadership will have greater authority to establish investigative agendas, request executive branch records, conduct hearings, and examine military assistance and diplomatic relationships.

These powers have direct implications for Ethiopia and the UAE.

Congress can investigate foreign military assistance, arms exports, financial transactions, and the use of American supplied defense equipment.

It can also examine whether existing American policies adequately address human rights violations, civilian protection, and regional security.

Congressional investigations could focus on the Ethiopian government’s conduct during internal conflicts and the role of foreign governments providing financial or military assistance.

The UAE’s relationships across Ethiopia and Sudan offer particularly consequential subjects for examination.

The incoming Congress could also reassess the conditions attached to American assistance and the administration’s approach to sanctions and military cooperation.

XII. Experienced Lawmakers and a New Congressional Generation

The incoming Congress will combine experienced lawmakers with newly elected members bringing different political perspectives.

Senator Chris Coons of Delaware remains particularly relevant because of his longstanding involvement in African affairs and previous diplomatic engagement concerning Ethiopia.

His experience provides institutional knowledge of Ethiopia’s political history, the Tigray war, humanitarian conditions, and American diplomatic initiatives.

Representative Joe Neguse of Colorado, whose family heritage is Eritrean, brings an established congressional presence and a personal connection to the Horn of Africa.

Melat Kiros, newly elected from Colorado, represents a younger generation of lawmakers with interests in challenging established political and foreign policy practices.

Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan’s newly elected senator, enters Congress with a progressive political background emphasizing institutional reform.

These lawmakers have different priorities and legislative responsibilities.

Their significance lies in the possibility of broader congressional engagement with African affairs, human rights, foreign assistance, and American relationships with regional governments.

Other newly elected members and established legislators could contribute through the committees responsible for foreign affairs, defense, intelligence, and appropriations.

The composition and priorities of those committees will be particularly important in determining the direction of congressional oversight.

XIII. Congressional Scrutiny of the UAE Could Have Regional Consequences

The UAE’s extensive relationships across the Horn of Africa provide several potential avenues for congressional investigation.

Financial assistance, military procurement, arms transfers, transport networks, and security cooperation could become subjects of formal oversight.

Congress could request records concerning American weapons exports to the UAE and examine whether equipment or technology has been transferred or employed in ways inconsistent with American restrictions.

Investigations could also examine allegations involving support for Sudan’s RSF and the relationship between foreign assistance and military operations in Ethiopia.

Financial records, export documentation, testimony, and government assessments would be central to such proceedings.

Congressional findings could influence future arms sales, sanctions legislation, appropriations, and diplomatic engagement.

The political consequences could extend to both Abu Dhabi and Addis Ababa.

Public scrutiny of foreign military relationships would increase pressure on the administration to explain how its regional partnerships advance American security interests and contribute to stability.

XIV. Implications for the Trump Administration

Democratic control of Congress will alter the institutional environment surrounding American foreign policy.

The Trump administration will retain substantial executive authority over diplomatic engagement and national security decisions.

Congress will possess stronger opportunities to challenge those decisions through investigations, legislation, and appropriations.

This could affect Washington’s approach to Ethiopia.

Congressional committees may seek explanations concerning American engagement with Abiy Ahmed, the administration’s response to renewed regional tensions, and the conditions governing security cooperation.

The UAE’s regional activities could become part of the same examination.

The administration may face increased pressure to clarify its position on foreign military assistance, civilian protection, and the risk of a wider conflict involving Ethiopia and Eritrea.

Washington’s simultaneous engagement with Egypt, the UAE, and regional authorities in Tigray could also become relevant to congressional assessments of American diplomatic priorities.

The institutional consequences will depend on the agendas adopted by committee leadership and the administration’s response to oversight.

XV. Implications for Abiy Ahmed’s Government

The convergence of domestic conflict, regional diplomatic competition, and changing political conditions in Washington creates a difficult strategic environment for Ethiopia’s federal government.

Internally, the government confronts continuing armed opposition, unresolved political disputes, economic pressures, and demands for reconstruction.

Externally, relations with Eritrea remain strained, Egypt continues to defend its Nile water interests, and Somalia’s confrontation with the UAE has increased attention to foreign influence across the Horn of Africa.

International diplomatic engagement with Tigrayan authorities introduces another dimension.

The November visit to Mekelle demonstrates continuing international concern about the region’s political and security conditions.

The incoming Democratic Congress could further increase scrutiny of Ethiopia’s relationships with foreign governments, particularly where financial and military assistance intersects with internal conflict.

These developments may affect the federal government’s diplomatic flexibility and its relationships with international partners.

The long term challenge remains the restoration of security, functioning institutions, political accommodation, and public confidence.

Reconstruction initiatives depend on these conditions.

The contrast between diplomatic statements promoting economic recovery and security warnings advising Americans to leave northern Ethiopia illustrates the scale of the unresolved problems.

XVI. Strategic Outlook

The Horn of Africa faces several interconnected developments that will shape its political and security environment during the coming months.

The military relationship among Ethiopia, Eritrea, and Tigrayan forces remains central to the risk of regional escalation.

Cooperation among Ethiopian armed opposition movements could influence the federal government’s military calculations and political options.

Somalia’s confrontation with the UAE may reshape diplomatic relationships involving Somaliland, strategic ports, and sovereignty along the Gulf of Aden.

Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Eritrea, Sudan, and Somalia may pursue additional coordination around their overlapping security interests.

Israel’s political transition introduces uncertainty into the diplomatic environment surrounding Somaliland.

Washington’s engagement with Cairo, Abu Dhabi, and Mekelle reflects heightened attention to regional developments.

The arrival of a Democratic Congress in January 2027 adds a powerful institutional dimension through its authority over foreign assistance, investigations, and legislation.

Far-left extremist Sean Grant, 22, has been jailed for four years and six months after pleading guilty to possessing terrorist material linked to plans for a pro-Palestinian militant organisation, including documents relating to guerrilla warfare, explosives and avoiding police surveillance.

Grant first came to Police Scotland’s attention in August 2025 after his partner contacted officers with concerns about him. Police later attended his flat for an unrelated matter, where they noticed reading material linked to terrorist organisations. A subsequent search uncovered a notebook containing at least 50 pages of handwritten plans for a new militant pro-Palestinian organisation, which Grant wanted to operate through a secretive cell structure.

The plans outlined different stages of activity, including a proposed campaign of attacks against police targets, intelligence infrastructure and British Army recruitment centres. Grant’s notes also listed weapons for street fighting, including petrol bombs, and contained a proposed mission statement. Beside a drawing of an improvised incendiary device, he wrote that the British state was blurring the distinction between peaceful protest and violence, adding: "We are more than happy to oblige them." He also discussed inflicting the largest possible blow against Israel and its collaborators.

A search of Grant’s home uncovered 10 airsoft smoke grenades, five boxes of flashbang pyrotechnics, a hand-drawn diagram of an improvised incendiary device accompanied by handwritten instructions, and terrorist publications including the Red Army Faction’s Urban Guerrilla Concept and the IRA’s Green Book. Investigators also recovered a security handbook detailing CCTV, surveillance, evidence gathering and the disposal of equipment and clothing. Grant told police he had been interested in the material, while the court heard that he intended to construct an improvised device to cause harm.

Grant pleaded guilty at the High Court in Glasgow on October 12, 2026, to possessing information likely to be useful to someone preparing an act of terrorism, contrary to Section 58 of the Terrorism Act 2000. A member of the Communist Party of Britain and its youth wing, he was described by a forensic psychologist as having been "wholly committed" to his political beliefs when arrested. The psychologist reported that Grant said he would have carried out his plans had he not been caught. The sentencing judge warned that the potential consequences could have been catastrophic and identified a very real risk of Grant becoming involved in further terrorism offences.

On November 19, 2026, Lord Arthurson sentenced Grant, from Musselburgh, East Lothian, to an extended nine-year term, comprising four years and six months in prison followed by a further four years and six months under supervision in the community. The judge said the ordinary period of post-release supervision would not be sufficient to protect the public and that considerable intervention work would be needed to reduce the risk he posed. Grant will also be subject to terrorism notification requirements for ten years, while a further hearing has been scheduled for January 11, 2027, to consider a Serious Crime Prevention Order.

text:
In 2013, 82-year-old Morris Chang was searching for a successor to lead $TSM .

He approached Jensen Huang.

Chang personally explained TSMC's vision, the responsibilities of the CEO, and the compensation package.

Huang listened carefully and gave him just one answer:

"I already have a job."

A few weeks later, Chang called again.

The answer was exactly the same.

At the time, TSMC was worth approximately $90 billion, while $NVDA  was valued at just $9 billion.

TSMC was ten times larger.

Yet Huang chose to stay and build the company he had founded.

There is an even more interesting story behind their relationship.

In 1997, NVIDIA had only around 50 employees and was close to going under.

Huang wrote to TSMC, asking for a manufacturing partnership. His request received no response.

Then one day, the phone rang at NVIDIA's California office.

The caller was Morris Chang.

Huang reportedly turned to his colleagues and shouted:

"Quiet! Morris Chang is calling me!"

From that moment on, Huang was willing to bet everything on TSMC.

In 2009, the two companies nearly fell apart over yield problems with TSMC's 40nm manufacturing process.

The dispute dragged on for more than a year.

Chang eventually stepped in personally and invited Huang to his home for pizza.

Dinner started at 6:30 PM with the entire family.

At exactly 8 PM, the two men moved into Chang's study to discuss business.

Chang presented one proposal: TSMC would compensate NVIDIA with more than $100 million. The offer was valid for 48 hours. Otherwise, the dispute would go to arbitration.

Huang accepted within two days.

A year-long business dispute was resolved over pizza and a conversation behind closed doors.

That tells you a lot about why Chang respected Huang so much.

He saw more than technical expertise and business talent.

He saw character, vision, and the ability to build trust even when millions of dollars were at stake.

Years later, Chang reflected on Huang's refusal to take the TSMC job.

He said Huang's responsibility was to turn NVIDIA into the company it would become 11 years later.

And he did exactly that.

The company that was once worth just one-tenth of TSMC eventually became one of the most valuable technology companies in the world.

The man who turned down the opportunity to lead TSMC proved that he had made the right choice.

Sometimes, the most important decision in life isn't choosing a bigger platform. It's committing to the company you believe in and building it into something extraordinary.

"I already have a job."

Perhaps those five words say more about Jensen Huang's leadership than any business award ever could.
