text:
$ANT went from rip to wipeout in under 24 hours: priced at $83, surged ~39% to $115.10, then dumped to ~$86.70 pre-market today, off nearly 25% from the top. Open buyers are down 22%+ in a day.

On 18.14B diluted shares, over $500B of value vanished from its $2.09T peak. Why the sudden dump?

I work in AI infra, so I went through the 424B4 filing line by line. The 12x revenue jump to $33.2B in the first nine months of 2026 is real, yet two numbers underneath jump off the page: customers have locked in only $13.8B of non-cancelable contracts, while Anthropic has signed up for $900.9B of compute and data-center commitments.

Start with where that "85.5% gross margin" actually comes from.

Anthropic doesn't break out cost of revenue or gross margin on its main income statement. It just reports $18.8B of compute and infrastructure for the nine months. Flip to Note 8, which splits expenses by function, and direct serving cost for paid customers was only $4.8B, implying an 85.5% serving margin. Free-user inference sits inside $6.6B of sales and marketing alongside cloud marketplace fees. The real weight is R&D at $19.2B, or 57.9% of revenue, mostly training compute and internal workloads. As a side note, Claude wrote over 90% of Anthropic's own internal code commits in September.

If you look at this through a traditional SaaS lens, you assume R&D tapers off later and 85.5% is steady-state margin. Frontier models don't age like Photoshop. The filing admits that over 80% of Q3 revenue came from model versions released in the prior six months, and 79.1% of revenue is billed by token usage. That $19.2B of training compute is basically maintenance cost to keep existing revenue from churning.

I ship code every day, and you can feel how fast the competitive moat has shifted on the ground. Back in the second half of last year around the Claude 4.5 era, Claude Code had a near-monopoly on serious software engineering. You basically had no real alternative, and that window is a big reason net revenue retention hit an eye-popping 900% in the filing. This year the table looks very different. OpenAI has Codex, Google's Antigravity has been getting strong word of mouth lately, and plenty of engineers around me now mix and switch between them daily. Switching coding agents or flipping an enterprise API router takes almost zero friction. API pricing between OpenAI and Claude is already matched down to the dollar at $2 input and $10 output per million tokens on the workhorse tier, and Q3 price cuts plus contractual discounts already shaved about $600M off Anthropic's top line.

There is another revenue hole Wall Street overlooks: its stance toward Chinese developers. Anthropic enforces almost paranoid risk controls against Chinese users with frequent, hair-trigger account bans, whereas Codex and Antigravity are noticeably more relaxed. China has millions of strong engineers running coding agents every day, making it one of the largest coding-token pools on earth. Whether out of compliance caution or its own strange fixation, Anthropic has effectively walked away from that entire market. You can see the footprint right in the prospectus: non-US revenue was just 29.4% in the first nine months, and the company admits it stepped up enforcement in August and September against accounts violating regional or usage rules, a bucket that generated 5% to 7% of nine-month revenue, or $1.7B to $2.3B in hard dollars. Handing a growth market that size straight to OpenAI and Google raises a real question about how long hyper-growth stays aloft.

Meanwhile, any hiccup in compute timing hits profits right away. Anthropic booked $974M of operating income in Q2. By Q3, quarterly revenue climbed to $17.0B, yet it swung back to a $567M operating loss after scrambling for $5.0B of pricey short-term compute and booking $2.0B of employee donation matching.

Now look at cash flow and that $900.9B tab.

Operating cash flow turned positive for the first time at $6.6B over the nine months (the $104.0B GAAP net loss is mostly non-cash fair-value marks on convertible notes as valuation rose). Subtract $925M of equipment purchases and $2.0B of data-center prepayments, factor back in $3.3B of stock-based comp, and common holders aren't left with much yet. Going public also triggers $14.7B of stored-up RSU expense and roughly $4.3B in cash tax withholding paid out by the company.

Anyone in infra sweats contract duration mismatch. On the customer side, non-cancelable RPO is just $13.8B, less than one quarter of Q3 revenue, with three-quarters burning off inside a year, and customer spend even dropped 20% over the two-week year-end holiday. On the supplier side, compute and data-center lease commitments stretch out to 2045 and total $900.9B, with $70.7B due in the next 12 months and $451.6B due by 2030, before counting another $125B to $150B of estimated Google TPU capacity without fixed dollar caps.

The contract terms are stiff too. Minimums of at least $121.3B to Google, $110.0B to Amazon, and $47.2B to $49.2B to Microsoft all carry true-up clauses whether Anthropic uses the capacity or not. It even signed up for as much as $120.5B of NVIDIA GPU compute from Elon Musk's https://t.co/RGB9OVT1Bd, though either party can cancel on 90 days' notice after early 2027.

Near-term cash obviously won't run dry. Roughly $104.8B in net proceeds from the IPO and concurrent private placement lifts pro forma cash and short-term investments to $232.4B. Look at the financing loop, though: Google, NVIDIA, Amazon, Microsoft, Broadcom, AMD, Micron, and TSMC collect those long-term compute checks while buying non-voting shares or extending backup convertible debt (Broadcom's $42B equipment lease line charges 9% to 13% interest and converts at a 10% to 15% discount to market). Future compute bills are wired directly into share dilution.

Finally, check the share count and voting rights.

Many quote apps show a market cap around $1.1T to $1.2T because they only count the 12.37B basic accounting shares (13.22B with the 847M public benefit fund shares). Sitting underneath are 1.55B Amazon rollover note shares converting at $2 to $5, 1.71B net option shares at a $2.91 average strike, 1.07B unvested RSUs, and 581M donation-matching shares. Put together, fully diluted shares reach 18.14B, or 46.6% above basic. From 2027 through 2036, the employee donation pool automatically adds up to 1% of shares a year, and every sustained 50% share-price step above $83 lets the board issue up to another 2% of fully diluted stock to the public benefit fund.

On governance, it's a Delaware Public Benefit Corporation. A single Class T share lets the Long-Term Benefit Trust elect a majority of the board, and a single Class F share locks in 50.1% of general stockholder voting power for the seven co-founders, capping all Class A public shareholders combined at 49.9%. And they really do sacrifice speed for safety: in April they held back broad commercial release of their cyber-capable Mythos model, and they recently delayed pretraining a next-gen frontier model by over a month to tighten weight security.

Over the next few quarters I'm watching four numbers:

1. Whether total R&D plus serving compute drops as a share of revenue, without more $5B emergency short-term compute buys.
2. How much revenue gets given back through price cuts and discounts ($600M in Q3), and whether token growth keeps outrunning lower prices as Codex and Antigravity siphon off demand.
3. Whether $1M+ enterprise accounts (over 1,900 today) sign longer non-cancelable deals to thicken that $13.8B RPO.
4. When real free cash flow shows up after data-center prepayments, equipment capex, and stock comp.

Facing a $900B compute tab, would you rather own the model lab itself or the chip and cloud vendors cashing the checks? Drop your thoughts below.

I don't hold ANT. This is my own note from reading the prospectus, not financial advice.

text:
SpaceX is running out of energy on Earth to power its compute as utilities struggle to build power plants fast enough for AI, with some now charging data centers just to get a place in line.

TVA, which supplies the power MLGW delivers to Colossus in Memphis, only began test runs at its newest gas plant, Cumberland, this year. Its next 1,550 MW of approved generation isn't due until 2032. Meanwhile, about 5 GW of data centers are in TVA's connection process, seeking access to power the grid cannot yet supply.

So TVA now charges new data centers about $1.5 million per MW just to reserve capacity. One customer has committed $1.7 billion under an agreement with TVA, with an initial $31 million payment and the rest spread across 59 installments. The customer's identity hasn't been disclosed.

That's not payment for electricity. It's payment for the right to wait into the 2030s. Absurd.

And SpaceX wants about 13 GW of compute by the end of next year alone. No utility can simply deliver that much power on demand, so SpaceX is building its own generation around the grid. It pays for its own substations and agrees to be cut off when the grid is stretched, running on its own turbines and Megapacks until grid power returns.

But building your own power doesn't make you immune to the bottlenecks. Mississippi is retiring the temporary Southaven turbines by July 2027, leaving the permanent plant at about 1.24 GW. Turbine manufacturers can also ship much of the equipment 12 to 18 months before the blades and vanes are ready. Those components set the pace, on top of political and endless other constraints that are getting tighter. 

If SpaceX, with its own power plants and batteries, is already running into these limits, imagine what they mean for everyone else trying to build AI infrastructure.

This is why space is the only way forward.

On Earth, scaling compute means permits, power plants, transmission infrastructure and years-long queues. In orbit, suitable sun-synchronous orbits offer near-constant sunlight without waiting for a grid connection. The main barrier is launch cost, and that's the problem SpaceX has spent more than 20 years solving.

Starship is designed to lift compute at gigawatts scale, with the first AI satellites targeted for 2027.

The bottleneck on Earth is increasingly power, and it will only get worse as AI adoption rapidly accelerates. SpaceX's bet is that it can move compute beyond the grid before those constraints become even more severe.

text:
President Trump said Friday, while discussing the Protect College Sports Act, “They’re paying quarterbacks $12 million a year.” He added that one quarterback has “a strong arm, but no accuracy” and “He’s 17 years old. It’s not going to work out.” He didn’t name anyone, and The Comeback and Yahoo read it as Michigan’s Bryce Underwood. If he meant Underwood, two numbers are off. Underwood is 19, and his reported deal is about $10 million to $12.5 million over four years, which is roughly $3 million a year.

Even the corrected number was large. SI reported in August 2025, citing On3, that Underwood’s roughly $3 million put him in the top five quarterbacks in pay, behind only Duke’s Darian Mensah at $4 million. LSU reportedly offered closer to $1.5 million a year, so Michigan paid about double (my math). Larry Ellison funded the deal, per Front Office Sports, and SI reports, citing On3, that it has no buyout. Underwood, the No. 1 prospect in the 2025 class, flipped from LSU weeks before the early signing period.

The return has been slower. Michigan benched Underwood at halftime of its 21-18 win over Penn State on Oct. 17 after two interceptions, and freshman Tommy Carr replaced him. Coach Kyle Whittingham said the offense had “absolutely nothing going.” The Comeback reports Underwood hasn’t started since and has completed 56.1% of his passes for 950 yards, five touchdowns and six interceptions this season. As a true freshman he threw for 2,428 yards with 11 touchdowns and nine interceptions in 13 games. On3’s current NIL valuation of him is $3 million.

The president’s remarks came as the Protect College Sports Act, which passed the Senate 77-22 in September, waits on a House vote that GOP leaders plan for the first week of December. The bill sets a federal framework for how much schools can share directly with athletes, and if the House hasn’t passed it by January it starts over. Underwood’s reported deal runs four years, and he is in his second.

For Dallas College, being named to this list highlights the breadth of work behind our mission: meeting students where they are, helping them reach their next goal and working alongside employers and community partners to support the future of North Texas.

Every day, students come to Dallas College to take the next step, whether that's earning college credit in high school, preparing for a career, transferring to a university, earning a degree or building new skills for emerging opportunities. Through those pathways and our partnerships across the region, we're helping create a stronger workforce, a stronger economy and greater opportunity for North Texans.
